in a kalpa called Dàbǎoyán,
in a world named Lígòu,
pure and without flaw or defilement,
with lapis lazuli for its ground,
golden cords dividing its roads,
trees of the seven treasures, multicolored,
always bearing flowers and fruits.
The Bodhisattvas of that land,
always resolute in mindfulness,
have perfected the spiritual powers of pāramitā,
all complete in every respect.
In the presence of countless Buddhas,
they have skillfully studied the Bodhisattva path.
Such great ones as these
are those transformed by Buddha Huāguāng.
When the Buddha was a prince,
he renounced his kingdom and left behind worldly glory,
in his very last body,
leaving home to accomplish the Buddha-way.
The Buddha Huāguāng abides in the world
for a lifespan of twelve small kalpas.
The multitudes of his land’s people
have a lifespan of eight small kalpas.
After the Buddha's extinction,
the True Dharma will abide in the world
for thirty-two small kalpas,
widely delivering all beings.
Once the True Dharma has entirely ended,
there will be thirty-two (kalpas of) the Counterfeit Dharma,
with relics widely distributed,
universally honored by deities and humans.
All the deeds accomplished by Buddha Huāguāng
are just thus;
his two-footed Honored One
excels, with none to compare.
That is your very self;
you ought to rejoice in yourself."
At that time, the fourfold assembly,
Bhikṣus, Bhikṣuṇīs, Upāsakas, and Upāsikās,
great multitudes of devas, nāgas, yaksas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas,
seeing Shèlìfú before the Buddha receive the prophecy of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
were filled with great joy, overwhelmed and immeasurable,
each taking off the upper garment they wore
to make offerings to the Buddha.
Shìdìhuán Yīn, Brahma King, and the like,
together with innumerable sons of the gods,
also with heavenly subtle garments, heavenly maṇḍarava flowers, great maṇḍarava flowers and such,
made offerings to the Buddha—
the scattered heavenly garments remained suspended in space,
circulating and revolving by themselves;
the music of the various heavens, with hundreds of thousands of myriads of kinds,
all played at once in the sky,
raining various heavenly flowers—uttering these words:
"Formerly, at Póluóniú, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma;
now again, he turns the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma."
At that time the sons of the gods,
wishing to further declare this meaning,
spoke in verse:
"In the past, at Póluóniú,
the wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths was turned,
discriminating and explaining the dharmas,
the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates.
Now again turns the most exquisite,
unsurpassed great wheel of Dharma;
this Dharma is extremely deep and profound,
rare are those who can believe.
From of old until now,
we have often heard the World-Honored One speak,
yet never have we heard such supreme, deep and wonderful Dharma as this.
The World-Honored One now expounds this Dharma,
and we all rejoice and delight.
The greatly wise Shèlìfú
now receives the exalted prophecy.
We, likewise,
shall surely attain buddhahood.
In all the worlds,
the most honored, none above,
the Buddha-way is inconceivable,
skillfully taught by means suitable to the occasion.
All the good karma I possess,
whether in this or future lives,
and the merit of seeing the Buddha,
I dedicate entirely to the Buddha-way."
At that time, Shèlìfú said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Now I have no further doubts or regrets,
and have personally, before the Buddha, received the prophecy of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Of these twelve hundred who dwell in freedom of mind,
in the past while dwelling in the state of study,
the Buddha always taught and guided, saying:
'My Dharma can free one from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and finally attain Nirvāṇa.'
Both those who are learning and those beyond learning
have each, by letting go of the view of self and of existence and non-existence, etc.,
thought that they had attained Nirvāṇa;
but now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, hearing what was unheard before, all have fallen into doubt and confusion.
Excellent, World-Honored One!
I wish that you would, for the fourfold assembly, speak of the causes and conditions, to remove their doubts and regrets."
Then the Buddha said to Shèlìfú:
"Have I not previously said: 'All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones,
expound the Dharma by means of various causes, analogies, phrases, and skillful means,
all for the sake of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi'?
All that I have said is for the purpose of transforming Bodhisattvas.
Yet, Shèlìfú!
Now I shall again use a parable to further clarify this meaning;
those endowed with wisdom can understand through parables.
Shèlìfú!
Suppose in a country, city, or village, there is a great elder,
elderly in years, with immeasurable wealth,
possessing many fields, houses, and various servants.
His house is vast and grand,
having only one door,
crowded with many people,
one hundred, two hundred, up to five hundred persons
reside within it.
The halls and chambers are old and decayed, the walls are crumbling,
the pillars at their base are rotten, the beams and rafters dangerously askew;
all around, suddenly, fire breaks out at one time, burning the house.
The elder's sons,
whether ten, twenty, or even thirty,
are within this house.
The elder sees the great fire rising on all four sides,
and is greatly alarmed and fearful, thinking:
'Though I can, through the burning door, escape safely,
my children, within the burning house, are engrossed in play,
unknowing and unaware, neither startled nor afraid;
as the fire approaches their bodies, the pain becomes intense,
yet they do not loathe their plight and have no wish to leave.'
Shèlìfú!
The elder then considers:
'I have strength in body and arms;
I could carry them out wrapped in cloth or on a desk.
Yet he further thinks:
'This house has only one door,
and it is narrow and small.
My children are young and ignorant,
attached to their place of play,
perhaps they may fall and be consumed by fire.
I should tell frightening things to them:
"This house is burning; you must leave quickly and at once,
lest you be burned by the fire."'
Having so considered,
as he has thought, he thoroughly informs his children:
"You must come out quickly!"
Although the father pities them and kindly exhorts and entreats,
the children, attached to their play, refuse to believe and accept,
neither startled nor afraid, utterly lacking the thought of leaving;
moreover, they do not know what fire is, nor what a house is,
nor what it is to lose or perish.
They only run east and west, playing and looking at their father.
Then the elder thinks:
'This house is already engulfed in great fire;
if I and my children do not leave at once,
we will surely be burned.
Now I must use skillful means, so that my children may escape this calamity.'"

The father knew that each of his sons, from the outset, had different preferences and delighted in various rare and exquisite treasures, and that their hearts would surely be attached to them with joy.
He then said to them:
‘The things you enjoy playing with and desire are rare and hard to obtain.
If you do not take them, you will surely regret it later.
There are now many sheep carts, deer carts, and ox carts outside the gate, with which you may amuse yourselves.
You should quickly come out of this burning house,
and you may have whichever you desire; I will give them all to you.’
At that time, upon hearing what their father said about
precious and marvelous things, which fit their wishes,
their hearts became eager and courageous. They pushed and jostled each other,
competing and running together to be the first to leave the burning house.
At this time, the elder
saw that all his sons had come out safely,
and that they were all sitting together in the open at the crossroads,
without any further obstacles or barriers.
His heart was calm and at ease; he was overjoyed and ecstatic.
Then the sons each said to their father:
‘Father, the playthings and treasures you promised us before,
the sheep carts, deer carts, and ox carts—we wish for you to give them to us now.’
Shèlìfú!
At that time, the elder gave each of his sons a great cart,
high and wide, adorned with many jewels,
surrounded by railings all around, with bells hanging on all four sides;
also, above, a canopy was set up,
which was likewise decorated and adorned with rare and precious jewels,
jeweled cords woven about and flowered tassels dangling down,
layers of decorated cloth with scarlet pillows placed within.
The carts were drawn by white oxen,
with pure and bright skin, beautiful form, great strength,
walking evenly and steadily, as swift as the wind;
and there were also many attendants serving and guarding them.
And why was this so?
That great elder's wealth was immeasurable;
all kinds of treasure-houses were completely filled to overflowing,
and he thought to himself:
‘My wealth and possessions are boundless;
I should not give such inferior little carts to my sons.
These young children are all my sons;
my love is impartial, with no favoritism.
I have such great jeweled carts, as many as can be counted without end;
I should give them all equally,
without making distinctions. Why is this?
Because even if I supplied an entire country with these things,
I would not run short;
how much less for just my sons!’
At that time, each of the sons rode a great cart, receiving something never before seen or hoped for,
not what they had originally expected.
"Shèlìfú!
What do you think,
when that elder gave his sons these great carts adorned with precious jewels,
was there any falsehood or deception?"
Shèlìfú replied:
"No, World-honored One!
That elder only wished his sons to escape the peril of fire
and preserve their bodies and lives; there was no falsehood in this.
Why is this?
If one's life is preserved,
that alone is obtaining the objects of play that were promised,
not to mention that he skillfully drew them from the burning house and rescued them.
World-honored One!
Even if that elder had not given them even the smallest cart,
still, there would have been no falsehood.
Why is this?
Because the elder had first made up his mind:
‘By skillful means, I will draw my children out.’
For this reason, there is no falsehood.
How much more so when the elder, knowing himself possessed of limitless wealth, wished to benefit his children and gave them all great carts equally."
The Buddha told Shèlìfú:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is as you have said.
Shèlìfú!
The Tathāgata is the same;
he is the father of all beings in the world.
Facing all fear, decline, distress, suffering, and the darkness caused by ignorance,
he brings these to an end, leaving nothing remaining,
and fully accomplishes immeasurable wisdom, powers, and fearlessness.
He possesses great miraculous power and the power of wisdom,
is complete in the perfections of skillful means and wisdom,
has great loving-kindness and great compassion, never becoming lax or tired,
always seeking good and benefiting all,
and is born within the decaying, burning house of the Three Realms,
to deliver living beings from the fires of birth, old age, sickness, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, ignorance, obscurity, and the three poisons.
He teaches and transforms, enabling them to attain Anuttarā-samyak-sambodhi.
Seeing that all living beings are tormented by the fires of birth, old age, sickness, and death, sorrow, and suffering,
as well as, for the sake of the five desires and material gain, endure all kinds of pain;
again, because of their greedy attachment and pursuit, they suffer in many ways now,
and later endure the sufferings of hell, of animals, and of hungry ghosts;
or even if born in heaven or as humans,
they suffer poverty, hardship, the pain of separation from beloved ones, and the meeting with those they resent,
and all manner of other such sufferings.
Living beings are submerged in these,
enjoy themselves and play,
without awareness or understanding, unalarmed and unafraid,
not feeling aversion nor seeking deliverance.
Within this burning house of the Three Realms, they run east and west;
though experiencing great suffering, they do not see it as distress.
Shèlìfú!
When the Buddha sees this, he thinks:
‘I am the father of all beings;
I should save them from their suffering
and give them the sublime bliss of Buddha's boundless, infinite wisdom,
enabling them to rejoice and play.’
Shèlìfú!
The Tathāgata again contemplates, thinking:
‘If I were to give living beings only the power of miracles and wisdom,
abandoning skillful means,
and merely praise for them the insight, powers, and fearlessness of the Tathāgata,
living beings would not thus be delivered. Why is this?
Because these living beings still have not escaped from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and suffering,
and are burning in the house of the Three Realms;
how could they possibly comprehend the wisdom of the Buddha?’
Shèlìfú!
As that elder,
though possessing strength and ability, did not use them directly,
but with earnest skillful means
strove to save his children from the peril of the burning house,
and only then gave them the great jewel-laden carts.
The Tathāgata is likewise;
though possessed of power and fearlessness,
he does not directly use them,
but by wisdom and skillful means, delivers beings from the burning house of the Three Realms,
and preaches three vehicles— Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Buddha vehicles—
saying this:
‘Do not delight to remain in the burning house of the Three Realms;
do not be greedy for gross and inferior forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and touches.
If you are attached and give rise to love, you will be burned by them.
Quickly leave the Three Realms,
and you will obtain the three vehicles— Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Buddha vehicles.
I now pledge to you this promise,
it will never be in vain.
You need only diligently cultivate and strive.’
The Tathāgata, by such skillful means, encourages living beings onward.
He further declares:
‘You should know
that these three vehicles are all praised by the sages,
free and unbound, needing nothing further.
Riding these three vehicles,
with the faculties, powers, awareness, paths, concentrations, liberations, and samādhi untainted by afflictions,
you will take delight in yourselves,
and soon attain immeasurable peace and happiness.’
Shèlìfú!
If there are beings who, inwardly possessing wisdom,
hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-honored One, and believe and accept it,
diligently cultivating and progressing, wishing quickly to leave the Three Realms,
seeking Nirvāṇa for themselves,
this is called the Śrāvaka vehicle,
just like those sons who sought the sheep cart and escaped the burning house.
If there are beings
who, on hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-honored One, believe and accept it,
diligently cultivating, seeking spontaneous wisdom,
delighting in solitary virtue and tranquility,
deeply understanding the causes and conditions of all phenomena,
this is called the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
just like those sons who sought the deer cart and escaped the burning house.
If there are beings
who, on hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-honored One, believe and accept it,
diligently cultivating,
seeking all-encompassing wisdom, Buddha wisdom, innate wisdom, and teacherless wisdom, the insight, powers, and fearlessness of the Tathāgata,
taking pity upon and bringing happiness to immeasurable beings,
benefiting gods and humans, delivering all,
this is called the Great Vehicle;
Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle, and are called mahasattvas,
just like those sons who sought the ox cart and escaped the burning house.
Shèlìfú!
As that elder saw his sons safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place free from fear,
and knowing his wealth to be limitless, he gave them all great carts equally.
The Tathāgata is the same;
as the father of all living beings,
when he sees incalculable billions of living beings emerge from the suffering of the Three Realms by means of the Buddha's teachings, escaping the perilous path and obtaining the joy of Nirvāṇa.
"At that time, the Tathāgata thinks:
‘I possess immeasurable, boundless wisdom, powers, fearlessness, and all the Dharma-treasures of the Buddhas;
these beings are all my children;
I must give them all the Great Vehicle equally,
permitting no one to attain final extinction alone,
but to attain extinction by means of the Tathāgata's own extinction.’
All those beings who have escaped the Three Realms,
are supplied with all the amusements of the meditative absorptions and liberations of the Buddhas;
all are of one form and one kind, praised by the sages,
capable of producing the purest and most wondrous joy.
Shèlìfú! Just as the elder at first used three carts to entice his children,
but then gave only great carts, adorned with jewels, the highest in safety and comfort;
yet that elder was never at fault for falsehood.
The Tathāgata is likewise,
without falsehood,
first preaching the three vehicles to guide living beings,
then finally delivers them all by means of the Great Vehicle alone.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata possesses the inexhaustible store of wisdom, powers, and fearlessness of all the Buddha-Dharmas,
able to give the Law of the Great Vehicle to all beings;
only not all are able fully to receive it.
"Shèlìfú!
For this reason,
you should know that by the skillful means of all the Buddhas,
there is expounded within a single Buddha Vehicle a division into three.
The Buddha, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke in verse:
It is like a wealthy elder,
who owns a great mansion.
This mansion has long been old,
and now is utterly decayed.
The halls and chambers are high and dangerous,
the pillars’ bases are cracked and rotten,
the beams and rafters lean askew, and
the foundations and steps have collapsed and crumbled,
the walls are crumbling and split,
the clay plaster has fallen away,
the roofing thatch drops down all in disorder,
the rafters and framework are coming loose, the encircling barriers are twisted and winding,
and filth and refuse fill it everywhere.
There are five hundred persons
dwelling inside it.
Kites and owls, vultures and eagles,
crows, magpies, pigeons, doves,
vipers, adders, scorpions,
centipedes and millipedes,
geckoes and hundred-legged insects,
macaques, civet cats, and field mice—
all kinds of malicious creatures and insects
weave and dart about.
Where filth of dung and urine stinks,
uncleanliness flows and overflows,
dung beetles and various insects gather upon it.
Foxes, wolves, and jackals
gnaw and trample,
dogs bite at corpses,
bones and flesh are scattered in disorder.
As a result, packs of dogs
compete to snatch and seize,
starving and frail, fearful and alarmed,
seeking food everywhere.
They fight, quarrel, pull and drag,
barking and snarling loudly.
The dwelling is full of terror,
and such are its conditions.
In every place within are
chīmèi-wǎngliǎng and
yèchā evil spirits,
who eat the flesh of people.
All manner of poisonous insects,
and vicious birds and beasts
breed and give birth,
each hiding themselves and protecting their young.
The yèchā spirit-ghosts rush about
vying for food;
once they are sated,
their evil minds only intensify,
and the sounds of their fighting and strife
are truly terrifying and dreadful.
Jīupántú-ghosts
squatting and crouching on earthen mounds,
sometimes floating above the ground, one or two feet,
roaming and wandering to and fro,
at their pleasure and in sport;
catching dogs by their hind legs,
muffling their cries,
then pressing the dogs’ necks with their feet,
terrifying the dogs, enjoying themselves.
Further, there are spirits
with great and tall bodies,
naked, black, and emaciated,
dwelling always within,
letting out big evil cries,
shouting out for food.
Again there are ghosts
whose throats are like needles,
and again ghosts
whose heads are like those of oxen—
some eat human flesh,
some devour dogs;
their hair is disheveled,
they are cruel and dangerous;
driven by hunger and thirst,
they cry out and rush about.
The yèchā hungry ghosts,
vicious birds and beasts,
in urgent hunger,
roam in all directions,
spying through windows and doors.
Such sufferings as these
are immeasurable in terror and dread.
This rotten and ruined house
belongs to one man.
Not long ago, this man
left the house;
shortly after, a sudden fire broke out in the dwelling,
all at once on every side,
its flames raging everywhere.
The beams, rafters, and pillars
crack and shatter with explosive sounds,
breaking and collapsing,
the walls caving in.
All the spirits and demons
raise their voices in loud cries.
Vultures and other birds,
jīupántú-ghosts and others,
are all in alarm and terror,
unable to make their way out.
Wild beasts and poisonous insects
hide and burrow in holes and crevices.
Píshézhé-ghosts
also live within,
and because of scant blessing and virtue,
are tormented by the fire;
they attack and harm each other,
drinking blood and eating flesh.
The jackals and their kind
were already dead before;
the great predators
flock to devour them;
rank smoke and blazing fumes
fill all sides.
Centipedes, millipedes,
poisonous snakes and the like,
are burned by the fire;
they scurry out of their holes,
and the jīupántú-ghosts
seize and eat them.
And there are hungry ghosts
whose heads are aflame,
who, tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat,
rush about in distress.
Such is this mansion—
most fearful and dreadful—
plagued by poison and fire,
with countless calamities.
At this time, the master of the house
stands outside the door
and hears someone say:
“Your sons
a while ago,
while playing,
entered this house.
Being young and ignorant,
they are delighted and attached to their games.”
Upon hearing this, the elder
rushes into the burning house,
intent on rescuing and saving them
so they will not be burned and harmed,
admonishing all his children,
describing the many disasters:
evil ghosts and poisonous insects,
the spreading fire,
all kinds of sufferings
proceeding without end—
poisonous snakes, vipers, adders,
and yèchā,
jīupánchá-ghosts,
jackals, foxes, dogs,
vultures, kites, and owls,
all manner of hundred-legged creatures,
tormented by hunger and thirst—
all are greatly to be feared.
This is a place of dire suffering—
how much more so now with the great fire!
The children, being ignorant,
though they hear their father’s admonition,
still delight and cling to their play,
never ceasing.
Then the elder
thinks to himself:
“These sons of mine
only increase my distress!
In this house
there is nothing pleasurable at all,
yet the children
are immersed in play,
not accepting my instruction,
and are sure to fall victim to the fire.”
He immediately considers
how to employ skillful means,
and says to his children:
“I have all kinds
of rare and precious things—
wonderful jeweled carts,
goat carts, deer carts,
and great ox carts.
They are now outside the door.
Come out, all of you!
For you I have made these carts,
for you to enjoy as you wish,
with which you can play.”
The children, hearing of such carts,
immediately rush and race,
sprinting out,
coming to open ground,
free from all suffering and calamity.
The elder, seeing his children
so escape from the burning house,
now stand at the crossroads.
Seated upon a lion throne,
he speaks, rejoicing:
“I am now joyful!
These many sons
are exceedingly hard to raise,
foolish and ignorant in youth,
and have entered a perilous house.
It is filled with many poisonous creatures,
terrifying chī mèi spirits,
fierce blazes of great fire,
rising on all sides.
And yet these sons
are engrossed in play and delight.
I have already saved them,
and caused them to escape misfortune.
Therefore, all people,
I am now joyful.”
At that time, the sons,
knowing their father was seated in safety,
all approached their father,
and addressed him, saying:
“We beseech you to grant us
the three kinds of jeweled carts
as earlier promised:
‘When the sons have come out,
I will indeed give three carts,
according to your wishes.’
Now is precisely the time,
we only ask you to bestow them.”
The Elder was immensely wealthy,
possessing great treasuries,
gold, silver, and lapis lazuli;
chariot-axles of mǎ nǎo and glāo nǎo,
and with many precious objects
constructed grand chariots.
Adorned and splendidly decorated,
encircled on all sides with railings,
bells hanging from all sides,
golden cords intertwined.
Nets of real pearls
were spread above,
golden blossoms and ornaments
hanging down everywhere,
adorned with various colors,
circling all around.
Soft silks and cotton
made the seat coverings;
atop were the finest fine woolens,
worth hundreds of billions,
fresh, white, and immaculate,
covering them above.
There were great white oxen,
plump and of great strength,
with fine forms and beauty,
to draw the jeweled carts.
Many attendants
followed in service and protection.
With these marvelous chariots,
he equally bestowed them upon his sons.
At that time, the sons
were full of joy and leapt for delight,
riding in these jeweled chariots,
traveling in all directions,
playing and rejoicing,
free and without hindrance.
He told Shèlìfú:
“So too am I:
honored among the assembly of sages,
the father of the world.
All sentient beings
are my sons;
so deeply attached to worldly pleasures,
lacking wisdom in their hearts.
The three realms are not at peace,
just like a burning house,
filled with manifold sufferings,
extremely fearful and terrifying.
Always there are birth, old age, sickness, death, and cares;
such fires as these
burn fiercely without ceasing.
The Tathāgata has already left
the burning house of the three realms,
dwelling in serene seclusion,
at ease in forest and wilderness.
Now these three realms
are all my possessions;
all the sentient beings within
are indeed my children.
But here and now,
there are many afflictions and calamities;
only I, alone,
am able to save and protect.
Though I teach and command them,
they do not believe or accept it,
being deeply attached to the defilements of desire,
their clinging is profound.
Therefore, by skillful means,
I teach the Three Vehicles,
to cause all sentient beings
to recognize the suffering of the three realms,
to open, explain, and expound
the path that goes beyond the world.
If these children
set their minds with determination,
and fully possess the three insights,
and the six spiritual powers,
attain the state of Pratyekabuddha,
or irreversible bodhisattvahood—
you, Shèlìfú!
It is for the sake of sentient beings
that I use this parable
to teach the One Buddha Vehicle.
If you and the others
can believe and accept these words,
then all will
attain the Buddha Way.
This vehicle is wondrous and subtle,
pure and supreme;
among all worlds,
none surpass it.
It is what brings joy to the Buddha.
It is that which all sentient beings
should praise,
revere, make offerings and obeisance to.
Innumerable hundreds of thousands,
the powers, liberations,
meditative concentrations and wisdoms,
and all other Buddha dharmas,
are attained through this vehicle.
It allows these sons
through days and kalpas,
to always enjoy play,
together with the bodhisattvas
and the multitude of śrāvakas,
riding in this jeweled vehicle
straight to enlightenment.
Because of this reason,
search as you may in all ten directions,
there is no other vehicle,
save for the Buddha’s skillful means.”
He told Shèlìfú:
“You and all beings
are my children;
I am the father.
Through countless kalpas,
burned by all manner of suffering,
I save and deliver you all,
leading you out of the three realms.
Though I have spoken before:
‘You shall attain extinction,’
this only ends birth and death,
but is not true extinction;
what should now be done
is only the Buddha’s wisdom.
If there is a bodhisattva
among this assembly
able to wholeheartedly listen
to the true Dharma of the Buddhas,
then the World-Honored Ones,
though using skillful means,
transform sentient beings,
all as bodhisattvas.
But if some are limited in wisdom,
deeply attached to love and desire,
for their sake
I teach the truth of suffering.
Sentient beings rejoice,
gaining the unprecedented;
the Buddha proclaims the truth of suffering,
it is true and not otherwise.
If there are sentient beings
who do not know the root of suffering,
deeply attached to its causes,
unable even briefly to relinquish,
for their sake,
I skillfully teach the Path.
The cause of all suffering
is rooted in craving and desire;
if craving and desire are extinguished,
there is nowhere for suffering to abide;
when all suffering is utterly ended,
this is called the third truth.
In order to realize the truth of cessation,
one cultivates the Path,
freeing oneself from all the bonds of suffering,
this is called attaining liberation.
But where is such a person
who truly attains liberation?
Only in leaving behind false delusions
is it called liberation;
In truth, he has not attained it,
nor complete liberation.
The Buddha says such a person
has not truly reached extinction.
This person has not attained
the unsurpassed path;
therefore, it is not my intention
to let him reach final extinction.
I am the Dharma King,
sovereign over the Dharma,
appearing in the world
to bring peace and security to living beings.
Rú Shèlìfú!
This seal of my Dharma,
I declare for the benefit of the world,
wherever you travel, do not propagate it carelessly.
If there are those who hear it
and joyfully receive it with reverence,
you should know that such a person
has entered Āpǐpózhì.
If there are those who faithfully accept
this sūtra and Dharma,
these people have already,
in the past, seen Buddhas,
honored and made offerings,
and also heard this Dharma.
If a person can
trust what you say,
it is as if he sees me,
sees you,
as well as the assembly of bhikṣus
and all the bodhisattvas.
This Lotus Sūtra
is spoken for those of profound wisdom;
those of shallow understanding,
upon hearing it become deluded and confused.
All the śrāvakas
and pratyekabuddhas
within this sūtra
cannot reach its depth.
Rú Shèlìfú!
Even for this sūtra,
you enter by faith;
how much more so for other śrāvakas.
These other śrāvakas,
because they believe the Buddha’s words,
comply with this sūtra
not by their own wisdom.
Again, Rú Shèlìfú!
To those who are arrogant and indolent,
attached to self-view,
do not expound this sūtra.
Ordinary people of shallow understanding,
deeply attached to the five desires,
on hearing cannot comprehend;
also do not preach to them.
If there are those who do not believe
and slander this sūtra,
they will sever all
seeds of Buddhahood in the world.
Or if they frown and scowl,
and harbor doubt and confusion,
you should listen
to the retribution for these offenses.
Whether while the Buddha is in the world
or after his extinction,
if there are any who slander
such sūtras,
see people who recite and read,
who copy and uphold the sūtra,
and treat them with contempt, loathing, and jealousy,
harboring grudges in their hearts,
the retribution for such a person,
listen again now.
When such a person’s life ends,
they fall into Avīci hell,
for a complete kalpa;
at the end of the kalpa they are reborn.
In this way, repeatedly,
for countless kalpas,
when freed from hell,
they are born as animals.
If as a dog or wild fox,
their body is scrawny and thin,
black, mangy, and leprous,
constantly harassed by people.
Again, people
regard them with contempt and disgust;
they constantly suffer from hunger and thirst,
their flesh and bones withered;
in life, enduring beatings and pain;
in death, struck by bricks and stones.
Because they have severed the seeds of Buddhahood,
they receive such retribution.
If born as camels,
or among donkeys,
their bodies always bear heavy burdens,
struck and beaten by sticks and whips,
thinking only of water and grass,
knowing nothing else.
Because they slandered this sūtra,
they receive such punishment.
Some are born as wild foxes
that enter villages,
with bodies diseased and mangy,
and lacking even one eye.
By groups of children
they are beaten and pelted,
suffering pain and injury,
sometimes resulting in death.
After such a death,
they are reborn as pythons.
Their bodies are long and huge,
five hundred yojanas,
deaf, stupid, and limbless,
twisting and crawling on their bellies,
preyed upon by countless small insects,
bitten and devoured,
suffering day and night,
never knowing respite.
Because they slandered this sūtra,
they receive such punishment.
If they are born as humans,
all faculties are dull and blind,
dwarfish, deformed, crippled, and lame,
blind, deaf, and hunched-backed.
When they speak,
people do not believe or accept them;
their mouths are always foul-smelling,
haunted by ghosts and spirits.
Poor and despised,
they are forced to labor for others,
constantly sick and emaciated,
having no one to depend on.
Even when they attach themselves to others,
they are disregarded,
and if they do obtain something,
they soon lose or forget it.
If they practice medicine,
and treat illness according to formulas,
they worsen others’ sicknesses,
sometimes even causing death.
If they themselves fall ill,
there is none to help or treat them;
even if they take excellent medicine,
their condition grows worse.
If others rebel,
rob or steal from them,
such woes and offenses
befall them without cause.
Such evil people
will never see the Buddha,
King of the assemblage of sages,
teaching the Dharma and transforming beings.
Such wicked beings
are always reborn in difficult conditions,
crazy, deaf, and disordered in mind,
never hearing the Dharma ever again.
For countless kalpas,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
they are always born deaf and mute,
with faculties incomplete.
Constantly abiding in hell
as if it were a pleasure garden,
on other evil paths
as if it were their own home,
camel, donkey, pig, dog —
such are the places they go.
Because they slandered this sūtra,
they receive such punishment.
If reborn as humans,
deaf, blind, mute, dumb,
poor and subject to all decline,
thus adorned.
Dropsy, emaciation,
scabies, sores, boils —
such kinds of disease
become their clothing.
Their body is constantly filthy,
soiled and unclean,
deeply attached to self-view,
their anger and resentment increase,
lust burns vigorously,
not discerning even between beasts.
Because they slandered this sūtra,
they receive such punishment.’
He said to Rú Shèlìfú:
‘The offenses of those who slander this sūtra, if fully described,
would not be exhausted in a kalpa.
For this reason,
I tell you:
Among those of no wisdom, do not speak this sūtra.
If there are those of keen faculties,
with wisdom and clarity,
much learning and strong memory,
seeking the Buddha path,
only to such people
should it be expounded.’
If a person has seen
hundreds, thousands, and millions of Buddhas,
planting all kinds of good roots,
with mind deep and steadfast,
such a person
can be taught.
If a person is diligent,
always cultivates a mind of compassion,
and is ungrudging with body or life,
such a person
can be taught.
If a person is respectful,
without a divergent mind,
separated from all the common and foolish,
dwelling alone in mountains and marshes,
such a person
can be taught.
Again, Shèlìfú!
If you see someone
abandoning evil friends,
and drawing near to good companions,
such a person
can be taught.
If you see a Buddha’s child
observing the precepts with purity,
like a bright and pure jewel,
and seeking the Mahāyāna scriptures,
such a person
can be taught.
If a person bears no anger,
upright and gentle,
constantly pities all,
respectfully worships all Buddhas,
such a person
can be taught.
There are also Buddha’s children
who, in great assemblies,
with pure minds,
using various causes and conditions,
metaphors and words,
preach the Dharma without obstruction—
such a person
can be taught.
If there is a bhikṣu
who seeks all-knowledge,
seeking the Dharma in all four directions,
presses palms together in reverence and receives it upon the crown,
only delights in accepting and holding
the Mahāyāna scriptures,
and does not even accept
a single gāthā from other sutras,
such a person
can be taught.
Just as if one, with utmost sincerity,
seeks the Buddha’s relics,
and likewise seeks the sutra,
afterward receives it upon the crown,
and never again
aspires after other scriptures,
nor ever thinks of
the texts of outside paths,
such a person
can be taught.
He said to Shèlìfú:
“I set forth these characteristics:
Those who seek the Buddha-way,
even if endless kalpas pass, will not finish describing them.”
People such as these
are able to believe and understand;
you should preach to them
the wondrous *Sūtra of the Lotus of the Wonderful Law*.
At that time, Huìmìng Xūpútí,
Móhē Jiāzhānyán,
Móhē Jiāyè,
Móhē Mùjiānlián,
after hearing from the Buddha such unprecedented Dharma,
and Śākyamuni bestowing upon Shèlìfú the prediction of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
gave rise to rare hearts, rejoiced and leapt for joy,
immediately rose from their seats and arranged their robes,
baring their right shoulders, right knee touching the ground,
with single mind, palms joined,
bent body in respect,
gazed up in reverence at the honored face
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We, as leaders of the Saṅgha,
and now aging,
always considered ourselves as having attained nirvāṇa and with nothing to shoulder,
and not to further seek Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The World-honored One has long expounded the Dharma in the past,
and I was always present among the assembly,
my body tired and weary,
thinking only on emptiness, signlessness, and non-action.
In the Bodhisattva Dharma—divine play in supernormal powers, purifying the Buddha lands, fulfilling beings—
my mind found no joy.
Why is this?
The World-honored One led us out of the three realms and allowed us to realize the proof of nirvāṇa.
Also, now we are aged,
in the Buddha’s teaching of Bodhisattvas and Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
not even a single thought of delight arises within.
Now before the Buddha,
upon hearing the bestowal of the prediction for Śrāvakas to attain Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
my heart is greatly gladdened,
such as never before.
It is unexpected that today, I suddenly hear such a rare Dharma,
and I deeply rejoice within, gaining great benefit—
innumerable treasures, acquired without seeking.
World-honored One!
Now I wish to speak a parable to clarify this meaning.
Suppose there is a person, still young and immature,
who abandons his father and flees, long staying in a different country,
for perhaps ten, twenty, up to fifty years,
and when grown older, becomes even more destitute,
wandering in all directions in search of clothing and food.
Gradually traveling, he chances to return to his native country.”
His father had come before and could not find his son,
and so stopped in a certain city.
His household was vastly wealthy, with limitless treasure—
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, pearls, and so on;
his storehouses were all filled to overflowing;
he had numerous servants, retainers, officials, and citizens;
elephants, horses, chariots, cattle, and sheep beyond count—
and his business transactions and profits extended to the neighboring countries,
and there were exceedingly many merchants and traders.
At that time, the poor son
wandered through various villages, passing through states and towns,
and thus arrived in the city where his father resided.
The father and mother thought of their son,
being separated for over fifty years,
and had never spoken of such things to others,
only pondering inwardly, filled with regret and longing.
Thinking of being aged and frail,
with much wealth,
gold, silver, precious treasures, storehouses overflowing,
yet without children,
that one day he would die and perish,
with his riches dispersed and lost,
having no one to whom to entrust them.
Thus, he would earnestly recall his son
and again thought:
‘If I could only gain my son, I would entrust him with my wealth and property,
be at ease and joyful, without further worry.’
World-honored One!
At that time, the poor son,
by chance being hired for wages, came near to his father’s house,
and stood by the gate. From afar, he saw his father
seated on a lion throne, with a jeweled footstool beneath his feet,
surrounded and revered by all the brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and householders;
adorned with pearl necklaces, worth millions, ornamenting his person;
officials and servants, bearing white fly-whisks, standing on left and right;
shaded by canopies of jewels,
with hanging flowered banners,
with fragrant waters sprinkled on the ground,
and with a profusion of fine flowers scattered about;
displayed precious objects, brought out and taken up from inside;
such were the various adornments,
his majesty and virtue uniquely exalted.
The poor son, seeing his father’s great power and prestige,
immediately became terrified,
and regretted having come there.
He secretly thought:
‘Perhaps this is a king,
or one of king's equals;
this is not a place where I, for hire, can obtain anything.
Better to leave and go to a poor hamlet, where labor will find its place,
and necessities of life will be easy to get.
If I stay long here,
perhaps I’ll be coerced or forced to work.’
Thinking thus,
he hurriedly ran away.
At that time, the wealthy elder,
on his lion seat, saw his son and recognized him at once,
and in his heart was filled with great joy.
He immediately thought:
‘My wealth and storehouses now have someone to whom they may be given.
I have always thought of this son,
yet had no way to see him,
and now he has suddenly come himself,
just as I had wished.
Though I am old, my attachments still linger.’
He then sent his attendants, urging them to chase after and bring [him] back at once.
At that time, the messengers, hurriedly running, seized him.
The poor son, stricken with fear, loudly cried out in protest:
‘I have done no wrong! Why am I seized?’
The messengers grasped him all the more tightly and forcibly dragged him back.
At that time, the poor son thought to himself,
‘With no crime, yet I am captured and held—
surely I will die;’
and, utterly terrified, he fainted and fell to the ground.
The father, seeing this from afar,
spoke to the messengers,
saying, ‘There is no need for this man,
do not force him to come.
Sprinkle cold water on his face to awaken him,
Why is this so?
Because the father knew that his son’s mind and aspirations were base and inferior,
and that his own wealth and nobility would be hard for his son to accept.
He understood this son well
and, using skillful means, did not tell others that this was his son.
He sent a messenger to him, saying:
‘I now release you; go wherever you wish.’
The impoverished son rejoiced, as if gaining something unprecedented,
rose from the ground, and went off to a poor neighborhood to seek clothing and food.
At that time, the elder
wishing to draw in his son,
devised a skillful means,
secretly sending two men, whose appearance was haggard and lacking dignity,
saying: ‘Go to him, and slowly speak to the impoverished son:
“There is work here, and the pay is double.”
If the impoverished son accepts, bring him to work.
If he asks, “What work is it?”
say, “We hire you to remove dung.
We two will also work together with you.”’
The two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son,
and having found him, conveyed all these matters.
At that time, the impoverished son first took his pay, and then began removing dung.
When his father saw his son, he pitied and found it strange.
On another day, from a window he saw his son in the distance,
emaciated, haggard, covered with dung and dust, filthy and unclean.
Immediately he removed his necklaces, fine soft garments, and adornments,
and put on coarse, tattered, dirty clothes,
covered himself with dust and dirt, holding a dung-carrying implement in his right hand,
appearing as if in fear. He spoke to the laborers,
‘Work diligently, and do not grow slack.’
By skillful means, he was able to come close to his son.
Later, he told him:
‘Hey, young man!
You should always work here and not go elsewhere,
and I will increase your pay.
If you need pots, rice, flour, salt, vinegar, or such things,
do not hesitate to ask.
There are also old, worn-out servants to attend to your needs,
so set your mind at ease.
I am like your father; do not worry or fret.
Why is this?
Because I am old and aged, and you are young and strong.
When you work, you are never dishonest, lazy, angry, or resentful.
I never see in you the faults I see in the other laborers.
From now on, be as if you were my own child.’
Then the elder again wrote up a contract, naming him as his son.
At that time, the impoverished son
was glad for this encounter,
yet still regarded himself as a hired laborer of low status.
Because of this, for twenty years he was constantly made to remove dung.
After this,
his heart and mind were in harmony and full of trust, entering and leaving at will,
but his place of residence remained unchanged.
World-Honored One,
at that time, the elder fell ill,
and knew he would not live much longer.
He spoke to the impoverished son, saying:
‘Now I have much gold, silver, precious treasures, and my storehouses are overflowing,
how much is in them, and what ought to be taken and given—you are thoroughly acquainted with it all.
Such is my intention; understand my meaning.
Why is this?
Now, between you and me, there is no difference,
so you should be diligent lest anything be lost.’
At that time, the impoverished son
accepted the instructions,
took charge of everything,
the gold, silver, precious treasures, and all the storehouses,
but had not a thought of taking a single meal’s worth for himself.
Still, he remained in his old dwelling,
his humble mind not yet cast off.
After a little while,
the father saw that his son’s mind had gradually opened up, his great resolve accomplished, and he now regarded his former heart as base.
When he was about to pass away, he summoned his son
and gathered together his relatives,
the king, great ministers, kṣatriyas, and laymen,
until all had assembled.
He himself proclaimed,
‘All of you, please know!
This is my son,
born of my body.
In such-and-such a city, he left me and fled,
wandering and suffering over fifty years.
His original name is such-and-such,
and my name is such-and-such.
In earlier days, in our native city,
I was anxious and sought for him,
and suddenly, here, by chance, we met.
He is truly my son,
and I am truly his father.
Now all I possess,
belongs to my son,
and all my former property within and without is known to him.’
World-Honored One!
At this time, when the impoverished son heard his father’s words,
he was overjoyed, gaining what he had never had before,
and thought to himself:
‘I originally had no intentions or hopes,
but now the precious treasure has come of itself.’
World-Honored One!
The great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata,
we are all like the Buddha’s children,
and the Tathāgata constantly says we are his sons.
World-Honored One!
Because of the three sufferings,
we experienced many torments in the cycle of birth and death,
confused and ignorant, attached to lesser teachings.
Today, the World-Honored One has caused us to contemplate,
to clear away the dung of vain debate on the various teachings,
and, by diligently striving, we have received a single day’s wage of nirvāṇa.
Having obtained this, our hearts are greatly joyful and self-satisfied,
so that we say to ourselves,
‘By diligent practice in the Buddha’s teachings,
we have gained so much.’
Yet the World-Honored One
already knew that our minds were attached to lowly desires and enjoyed the lesser teachings,
so he permitted us to be let go without distinction:
‘You all have a share in the Tathāgata’s treasury of wisdom and insight.’
By the power of skillful means, the World-Honored One expounded the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
We, attending the Buddha, obtained a day’s wage of nirvāṇa
and thought it a great gain,
having no aspiration for the Great Vehicle.
Yet, because of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, when the Buddha revealed and taught it to the bodhisattvas,
we ourselves had no wish for it.
Why is this?
The Buddha knew our minds delighted in lesser teachings
and, by skillful means, followed our preferences;
we did not realize we were truly the Buddha’s children.
Now we finally realize
that the World-Honored One, as to the Buddha’s wisdom,
withholds
nothing.
Why is this?
For from the beginning, we truly have been the Buddha’s children,
yet we only delighted in lesser teachings,
but if we had inclined our minds to the greater,
the Buddha would have taught us the Great Vehicle.
In this sūtra only the One Vehicle is expounded,
yet before, in front of the bodhisattvas, those who criticized the śrāvakas’ preference for lesser teachings—
even so, the Buddha truly was teaching with the Great Vehicle.
Therefore, we have said we truly had no intention or hope.
Now, the great treasure of the Dharma King has come of itself,
and the Buddha’s children have all received what they ought to obtain.’
At that time, Móhē Jiāshè
wishing to further express this meaning,
spoke in verse:
Today we,
hearing the Buddha’s teaching,
delight and leap for joy,
attaining what we have never had.
The Buddha says that śrāvakas
will become Buddhas,
gaining the supreme heap of treasures,
unasked, it is freely given.
For example, a child,
young and ignorant,
leaves his father and flees,
wandering far to another land,
roaming all the countries,
for more than fifty years.
His father, grieved,
searched everywhere,
and when weary from seeking,
stayed at a city,
built a house,
and enjoyed the five desires.
His household was extremely wealthy,
having much gold and silver,
with carriages and horses,
pearls and lapis lazuli;
elephants, horses, cattle, sheep,
litters, carriages, and carts;
fields and estates, male and female servants,
and a great multitude of people.
His business profits and losses
extended to other countries;
merchants and traders—
there was no place they were not found.
Crowds in the tens of thousands,
gathered around in reverence;
he was always beloved [by] kings,
nobles and great clans,
who all esteemed him.
For these reasons,
many people came and went;
his wealth and power were thus immense.
He had great might.
But, as he aged,
he only missed his son more,
thinking of him day and night,
The time of death is approaching.
The foolish child abandoned me, for more than fifty years,
all the stores and possessions in the treasury,
what should be done with them?
Then the poor son
sought clothing and food,
going from town to town,
from state to state.
Sometimes he obtained something,
sometimes he obtained nothing,
hungry and emaciated,
his body developed sores and scabs.
Gradually passing through,
he arrived at the city where his father lived,
working as a hired laborer in various places,
until he finally reached his father’s house.
At that time, the elder
within his gate had a great jeweled canopy set up
and sat on a lion’s seat;
relatives and dependents gathered around,
various people served and guarded him,
some were making calculations,
checking the gold, silver, and treasures,
managing internal and external assets,
and recording contracts and records.
The poor son saw his father’s
wealth, nobility, and dignity,
and thought he must be the king,
or someone like a king.
Startled and afraid, he blamed himself,
wondering why he came here.
He reflected inwardly, saying:
“If I stay long,
I might be forced or
driven to work.”
Having thought this over,
he hurried away and left;
asking among the poor,
he sought work as a laborer.
At that time, the elder
from his lion’s seat
saw his son from afar
and silently recognized him.
Immediately he ordered a servant
to pursue and bring him back.
The poor son, startled, cried out
and fainted, collapsing to the ground:
“These people are arresting me,
surely I will be put to death;
what use is clothing and food
if I am brought to this?”
The elder knew his son was
ignorant, foolish, narrow, and lowly,
that he would not believe his words
or believe that he was his father.
So, by skillful means,
he sent other people instead,
one-eyed, short, and ugly,
without dignity or power,
saying: “You go and speak to him;
tell him I will hire him,
to remove excrement and filth,
and I will pay him double.”
The poor son, hearing this,
was glad and followed,
removing excrement and filth,
cleaning all the rooms and houses.
The elder, through a window,
constantly watched his son,
knowing his son was dull and lowly,
content to do base work.
Then the elder
put on filthy, tattered clothes,
took a container for excrement,
and went to his son’s place,
using skillful means to get close
and spoke, urging him to work diligently:
“I will increase your pay,
and oil your feet as well,
give you plenty of food and drink,
with thick and warm bedding.”
He spoke harshly to him:
“You must work diligently.”
But also spoke gently:
“You are like a son to me.”
The elder was wise,
and gradually allowed him to come and go in the house;
after twenty years,
he had him manage the household affairs.
He showed him the gold and silver,
the pearls and crystals;
all the goods coming in and out
were entrusted to his knowledge.
Yet still, he stayed outside the gate,
lodging in a grass hut,
reflecting on his poverty,
“I do not possess these things.”
The father knew his son’s mind
had gradually become broad,
and desired to give him his wealth and possessions.
So he gathered his relatives,
kings and great ministers,
kṣatriyas and householders.
Before this great assembly,
he declared, “This is my son,
who left me and went elsewhere,
for fifty years.
Since I saw my son return,
it has been twenty years.
Long ago, in a certain city,
I lost this son;
I traveled everywhere seeking him
until I came here.
All that I possess
—house, estates, and people—
I now entrust entirely to him,
letting him use them as he wills.
My son remembers his former poverty,
his aspirations and spirit were base;
now, in his father’s house,
he has greatly acquired precious treasures,
together with house and estate,
and all wealth and riches.
He is exceedingly joyful,
having attained what he never had before.”
Likewise, the Fó
knows that we delight in lesser things,
and has never spoken, saying:
“You shall become Buddhas.”
Instead, he has taught that we
attain the unconditioned,
achieve the Hīnayāna,
as Śrāvaka disciples.
The Fó instructed us
to expound the supreme path;
those who practice this
shall attain buddhahood.
I follow the teaching of the Fó,
acting as great bodhisattvas,
by various causes and conditions,
all kinds of parables,
with many words,
to expound the unsurpassed path.
All the sons of the Buddhas,
hearing the Dharma from me,
think on it day and night,
diligently practicing.
At that time all Buddhas
immediately bestowed predictions,
“In the future,
you shall attain buddhahood.”
All the teachings
hidden in the Buddhas’ treasury,
are taught only for bodhisattvas, revealing the true matter,
but not to us
are the real essentials revealed.
Just like that poor son,
who could approach his father,
though he knew of all the goods,
his mind did not covet them.
Even as we speak of
the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma,
we have no aspiration,
it is likewise with us.
Within, we quench ourselves,
claim self-sufficiency,
thinking this is complete,
with nothing more to pursue.
If we hear of
the pure Buddha-lands,
transforming and teaching beings,
we feel no delight at all.
Why is this?
All dharmas
are empty and still,
unborn and undying,
neither great nor small,
neither defiled nor produced.
Reflecting thus,
we do not generate joy.
Through long nights,
in the Buddha’s wisdom,
we have no greed or attachment,
and no further aspirations;
and within the Dharma,
think it is ultimate.
Through countless nights,
we have practiced the Dharma of emptiness,
escaping the three realms
and the afflictions of suffering.
Dwelling in the final body,
possessing remainder nirvāṇa.
Those whom the Buddha has taught and transformed,
their attainment of the Way is not in vain,
thus they have attained it,
and repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Although we are considered,
all as sons of the Buddhas,
and practice the Bodhisattva path,
seeking the Buddha-way;
yet with regard to this Dharma,
we have never harbored wish or delight.
The Teacher, seeing us cast aside,
and observing our minds,
at first did not encourage us,
or speak of real benefit.
It is like a wealthy elder,
who knows his son’s aspiration is base,
and with skillful means,
gently subdues his mind,
and only then entrusts
all his goods and treasures.
The Buddha is likewise:
manifesting rare and marvelous deeds,
knowing those who delight in lesser things,
through skillful means,
tames and subdues their minds,
and then teaches great wisdom.
Today, we have
obtained what has never been before,
not what we previously expected,
but now we ourselves attain,
like that poor son
who gains limitless treasures.
World-Honored One, today I,
have attained the Way and its fruit,
in the undefiled Dharma
I have obtained the pure eye.
For countless nights, we have
upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts,
but only from today
do we gain their reward.
Long have we cultivated the pure conduct
within the Dharma of the Dharma-King,
now attaining the undefiled,
supreme great fruit.
Now we,
are truly Śrāvakas,
with the voice of the Buddha-way,
making all hear it.
Now we,
are true Arhats,
among all in the world,
devas, humans, Māra, Brahmā,
universally among them,
worthy to receive offerings.
The World-Honored One’s great kindness,
by means of rare marvels,
in compassion teaches and transforms,
and benefits us,
for innumerable hundreds of millions of kalpas;
who could repay this?
Supplying our hands and feet,
bowing with our heads,
making all offerings—
none could suffice as repayment.
Even if, with head bowed,
bearing him on our shoulders,
for kalpas as innumerable as the sands of the Ganges,
with utmost reverence;
and with fine food,
limitless jeweled garments,
and all manner of bedding,
various soups and medicines,
candana from ox-heads,
and precious jewels,
to build stūpas and temples,
spreading jeweled clothes upon the ground—
such acts as these,
in making offerings,
for kalpas as countless as the sands of the Ganges,
could not requite his kindness.
The Buddhas are rare,
boundless in number,
inconceivable,
of great spiritual power,
without outflows, unconditioned,
kings of the Dharma.
Able, for the sake of those of lowly station,
to endure these situations,
taking as real the forms of common beings,
and teaching as appropriate.
The Buddhas, in the Dharma,
have gained the utmost freedom;
they know the various desires and delights of beings,
as well as their strength of intent.
According to what they can bear,
with countless parables,
they expound the Dharma.
In accord with all beings’ [past] roots of goodness,
also knowing who is mature and who is not yet mature,
they weigh various factors,
distinguish and discern,
and regarding the One Vehicle Way,
as appropriate, they teach three.
The Lotus Sūtra of Wonderful Dharma
Scroll the Third of The Lotus Sūtra of Wonderful Dharma
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Qiūcí of Later Qín,
Kumārajīva, by imperial command
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Mahā Kāśyapa and all the great disciples:
"Excellent, excellent! Kāśyapa,
you have well spoken the Tathāgata’s true and real merit.
As you have said,
the Tathāgata furthermore possesses boundless and limitless asaṃkhyeya merits.
Even if you were to speak for innumerable hundreds of millions of kalpas, you could not exhaust them.
Kāśyapa! Know
the Tathāgata is king of all dharmas.
Anything he teaches is never in vain.
For all dharmas,
with wisdom and skillful means he proclaims them,
and his teachings
all reach the ground of all-knowing wisdom.
The Tathāgata observes and knows the ultimate tendency of all dharmas,
and likewise knows the deep workings in the minds of all sentient beings,
penetrating freely without obstruction.
And again, he is ultimately clear and fully realized in all dharmas,
revealing to beings all wisdom.
Kāśyapa!

It is like the Three Thousand Great Thousand World; the mountains, rivers, valleys, the land, the vegetation, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs, their types are many, with differing names and appearances.
Dense clouds spread everywhere, covering the Three Thousand Great Thousand World,
at once raining evenly, the moisture soaking all. The vegetation, trees, forests, and herbs—
those with small roots and stalks, with small branches and leaves,
those with medium roots and stalks, medium branches and leaves,
and those with large roots and stalks, large branches and leaves,
trees large and small—
each receives according to its superior, middle, or lower capacity.
From the same raincloud,
in accord with their natures
they grow and develop,
blossoming and bearing fruit.
Though all are born in one land and moistened by one rain,
yet all the grasses and trees
each have differences.
Kāśyapa, you should know:
The Tathāgata is likewise,
appearing in the world, as great clouds arise,
with a great voice resounding through the world of devas, humans, asuras,
just as the great cloud covers the Three Thousand Great Thousand Lands.
In the great assembly, he proclaims:

‘I am the Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Complete in Understanding and Practice, Well Gone, Knower of the World, Supreme Guiding Man, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Devas and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
Those not yet crossed over, I cause to cross;
those not yet understood, I cause to understand;
those not yet at peace, I cause to have peace;
those not yet in nirvāṇa, I cause to attain nirvāṇa.
Of the present and future lifetimes, I know as they truly are.
I am the knower of all,
the seer of all,
the knower of the Way,
the revealer of the Way,
the instructor of the Way.
All you devas, humans, and asuras,
should assemble here,
to hear the Dharma.’
Then countless tens of thousands of millions of beings
come to the presence of the Buddha and listen to the Dharma.
The Tathāgata at that time, observing the faculties of these beings, their sharpness or dullness, their diligence or laziness,
in accord with their capacity, teaches the Dharma,
by various and countless methods,
causing them all to rejoice and swiftly gain benefit.
These beings, having heard this Dharma,
are at peace and secure in this life and are born in good destinations hereafter;
by the Way, they experience happiness, and, again, hear the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, they are freed from all obstacles;
with regard to all dharmas,
according to their ability, gradually enter into the Way.
Just as that great cloud rains upon all the grass, forests, trees, and medicinal herbs,
according to their nature,
each is fully moistened and grows.
The Tathāgata expounds the Dharma with one mark and one flavor—
namely: the mark of liberation, the mark of separation, the mark of extinction,
ultimately reaching the wisdom of all modes.
If there are beings who hear the Tathāgata’s Dharma,
and uphold, read, recite, and practice as taught,
the merits they obtain they are themselves unaware of.
Why is this?
Only the Tathāgata knows the various kinds, characteristics, and natures of beings,
what they ponder,
what they contemplate,
what they cultivate,
how they ponder,
how they contemplate,
how they cultivate,
by which Dharma they ponder,
by which Dharma they contemplate,
by which Dharma they cultivate,
and by means of which Dharma they attain which Dharma.
Sentient beings dwell in various places;
only the Tathāgata sees this as it truly is, clear and unobstructed.
Just as with grasses, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs,
they themselves do not know if their natures are superior, average, or inferior.
The Tathāgata knows the Dharma to be of one aspect and one flavor—
namely, the aspect of liberation, the aspect of separation, the aspect of extinction—
ultimately the eternal, tranquil, and extinct aspect of Nirvāṇa, finally returning to emptiness.
The Buddha, knowing this, observes the minds and desires of sentient beings and seeks to protect them.
Therefore, he does not immediately teach the wisdom of all modes.
"You, Jiāshè! This is most rare:
to be able to know that the Tathāgata preaches according to what is appropriate, to be able to believe and accept it.
Why is this so? The various Buddhas, Bhagavāns, teach dharma as appropriate, which is difficult to understand and difficult to know."
At that time, the Bhagavān, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse, saying:
The King of Dharma who dispels being,
appears in the world,
responding to the desires of sentient beings,
and preaches dharma in various ways.
The Tathāgata is worthy of reverence,
his wisdom deep and far-reaching.
Long has he maintained silence on this essential matter,
not hastily expounding it.
If the wise hear it,
then they are able to believe and understand;
if the unwise, in doubt and regret,
then they forever lose it.
Therefore, Jiāshè!
He preaches according to their capacity,
with various conditions,
enabling them to gain right view.
Jiāshè, you should know!
It is like a great cloud
rising in the world,
covering everything everywhere;
the cloud of wisdom contains moisture,
its lightning dazzling and bright,
thunder rumbling far away,
bringing joy and delight to all.
The sunlight is covered,
the ground becomes cool and fresh,
dark and dense layers hang down,
as if they could be gathered in the hands.
Its rain is impartial,
falls equally in all directions;
the streaming and soaking is limitless,
blessing all the land with abundance.
Mountains, rivers, and deep ravines,
and secluded, remote places;
grasses, trees, medicinal herbs,
trees great and small,
the seeds and shoots of all grains,
sugarcane and grape vines—
all those moistened by the rain
are abundantly nourished.
The dry earth is thoroughly soaked,
and medicinal shrubs flourish together.
What comes from that cloud
is water of one flavor;
grasses, trees, and forests,
each receive moisture according to their share.
All kinds of trees,
superior, average, and inferior,
according to their size,
each grows and develops;
roots, stalks, branches, and leaves,
flowers and fruits, brightness and color,
all that the rain reaches,
is made fresh and lustrous.
According to their form and aspect,
their natures and sizes differ,
yet what moistens them is one,
and each flourishes anew.
So too is the Buddha:
he appears in the world,
like a great cloud,
universally covering all.
Upon appearing in the world,
for all beings,
he distinguishes and preaches
the true reality of dharmas.
The Great Sage, the Bhagavān,
among gods and humans,
in the midst of all beings,
declares these words:
"I am the Tathāgata,
the Most Honored among bipeds,
appearing in the world,
just like a great cloud,
filling and nourishing all.
All withered sentient beings,
I enable to leave suffering,
and gain ease and happiness—
the joys of the world
as well as the joy of Nirvāṇa.
All gods and humans,
gather with focused minds,
all should come here
to behold the unsurpassed Honored One."
I am the Bhagavān,
unmatched by any,
appearing in the world
to bring ease and peace to sentient beings.
For the great assembly, I preach
the nectar-like pure Dharma,
this Dharma of one flavor:
liberation and Nirvāṇa.
With one wondrous sound,
I expound and clarify this meaning,
always for the Mahāyāna
creating the conditions.
I see all
universally as equal,
with no bias of this or that,
no mind of love or hate.
I possess no greed or attachment,
nor any limitations or hindrances,
always for all alike,
preaching Dharma equally.
As for one person,
so for many as well,
I always expound Dharma,
never occupied with anything else.
Whether coming, going, sitting, or standing,
ultimately I never grow weary or disheartened,
filling the world
like the rain moistening all.
Noble or base, superior or inferior,
those who keep precepts or break the precepts,
those fully endowed with decorum,
and those not fully endowed,
those with right view or wrong view,
sharp faculties or dull faculties—
I rain the Dharma equally,
without laziness or fatigue.
All sentient beings,
who hear my Dharma,
according to the capacity they receive,
abide in various situations.
Some dwelling among humans and gods,
Cakravartin kings,
the kings Śakra and Brahmā—
these are the small medicinal herbs.
Those who know the flawless Dharma,
attain Nirvāṇa,
arise with the six supernormal powers,
and obtain the three knowledges,
dwelling alone in mountain forests,
always practicing meditative absorption,
attaining Pratyekabuddha realization—
these are the middle medicinal herbs.
Those who seek the seat of the Bhagavān,
who resolve to become Buddhas,
practice diligence and concentration—
these are the superior medicinal herbs.
Moreover, the Buddha-children,
wholeheartedly pursuing Buddhahood,
always practicing kindness and compassion,
knowing themselves to be Buddhas,
determined and without doubt—
these are called small trees.
Those abiding in supernormal powers,
turning the wheel of non-retreat,
delivering innumerable millions,
hundreds of thousands of sentient beings—
these Bodhisattvas,
are called great trees.
The Buddha preaches equally,
like rain of one flavor;
but according to beings' natures,
what they receive is not the same,
just as with the grasses and trees,
what they take up differs each according to its kind.
The Buddha uses this metaphor,
expediently teaching,
with various words and expressions,
to expound but one Dharma;
yet the Buddha's wisdom
is but like a drop in the sea.
I rain the Dharma-rain,
filling the world,
the Dharma of one flavor—
for each, practice follows their strength.
Just as with the forests,
the medicinal herbs and trees,
according to their size,
gradually increase and flourish.
So too, the Dharma of the Buddhas
is always one in flavor,
enabling all the world
to completely attain sufficiency,
cultivating step by step,
all achieve the fruit of the Way.
Śrāvakās and Pratyekabuddhas,
dwelling in mountain forests,
reside in their final body,
hear the Dharma and attain the fruit,
these are called medicinal herbs,
each gaining increase and growth.
If there are Bodhisattvas,
whose wisdom is firm,
who thoroughly comprehend the three realms,
and seek the supreme vehicle,
these are called small trees,
and they too gain increase and growth.
Further, there are those abiding in meditation,
who obtain spiritual powers,
who hear that all dharmas are empty,
whose hearts are greatly joyful,
radiating immeasurable light,
delivering all sentient beings,
these are called great trees,
and they too gain increase and growth.
Thus, Jiāshè!
The Dharma spoken by the Buddha
is like a great cloud,
with a single-flavored rain,
moistening the flowers of people,
so each may reach fruition.
Jiāshè, you should know!
Using various causes and conditions,
and all manner of similes,
I reveal and demonstrate the Buddha Path;
this is my skillful means,
and all Buddhas are likewise.
Now, for your sake,
I speak the truest matter:
“All the Śrāvakā assemblies
have not truly entered extinction.
What you all practice
is the Bodhisattva path;
gradually cultivating and learning,
you will assuredly become Buddhas.”
At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this verse,
he addressed the great assembly and proclaimed, saying:
“My disciple Mahā Kāshyapa,
in a future age, will come to personally see three trillion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
make offerings with reverence, respect, and praise,
and widely declare the Buddhas’ measureless great Dharma.
In his final body, he will achieve Buddhahood,

and be named Guāngmíng Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Clarity and Practice, Well Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
The land will be called Guāngdé,
and the kalpa will be named Dàzhuāngyán.
The Buddha’s lifespan will be twelve small kalpas,
the True Dharma will abide in the world for twenty small kalpas,
and the Counterfeit Dharma will likewise abide for twenty small kalpas.
The land will be adorned magnificently,
without any filth or evil,
rubble, thorns,
filth or impurities.
The land will be level and proper,
with neither high nor low,
no pits, mounds, or knolls.
The ground will be of lapis-lazuli,
jewel trees in rows,
golden cords as boundaries along the paths,
all kinds of precious flowers strewn about, everywhere pure and clean.
The country’s Bodhisattvas will number limitless hundreds of millions,
and the assembly of Śrāvakās will also be numberless.
There will be no mara incidents,
and while there will be māras and māra’s followers,
all will protect the Buddha Dharma.”
Then, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this intention,
spoke in verse:
“Addressing the Bhikṣus:
With the Buddha eye,
I see this Kāshyapa,
in a future age,
after countless kalpas,
will assuredly become a Buddha.
In the ages to come,
he will make offerings and personally see
three trillion,
Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
For Buddha wisdom,
he will purely cultivate Brahma practice.
Having made the highest offerings
to the Two-Footed Honored Ones,
he will cultivate all
unsurpassed wisdom.
In his final body
he will attain Buddhahood.
His land will be pure,
with lapis-lazuli ground,
many precious trees
arranged in rows beside the paths,
golden cords as boundaries,
those who see it rejoice.
Fragrant scents will always arise,
scattering famous flowers,
of various wondrous kinds,
as adornments.
The land is level and proper,
without hills or pits.
The Bodhisattva assembly
is beyond reckoning,
their minds gentle and tame,
achieving great spiritual powers,
upholding all Buddhas’
Mahāyāna sūtras.
The assembly of Śrāvakās,
in their final body without outflows,
children of the Dharma King,
too numerous to reckon,
even with the heavenly eye,
they cannot be counted or known.
The Buddha’s lifespan
will be twelve small kalpas;
the True Dharma will abide in the world
for twenty small kalpas;
the Counterfeit Dharma will likewise abide;
the honored Guāngmíng Buddha,
it will be thus.”
At that time Dà Mùjiānlián,
Xū Pútí, Mahā Kātiānyán, and others,
all became fearful and trembling,
single-mindedly joined palms,
gazed upon the Honored Face,
eyes never leaving him even briefly,
and together in one voice,
spoke this verse:
“Great hero, mighty World-Honored One,
Dharma King among all Shìjiā,
out of pity and compassion for us,
you have bestowed the Buddha’s voice.
If you know our innermost minds,
and see that we receive this prediction,
it is like being sprinkled with nectar,
cooling us and relieving our heat.
It is as if coming from a famine-stricken land,
suddenly encountering the king’s feast,
still harboring doubt and fear,
not daring to eat right away;
if granted the king’s command,
then one dares to eat.
We are likewise:
ever aware of the shortcomings of the Lesser Vehicle,
not knowing how
to attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom.
Although we heard the Buddha’s voice
saying we will become Buddhas,
our hearts still feel anxious and afraid,
as not daring to eat immediately;
if we would receive the Buddha’s prediction,
only then would we be truly joyful and at peace.
Great hero, mighty World-Honored One,
ever willing to bring peace to the world,
please grant us your prediction,
like teaching the hungry to eat.”
At that time, the World-Honored One,
knowing the thoughts in the hearts of all the great disciples,
addressed the Bhikṣus:
“This Xū Pútí, in the future, will personally see three trillion nayutas of Buddhas,
making offerings with reverence, respect, and praise,
constantly cultivating Brahma conduct, and fully engaging in the Bodhisattva Path.
In his final body, he will become a Buddha,

titled Míngxiàng Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Clarity and Practice, Well Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
The kalpa will be called Yǒubǎo.
The land will be called Bǎoshēng.
The land will be level and proper,
with beryl as its ground,
wondrously adorned with jeweled trees,
with no hills, pits, sand, gravel, thorns, or impure filth,
jeweled flowers covering the ground, everywhere pure and clean.
The people of that land will all reside on jeweled terraces and exquisite towers and pavilions.
The Śrāvakā disciples, in numbers immeasurable and boundless,
far beyond what can be known by calculation or analogy.
The Bodhisattva assemblies will also be innumerable, in the thousands, millions, billions, nayutas.
The Buddha’s lifespan will be twelve small kalpas,
the True Dharma will abide in the world for twenty small kalpas,
and the Counterfeit Dharma will likewise abide for twenty small kalpas.
That Buddha will always reside in the sky,
expounding the Dharma for the multitudes,
delivering limitless Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakā assemblies.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this intention,
spoke in verse:
All the assembly of bhikṣus,
I now tell you,
you should all set your minds as one,
and listen to what I declare:
My great disciple,
Xū Pútí,
will in the future become a Buddha,
with the name and title “Míng Xiàng.”
He will serve and honor countless
myriads of kotis of Buddhas,
following the practices carried out by the Buddhas,
and gradually accomplish the Great Way.
In his final body, he will attain
the thirty-two marks,
upright and exquisitely beautiful,
like a precious mountain.
His Buddha-land
will be supreme in purity and adornment,
and all sentient beings who see it
will love and delight in it without exception.
The Buddha, therein,
will deliver immeasurable beings.
Within his Buddha-dharma,
there will be many bodhisattvas,
all of sharp faculties,
circling the Wheel of Non-Retrogression—
his land will ever
be adorned with bodhisattvas.
The assembly of śrāvakas
are beyond reckoning,
all possessing the Three Insights,
endowed with the Six Supernatural Powers,
abiding in the Eight Liberations,
and commanding great spiritual potency.
That Buddha’s teaching
will manifest infinite
supernatural transformations,
inconceivable to ordinary thought.
The assemblage of gods and humans
is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
all raise their palms together,
listening and accepting the Buddha’s teaching.
That Buddha’s lifespan
will be twelve minor kalpas;
the True Dharma will abide in the world
for twenty minor kalpas;
the Semblance Dharma will also abide
for twenty minor kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
“I now tell you,
this Mahākātyāyana, in times to come,
will render all manner of offerings and serve eight thousand kotis of Buddhas, with utmost honor and respect.
After those Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa,
stūpas and shrines will be raised for each, a thousand yojanas tall,
with length and breadth equal, five hundred yojanas each,
all formed from gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, pearl, rose quartz, and seven jewels fused together,
adorned with multitudes of flowers, necklaces, incense paste, powdered incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and pennants,
offered before the stūpas and shrines.
After this,
he will again make offerings to twenty thousand kotis of Buddhas,
likewise as before.
After making offerings to these Buddhas,
with the bodhisattva way complete, he shall become a Buddha,

with the name Yánfú Nátí Jīnguāng Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Complete in Wisdom and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Hero, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Men, Buddha, World-Honored One.
His land will be level and straight,
with the ground of beryl and adorned with jeweled trees;
golden lines will border the pathways,
the earth will be covered with wondrous flowers, pure and unstained throughout,
bringing joy to those who behold it.
There will be none of the four evil destinies—hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or asura realms.
