he should enter the Thus-Come One's chamber,
wear the Thus-Come One's robe,
and sit upon the Thus-Come One's seat.
Dwelling among the assembly, he will have no fear,
and widely and clearly explain it.
Great compassion is his chamber,
gentleness and patience his robe,
the emptiness of all dharmas his seat;
dwelling thus, he preaches the Dharma.
If, while expounding this sūtra,
someone reviles with harsh words,
or attacks with knives, staves, tiles or stones,
he should endure because he remembers the Buddha.
Throughout a thousand myriad kotis of lands,
I manifest a pure and solid body,
and for limitless aeons asankhya,
I preach the Dharma to sentient beings.
If after my extinction
there is one who can preach this sūtra,
I will send transformation bodies from among the fourfold assembly—
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs,
male and female lay faithful—
to honor and make offerings to the Dharma teacher,
to guide all sentient beings,
gathering them to listen to the Dharma.
If anyone wishes to do harm,
with knives, staves, tiles, or stones,
I will then dispatch transformation beings
to act as their guards and protectors.
If the person expounding the Dharma
is alone in a quiet place,
silent and without a sound from others,
reciting or reading this sūtra,
at that time I will manifest
a pure and bright body before him.
If he forgets or loses passages and verses,
I will speak them for him to render understanding clear and fluent.
If someone possesses these virtues,
whether preaching to the fourfold assembly
or reciting the sūtra alone in solitude,
all shall obtain a vision of my body.
If a person is in solitude,
I send the heavenly Nāga kings,
yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth,
to form an audience for hearing the Dharma.
This person delights in preaching the Dharma,
he distinguishes and explains without hindrance;
because all Buddhas protect and remember him,
he can cause the great assembly to rejoice.
If one draws near to the Dharma teacher,
one quickly attains the bodhisattva path,
studying in accord with this teacher,
one shall see buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Then, in front of the Buddha, there was a jeweled stūpa of seven treasures,
five hundred yojanas high,
two hundred fifty yojanas in breadth and depth,
emerging from the earth, dwelling in the sky,
adorned with various kinds of jewels.
There were five thousand balustrades,
tens of thousands of niches,
countless banners and canopies embellishing it,
countless jeweled necklaces, jeweled bells, hung above by the myriads and millions.
On all four sides wafted the scent of tamāla and sandalwood, pervading throughout the world.
Its many banners and parasols were composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, pearls, rose quartz, the seven treasures combined,
reaching up to the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.
The Thirty-three Gods rained heavenly mandārava flowers
as offerings to the jeweled stūpa.
Additionally, the other gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṁnaras, mahoragas, humans and nonhumans,
myriad kotis in number,
with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, music,
made offerings to the jeweled stūpa,
reverently respecting, honoring, and praising it.
At that time, from within the jeweled stūpa came a great sound of praise, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Śìjiāmóuní World Honored One!
Able, with equal and great wisdom,
to teach the bodhisattva path,
guarded and remembered by the Buddhas—the wonderful Dharma Flower Sūtra,
preached for this great assembly.
So it is, so it is! Śìjiāmóuní World Honored One!
What you have spoken is entirely true.”
Then the fourfold assembly,
seeing the great jeweled stūpa dwelling in the air,
also hearing the sound coming from within the stūpa,
all felt Dharma joy,
marveled at this unprecedented event,
rose from their seats,
reverently joined their palms
and stood to one side.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Dàlèshuō,
who understood the doubts in the minds of all the devas, humans, asuras, and so forth in the world,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World Honored One, for what reason and cause has this jeweled stūpa risen from the earth,
and why does it emit this sound?”
At this time, the Buddha told the bodhisattva Dàlèshuō:
“Within this jeweled stūpa is the complete body of a Thus-Come One.
Long ago, in the east, beyond numberless myriads of kotis asankhya worlds,
there was a land named Bǎojìng.
There, a Buddha appeared, named Duōbǎo.
When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path,
he made a great vow:
‘If, after I attain Buddhahood and enter nirvana,
in any land in the ten directions there is a place where the Dharma Flower Sūtra is taught,
my stūpa and shrine,
in order to hear this sūtra,
will emerge in front of them,
to remain as a testimony
and praise it, saying “Excellent!”’
After becoming a Buddha,
at the time of his extinction,
in the midst of the assembly of devas, humans, and so forth, he told the bhikṣus:
‘After my extinction,
those who wish to make offerings to my complete body
should erect a great stūpa.’
By the Buddha’s supernatural power and vow,
wherever in the ten directions,
in all places,
if there is one expounding the Dharma Flower Sūtra,
his jeweled stūpa will always emerge before him,
his complete body within the stūpa,
praising, “Excellent, excellent!”’
Dàlèshuō,
now, the stūpa of the Thus-Come One Duōbǎo,
hearing the Dharma Flower Sūtra preached,
has risen from the earth and praised,
‘Excellent, excellent!’”
At this time, the bodhisattva Dàlèshuō,
by the power of the Thus-Come One,
addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World Honored One,
we wish to see this Buddha’s body.”
The Buddha told the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Dàlèshuō:
This Buddha Duōbǎo
has a profound vow:
‘If my jeweled stūpa,
for the sake of hearing the Dharma Flower Sūtra,
appears before the various Buddhas,
if there are those who wish my body to be shown to the fourfold assembly,
the divided bodies of those Buddhas—
who are preaching in worlds of the ten directions—
must all gather together in one place;
only after that will my body be revealed.’
Dàlèshuō,
my divided bodies—the Buddhas
in the worlds of the ten directions expounding the Dharma—
should now be gathered together.”
Dàlèshuō addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World Honored One,
we too wish to see the World Honored One’s divided bodies,
to pay homage and make offerings.”
At this time, the Buddha released a light from the white hair mark between his brows,
and instantly the Buddhas of five hundred myriad kotis of nayutas of Ganges sands of lands in the east became visible,
and in those lands, all had crystal for ground,
adorned with jeweled trees and jeweled robes,
filled with innumerable thousands of myriads of kotis of bodhisattvas,
with jeweled canopies spread everywhere,
jeweled nets arrayed overhead.
In those lands, the Buddhas proclaimed the Dharma with marvelous voices,
and were seen by numberless countless myriads of kotis of bodhisattvas who filled those realms,
preaching the Dharma for the crowd.
In the south, west, north, four corners and upward,
everywhere the light of the white hair mark reached,
it was likewise so.
Then, the Buddhas in the ten directions each told their assembly of bodhisattvas:
“Good sons, I now should go to the Sahā world,
to Śìjiāmóuní Buddha,
and together make offerings to the jeweled stūpa of the Thus-Come One Duōbǎo.”
At that time, the Sahā world was instantly transformed into purity,
with lapis lazuli for ground,
adorned with jeweled trees,
with ropes of gold marking off eight highways,
and no towns, villages, cities, seas, rivers, mountains, valleys, forests, or thickets remaining.
Precious incenses were burned,
mandārava flowers were scattered everywhere,
jeweled nets and banners canopied the sky above,
with countless jeweled bells dangling.
Only this assembly was left,
while gods and humans were removed and sent to other lands.
At this time, each of the Buddhas brought one great bodhisattva as attendant
and came to the Sahā world,
each arriving beneath a jeweled tree.
Each of those jeweled trees was five hundred yojanas tall,
their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit adorning them in succession,
and beneath each jeweled tree was a lion throne five yojanas high,
also decorated and adorned with great gems.
Then, each of the Buddhas
sat down cross-legged on this seat.
Thus, in succession, they filled the three thousand great thousand worlds,
yet the divided bodies of Śìjiāmóuní Buddha appearing in but one quarter were not yet exhausted.
At that time, Shìjiā Móuní Fó,
wishing to make room to receive all the many emanated Buddhas,
transformed two hundred million nayuta countries in each of the eight directions,
making them all pure,
with none of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or Asuras.
Again, the gods and humans were moved to other lands.
The lands thus transformed
also had jeweled ground of crystal, adorned with precious trees;
the trees were five hundred yojanas high,
their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits wonderfully arrayed in order.
Beneath each tree was a jeweled lion throne,
five yojanas in height,
ornamented and adorned with various kinds of jewels.
There were also no great oceans or rivers,
nor Mount Móuzhēnlíntuó,
Mahā-Móuzhēnlíntuó, the Iron Encircling Mountains, the Great Iron Encircling Mountains, Mount Xūmí, and other such kingly mountains.
All became a single land of a Buddha.
The jeweled ground was level and even,
covered everywhere with canopies of interwoven precious nets;
with banners and canopies hanging,
and great incense of jewels being burned,
and heavenly jeweled flowers scattered across the ground.
Shìjiā Móuní Fó, for the future seating of all the Buddhas,
again in each of the eight directions transformed two hundred million nayuta countries,
making them all pure,
with none of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or Asuras,
and again moved the gods and humans to other lands.
The lands thus transformed
also had jeweled ground of crystal,
adorned with precious trees,
the trees five hundred yojanas high, with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits splendidly adorned in order,
underneath each tree a jeweled lion throne,
five yojanas high,
likewise splendidly adorned with great jewels.
There were also no great oceans or rivers,
nor Mount Móuzhēnlíntuó, Mahā-Móuzhēnlíntuó, the Iron Encircling Mountains, the Great Iron Encircling Mountains, Mount Xūmí, and the other kingly mountains.
All became a single land of a Buddha. The jeweled ground was level and even,
covered everywhere with canopies of interwoven jewels;
banners and canopies hung,
great incense of jewels being burned,
and heavenly jeweled flowers scattered throughout the land.
Then, in the East, the emanated bodies of Shìjiā Móuní Fó—
the Buddhas in the hundred thousand million nayuta Ganges sands-like lands—
each expounding the Dharma,
all gathered here;
and so in order from all ten directions, all Buddhas came and assembled,
seated in the eight directions.
Then, in each direction, four hundred million nayuta Buddhakṣetras were utterly filled with Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
At that time each Buddha, seated beneath the precious trees on lion thrones,
sent attendants to greet Shìjiā Móuní Fó,
each bringing handfuls of jeweled flowers, saying:
“Virtuous one!
Go to Mount Qíchéjué and present yourself before Shìjiā Móuní Fó,
and in my stead say:
‘May you be free from illness and suffering, may your energy be at ease,
and may all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas be peaceful as well?’
Scatter these jeweled flowers in offering to the Buddha, and say:
‘Such-and-such Buddha wishes to open this jeweled stūpa.’”
The Buddhas all sent messengers in this way.
At that time, Shìjiā Móuní Fó,
seeing that all the emanated Buddhas had come and assembled,
each sitting upon a lion throne,
all having heard that the Buddhas wished to join in opening the jeweled stūpa,
immediately arose from his seat,
and stood in empty space.
All of the four assemblies also rose, put their palms together,
and single-mindedly gazed at the Buddha.
Then Shìjiā Móuní Fó, with his right finger, opened the door of the seven-jeweled stūpa,
producing a great sound,
like a mighty city gate unlocked.
At that moment the entire assembly
saw Duōbǎo Tathāgata seated inside the jeweled stūpa upon a lion throne,
his entire body undispersed,
as if in meditative absorption.
They also heard him say:
“Excellent, excellent! Shìjiā Móuní Fó!
Quickly proclaim this Lotus Sūtra;
I have come here especially to hear it.”
Thereupon, the four assemblies and others,
seeing a Buddha of innumerable millions of aeons past, one who had entered extinction, speaking in this way,
marveled at what they had never before encountered,
gathering heavenly jeweled flowers
and scattering them upon Duōbǎo Buddha and Shìjiā Móuní Fó.
Then, Duōbǎo Buddha,
within the stūpa, shared half his seat with Shìjiā Móuní Fó, saying:
“Shìjiā Móuní Fó! Please sit here on this seat.”
Instantly, Shìjiā Móuní Fó entered the stūpa,
sat upon the half-seat,
and assumed the lotus posture.
At that time, the great assembly
saw the two Tathāgatas on the lion throne in the seven-jeweled stūpa, both seated cross-legged,
and each thought:
“The Buddha seat is so high and distant—
may the Tathāgata use his supernatural powers
to allow us all to dwell together in the sky!”
Immediately, Shìjiā Móuní Fó, with his supernatural power,
lifted all the assembled and placed them in the sky,
and in a great voice announced to the four assemblies:
“Who is able, in this Śāhā World, to broadly preach the wondrous Lotus Sūtra?
Now is truly the time.
The Tathāgata shall soon enter nirvāṇa.
The Buddha wishes, with this wondrous Lotus Sūtra, to entrust it to those who remain.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate these points,
spoke in verse:
The Holy, Venerable Lord,
though long in extinction,
is still within the precious stūpa,
and yet comes for the sake of the Dharma.
Why do people
not strive for the Dharma?
This Buddha, after extinction,
through boundless aeons,
in place after place, hears the Dharma
because it is so hard to encounter.
That Buddha’s original vow:
After my extinction,
wherever he may go,
it will always be for hearing the Dharma.
And my own emanated bodies,
the countless Buddhas
as numerous as Ganges sands,
all have come wishing to hear the Dharma,
and to see the extinct Duōbǎo Tathāgata.
Each leaves his wondrous land,
his assembly of disciples,
gods, humans, dragons, and spirits,
together with all offerings,
so that the Dharma may long abide, and thus have come here.
That all Buddhas may sit,
through supernatural power,
countless multitudes are relocated,
and the lands made pure.
Each Buddha,
proceeds beneath a jeweled tree,
like a clear pond, adorned with lotus flowers.
Beneath these precious trees,
are lion thrones,
upon which Buddhas sit,
shining with radiance,
like a great torch blazing in the darkness of night.
Their bodies emit exquisite fragrance,
pervading the countries of the ten directions,
and all living beings, bathed in this scent,
are overcome with joy.
It is like a great wind
stirring the branches of small trees.
With such skillful means,
the Dharma is made to abide long.
He addresses the great assembly:
‘After my extinction,
who will protect and sustain
and recite and explain this sūtra?
Now, before the Buddha,
declare your vows yourself.
Duōbǎo Buddha,
though long since entered extinction,
by the power of a great vow
still gives a lion’s roar.
Duōbǎo Tathāgata,
together with myself,
and all the emanated Buddhas who have gathered,
all should comprehend this intention.
All you sons of the Buddha,
who can protect the Dharma,
ought to make great vows,
that it may long abide.
Whoever is able to protect
this sūtra and Dharma
will be serving offerings
to myself and to Duōbǎo.
This Duōbǎo Buddha,
dwelling in the jeweled stūpa,
eternally travels the ten directions,
for the sake of this sūtra,
likewise receives offerings
from all the visiting Buddhas,
adorned with radiance
in all the worlds.
One who explains this sūtra
will see myself,
Duōbǎo Tathāgata,
and all the emanated Buddhas.
Good sons!
Each of you earnestly reflect,
for this is a difficult task,
and you should make great vows.
As for other sūtras,
though they are as numerous as sands of the Ganges,
and are expounded,
none are as difficult as this.
If one were to lift Mount Xūmí
and fling it to another place,
across countless lands of Buddhas,
that would still not be difficult.
If with the tip of a toe
one were to move the great trichiliocosm
and hurl it far into another country,
that too would not be difficult.
If one were to ascend to the summit of existence,
and expound to the multitudes,
the immeasurable remainder of the scriptures,
this would yet not be difficult.
But if, after the Buddha’s extinction,
in the evil world,
one can teach this scripture,
this, then, is indeed difficult.
Suppose there is someone
who grasps empty space in their hand
and roams about with it—
also, this would not be difficult.
After my extinction,
whether one copies this scripture oneself,
or has others write it,
this, then, is indeed difficult.
If one were to place the great earth
atop the nail of one’s foot,
and ascend to Fàntiān,
even this would not be difficult.
After the Buddha’s extinction,
in the evil world,
even to briefly read this scripture,
this, then, is indeed difficult.
Suppose in a kalpa-conflagration,
one carries dry grass
into the flames without being burned—
even this is not difficult.
After my extinction,
if one holds to this scripture,
and expounds it to a single person,
this, then, is indeed difficult.
If one holds the eighty-four thousand Dharma-treasuries,
and the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
and expounds them for others,
causing all listeners
to attain the six supernatural powers—
even though one is able so,
this is still not difficult.
After my extinction,
to listen to and accept this scripture,
and inquire about its meaning and intent,
this, then, is indeed difficult.
If one expounds the Dharma,
enabling billions and trillions,
countless, numberless sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges
to attain Arhatship,
replete with the six supernatural powers—
although there is this benefit,
even this is not difficult.
After my extinction,
if one is able to uphold
scriptures such as this,
this, then, is indeed difficult.
For the sake of the Buddha Way,
throughout immeasurable realms,
from the beginning until now,
I have extensively preached various scriptures,
and among them,
this scripture is the foremost.
If there are those who can uphold it,
then they uphold the Buddha’s body.
All virtuous men!
After my extinction,
whoever can receive, uphold,
read, or recite this scripture,
now before the Buddha,
should declare their vows themselves.
This scripture is difficult to uphold;
if for even a moment one can uphold it,
I will rejoice,
and so will all Buddhas.
People such as these
are praised by all Buddhas.
These are truly courageous;
these are truly diligent;
these are called upholders of morality,
those who practice ascetic conduct,
they will quickly attain
the supreme Buddha Way.
Able in the ages to come
to read and uphold this scripture,
they are true children of the Buddha,
abiding in the state of pure goodness.
After the Buddha’s extinction,
those able to understand its meaning,
these are the eyes of gods and humans in the world.
In an age of fear and dread,
if one can speak even briefly,
all gods and humans ought to make offerings.
At that time the Buddha said to the bodhisattvas, the gods, and the fourfold assembly:
"For past, immeasurable kalpas,
I have sought the Fǎhuá Jīng, never lax or weary.
Throughout many kalpas I was always a king,
vowing to seek unsurpassed bodhi,
my mind never turning back.
In order to perfect the six pāramitās,
I diligently practiced giving,
with no stinginess in my heart:
elephants, horses, the seven treasures, country, city, wives, sons, slaves, attendants,
head, eyes, marrow, brain,
body, flesh, hands, feet—
I did not begrudge my life.
In that era, people’s lifespans were immeasurable;
for the sake of the Dharma,
I relinquished the throne,
entrusted government to the crown prince,
struck the drum and proclaimed a decree,
seeking the Dharma in all directions:
‘Who is able to preach the Mahāyāna for me?
I will serve as a messenger for my entire life!’
At that time, a rishi came and said to the king:
‘I have the Mahāyāna,
named the marvelous Fǎhuá Jīng.
If you do not oppose me,
I will preach it for you.’
Hearing the words of the rishi,
the king rejoiced and leapt for joy,
at once following the rishi,
providing whatever was needed—
gathering fruits, drawing water, collecting firewood, preparing food,
even using his own body as a bed or seat—
in body and mind never weary,
always serving at that time. For a thousand years,
for the sake of the Dharma,
he served diligently,
ensuring there was nothing lacking."
At that time the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke in verse, saying:
"I recall past kalpas,
seeking the great Dharma:
though I was king of the world,
I was not attached to the pleasures of the five desires.
I struck the bell to announce to all directions:
Who possesses the great Dharma?
If you can explain it to me,
I will become your servant.
Then there was the rishi Āshī,
who came and said to the great king:
‘I have a subtle Dharma,
rare in the world.
If you are able to practice it,
I shall preach it for you.’
Then the king, hearing the rishi’s words,
was greatly delighted,
and at once followed the rishi,
providing whatever was needed,
gathering firewood and fruits,
offering them respectfully as needed,
always keeping in mind the marvelous Dharma,
never weary in body and mind.
Universally for all sentient beings,
he diligently sought the great Dharma,
not for his own sake,
nor for the pleasures of the five desires.
Thus as a great king,
he diligently sought and gained this Dharma,
thereby came to attain Buddhahood,
and now I preach it for you."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the king— that was me;
and the rishi— now is Dípó Dátuó.
It was because of Dípó Dátuó, the good spiritual friend,
that I perfected the six pāramitās,
kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity,
the thirty-two marks,
the eighty excellent characteristics,
the color of pure gold,
the ten powers,
the four fearlessnesses,
the four means of unification,
the eighteen distinct Dharma qualities,
attained perfect enlightenment, and vastly liberated sentient beings—
all due to the good spiritual friend Dípó Dátuó."
He said to the fourfold assembly:
"After innumerable kalpas in the future, Dípó Dátuó
will become a Buddha

named Tiānwáng Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Fully Accomplished in Wisdom and Conduct, Well Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Hero, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
The world will be called Tiāndào.
At that time, the Tiānwáng Buddha will dwell in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas,
extensively preaching the marvelous Dharma to sentient beings,
and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will attain the fruit of Arhatship;
innumerable beings will give rise to the heart of solitary enlightenment;
as many as the sands of the Ganges will give rise to bodhicitta;
attaining the patience with the non-arising of dharmas,
and reach non-retrogression.
After the Nirvana of the Tiānwáng Buddha,
the true Dharma will abide in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas.
Relics of the entire body will give rise to a stupa of seven treasures,
sixty yojanas in height,
and forty yojanas in width and breadth.
All gods and humans will offer miscellaneous flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, paste incense, garments, necklaces, banners, canopies of jewels, music, and hymns,
worshiping and making offerings to the marvelous stupa of seven treasures.
Immeasurable sentient beings will attain the fruit of Arhatship;
immeasurable sentient beings will awaken to pratyekabuddhahood;
inconceivable sentient beings will give rise to the aspiration for awakening,
and reach non-retrogression."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“In future ages, if there are good men or good women
who hear the ‘Devadatta’ chapter of the wondrous *Fǎhuá Jīng*,
and, with pure mind, believe and revere it without doubt or hesitation,
they will not fall into hell, hungry ghost, or animal realms.
They will be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions,
and wherever they are born, they will constantly hear this sūtra.
If they are born among humans or devas,
they will receive supreme and wondrous happiness;
if in front of a Buddha,
they will be born by transformation from a lotus flower.”
At that time, a bodhisattva in the assembly of the Bhagavān Duōbǎo in the lower direction,
named Zhìjī,
said to the Buddha Duōbǎo:
“I wish to return to my own land.”
*Shìjiāmóuní* Buddha said to Zhìjī:
“Good man, wait for a little while.
Here there is a bodhisattva named Wénshūshīlì, with whom you may meet,
discuss the wondrous Dharma,
and then return to your homeland.”
At that time Wénshūshīlì,
seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel—
together with the accompanying bodhisattvas, who were also seated upon jeweled lotus flowers—
spontaneously rose up from the great ocean and the palace of the nāga king Sājiéluó,
and remained in empty space.
They went to Língjiǔ Mountain,
descended from the lotus blossoms,
and arrived where the Buddha was.
They bowed their heads and reverentially paid homage at the feet of the two Bhagavāns.
After paying homage,
they went to Zhìjī,
exchanged greetings,
and sat to one side.
The bodhisattva Zhìjī asked Wénshūshīlì:
“When you went to the nāga palace,
how many beings have you transformed?”
Wénshūshīlì replied:
“The number is limitless,
beyond reckoning,
beyond what lips can express,
and beyond what mind can comprehend.
Please wait a moment;
evidence will naturally appear.”
Even before he finished speaking,
countless bodhisattvas, seated upon jeweled lotus flowers,
rose up from the ocean
and came to Língjiǔ Mountain,
remaining in empty space.
All these bodhisattvas had been taught and liberated by Wénshūshīlì,
possessing the practices of bodhisattvas,
and together discoursed upon the six pāramitās.
Those who were originally śrāvakas
now, while staying in the sky, discoursed on śrāvaka practices—
yet were all now cultivating the Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness.
Wénshūshīlì said to Zhìjī:
“Thus is the teaching among the ocean beings.”
At that time the bodhisattva Zhìjī praised him in verse:
“Vast is your wisdom, virtue, vigor, and courage;
you have liberated countless beings.
Now this great assembly,
including myself, has seen it all.
You fully expound the meaning of true reality,
elucidate the teaching of the One Vehicle,
widely lead all beings
to quickly reach bodhi.”
Wénshūshīlì said:
“When in the ocean,
I always proclaim only the wondrous *Fǎhuá Jīng*.”
Zhìjī asked Wénshūshīlì:
“This sūtra is extremely profound and subtle,
the jewel among all sūtras,
rare in the world.
Are there any beings
who diligently cultivate it
and quickly attain Buddhahood?”
Wénshūshīlì said:
“There is the nāga king Sājiéluó’s daughter,
just eight years old.
Her wisdom is sharp,
she well understands the faculties and actions of all beings,
has attained dhāraṇī,
and is able to uphold and retain all the profound secret treasures spoken by the Buddhas.
She dwells deeply in meditation,
comprehends all dharmas,
and in an instant arouses the bodhicitta,
achieves non-retrogression,
and has unhindered eloquence.
Her compassion for all beings
is like that of a mother for her child.
Her virtues are perfected;
her words and thoughts
are subtle, vast, and wondrous;
her kindness, compassion, benevolence, and yielding spirit,
and harmonious intent
enable her to reach bodhi.”
The bodhisattva Zhìjī said:
“I see *Shìjiā* Tathāgata,
over countless kalpas, engaged in difficult, painstaking practices
and accumulated merits and virtues,
seeking the path to bodhi without ever resting.
Contemplating the three thousand great thousand worlds,
there is not so much as a mustard seed-sized place
where, as a bodhisattva, he did not give his life for beings.
Only for the sake of all beings
did he eventually attain the path of bodhi.
I do not believe that this girl can, in but a moment,
achieve right enlightenment.”
Before the conversation was finished,
the nāga girl suddenly appeared before them,
bowed her head in reverence,
stood to one side,
and praised them in verse:
“He thoroughly understands the workings of karma,
shines upon the ten directions;
his wondrous, pure Dharma body
is endowed with thirty-two marks,
adorned with eighty kinds of excellences.
He is revered by gods and men,
and honored by nāgas and spirits.
There is no being who does not esteem and serve him.
To witness the attainment of bodhi—
only the Buddha can know and prove this.
I expound the Mahāyāna teaching
to deliver suffering beings.”
At that time *Shèlìfú* addressed the nāga girl, saying:
“You claim that you will soon attain supreme enlightenment—
this is hard to believe.
Why is this so?
A female body is defiled and not a proper vessel for the Dharma;
how could one in such a form attain unsurpassed bodhi?
The Buddha path is vast and long;
through countless kalpas of diligent cultivation and thorough perfection of the pāramitās,
only then is attainment possible.
Moreover, a woman’s body has five obstacles:
first, unable to become Brahmā,
second, Śakra,
third, Māra,
fourth, a wheel-turning king,
and fifth, a Buddha.
How can a woman quickly achieve Buddhahood?”
At that time, the nāga girl had a precious jewel
worth as much as the three thousand great thousand worlds.
She offered it to the Buddha,
and the Buddha accepted it.
The nāga girl said to the bodhisattva Zhìjī and Elder *Shèlìfú*:
“I offer this jewel
and the Bhagavān accepts it—
is this not swift?”
They replied: “Very swift.”
She said: “Relying on your spiritual power,
observe me become a Buddha,
more swiftly than this.”
At that time, in the assembly,
all saw the nāga girl suddenly transform into a man,
complete in bodhisattva practices,
immediately proceed to the southern Immaculate World,
sit upon a jeweled lotus flower,
attain perfect enlightenment,
with thirty-two marks,
eighty excellent characteristics,
and universally expound the wondrous Dharma to all beings in the ten directions.
Then, in the Sahā World,
bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, the eight classes, humans and non-humans,
all from afar witnessed the nāga girl’s attainment of Buddhahood,
universally teaching Dharma to gods and humans gathered for the occasion.
Their hearts rejoiced greatly,
and they all respectfully paid homage from afar.
Immeasurable beings,
on hearing the Dharma, awakened to understanding
and achieved non-retrogression;
immeasurable beings
received predictions of enlightenment.
The Immaculate World
shook in six ways;
in the Sahā World, three thousand beings abided on the stage of non-retrogression,
and three thousand beings aroused bodhicitta and obtained assurance.
The bodhisattva Zhìjī and *Shèlìfú*,
as well as the entire assembly,
quietly accepted and believed.
At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Yàowáng and the bodhisattva mahāsattva Dàlèshuō,
with their retinues of twenty thousand bodhisattvas,
all before the Buddha, made this vow, saying:
“We earnestly pray that the Bhagavān do not worry.
After the Buddha’s extinction,
we shall uphold, recite, and expound this scripture.
When, in the evil ages to come,
beings have ever fewer roots of goodness,
are increasingly arrogant,
seek gain and offerings,
increase in unwholesome roots,
and distance themselves from liberation.”
Though they are difficult to transform,
we ought to arouse great patience and strength,
recite and study this sūtra,
uphold, explain, and copy it,
making various kinds of offerings,
without sparing even our lives.”
At that time, among the assembly, the five hundred Āluóhàn who had received prediction
spoke to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! We too vow
to widely expound this sūtra in other lands.”
Furthermore, there were eight thousand trainees and adepts who had received prediction,
who rose from their seats,
put their palms together and made this vow to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! We too shall widely expound this sūtra in other lands.
And why is this?
In the land of Shāpo,
people are full of faults and evil,
harboring excessive pride,
with shallow merit, anger, defilement, flattery, and crookedness,
because their minds are not sincere.”
Then the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Móhē Bōjiāpótí Bhikṣuṇī,
together with six thousand trainee and adept bhikṣuṇīs,
rose from their seats,
single-mindedly joined their palms,
looked up at the honored countenance,
and did not avert their gaze even for a moment.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Jiāotánmí:
“Why do you look at the Tathāgata with a worried expression?
Are you thinking in your heart that I do not mention your name,
and have not given you the prediction of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Jiāotánmí! Earlier, I gave a general prediction to all the śrāvakas,
if now you wish to know specifically,
in the future
amongst the teachings of sixty-eight thousand billion Buddhas you shall be a great Dharma teacher,
and together with six thousand trainee and adept bhikṣuṇīs, all will be Dharma teachers.
In this way you shall gradually fulfill the bodhisattva path,
and will become a Buddha,
with the name ‘All Sentient Beings Joyous-to-Behold Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Complete in Knowledge and Conduct,
Well Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.’
Jiāotánmí! This ‘All Sentient Beings Joyous-to-Behold’ Buddha and the six thousand bodhisattvas
will, in turn, receive the prediction of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, Rāhula’s mother, Yéshūtuóluó Bhikṣuṇī, thought to herself:
“Among those who have received prediction, the World-Honored One alone does not mention my name.”
The Buddha said to Yéshūtuóluó:
“In future worlds, among the Dharma of hundred thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, you shall cultivate the bodhisattva path,
be a great Dharma teacher,
and gradually complete the Buddha path.
In the realm of Shànguó you will become a Buddha,
named ‘Perfectly Endowed with Myriad Radiant Marks Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings,
Perfectly Enlightened, Complete in Knowledge and Conduct, Well Gone,
Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.’
The Buddha’s lifespan will be immeasurable asamkhyeya kalpas.”
At that time, Móhē Bōjiāpótí Bhikṣuṇī and Yéshūtuóluó Bhikṣuṇī,
together with their families and followers, were all greatly joyful,
obtaining what they had never before attained.
Immediately in front of the Buddha they spoke in verse:
“World-Honored One, guiding teacher,
peace and comfort to gods and humans,
we, hearing our predictions,
feel assured and fully content.”
When the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken this verse,
they said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! We too are able to widely propagate this sūtra in other lands.”
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed at the eighty thousand billion nayuta great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
All these bodhisattvas—who were abhirati-avīvarthaka,
turning the wheel of the unregressing Dharma,
and had attained all dhāraṇīs—
rose from their seats,
came before the Buddha,
joined their palms single-mindedly,
and thought to themselves:
“If the World-Honored One instructs us to uphold and expound this sūtra,
we shall, according to the Buddha’s teaching,
widely proclaim this Dharma.”
Again, they thought:
“Now the Buddha remains silent;
he does not issue the instruction;
what should we do?”
Then these bodhisattvas, reverently complying with the Buddha’s intent,
and desiring self-fulfillment of their original vows,
in front of the Buddha let out a lion’s roar and made a vow, saying:
“World-Honored One!
After the Tathāgata's extinction,
we will travel to and fro throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
enabling sentient beings to copy this sūtra, accept, uphold, recite,
and explain its meaning,
practice it as prescribed,
and maintain correct mindfulness;
all of this is due to the Buddha’s power.
We only wish that the World-Honored One,
from afar in other places, will watch over and protect us.”
Immediately all the bodhisattvas together raised their voices and spoke in verse:
“We only wish that there be no anxiety,
for after the Buddha’s extinction,
amidst the fearful, evil world,
we shall widely expound.
There will be ignorant people,
who will revile and curse us with harsh words,
or inflict harm with swords and staves;
we shall endure it all.
In the evil world, there will be monks
with perverse wisdom, insincere,
claiming attainment when they have not attained,
filled with arrogance.
Some may dwell in a forest retreat,
wearing robes, sitting in seclusion,
claiming that they practice the true path,
despising people of the world.
Craving for gain and support,
they preach the Dharma to laypeople,
receiving worldly honor and respect,
as if they were an arhat with six supernatural powers.
These people harbor evil motives,
constantly thinking of worldly affairs,
falsely bearing the name of forest-dweller,
delighting in finding fault with us, and saying:
‘These monks, out of craving for gain and support,
preach the doctrines of heretics;
they themselves composed these scriptures,
deceiving the people of the world,
and for the sake of fame
distinguish and comment on this sūtra.’
Always in the midst of great assemblies
they slander us,
before kings and ministers,
Brāhmaṇas and householders,
as well as other assemblies of monks,
speaking ill of us,
calling us people of mistaken views,
and saying we preach heretical doctrines.
Because we venerate the Buddha,
we endure all such evils.
If they speak lightly of us, saying,
‘You are all Buddhas,’
and utter such scornful words,
we shall endure them.
In the corrupt, evil age,
there will be many terrors,
evil spirits possessing people,
reviling and humiliating us.
We, out of veneration and faith in the Buddha,
will wear the armor of forbearance,
and for the sake of preaching this sūtra,
endure all such hardships.
We do not value our bodies and lives,
but only cherish the unsurpassed path.
In the future,
we will protect and uphold what the Buddha entrusted to us;
the World-Honored One himself knows this.
In the corrupt world, evil monks,
not knowing the Buddha’s expedient means,
speak the Dharma as they please,
with harsh words and frowns,
often casting us out,
driving us far from stupas and temples.
All such evils,
because we remember the Buddha’s exhortation,
we will endure.
In all villages and cities,
wherever there are seekers of the Dharma,
we will go to them all,
to teach the Dharma entrusted by the Buddha.
We are messengers of the World-Honored One,
and within the assembly have no fear;
we will skillfully expound the Dharma,
wishing the Buddha peaceful abiding.
Before the World-Honored One,
and the Buddhas of the ten directions who have come,
we thus make our vow;
the Buddha himself knows our hearts.”
Scroll Four of the *Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sūtra*
Scroll Five of the *Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sūtra*
Translated on imperial command by Tripiṭaka Dharma Master
Jiūmóluóshí of the country of Kucha in Later Qin
At that time,
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Wénshūshīlì, Prince of the Dharma, spoke to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
These bodhisattvas are truly rare,
because of their reverence for the Buddha
making great vows,
in the future evil world
upholding, reading, and preaching this Lotus Sūtra.
World-Honored One!
How can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva in the future evil world expound this sūtra?”
The Buddha said to Wénshū Shīlì:
“If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva
wishes to expound this sūtra in the evil world to come,
he should abide by four practices.
First, he should abide in the places of the Bodhisattva’s practice and the places for close association.
Thus he is able to expound this sūtra for sentient beings.
Wénshū Shīlì,
what is called the place of practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides on the ground of patience,
gentle, harmonious, free of sudden rage,
his mind never shaken;
further, with respect to the Dharma, engages in nothing,
but contemplates all dharmas according to their true aspect;
he neither acts nor discriminates,
this is called the place of practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
What is called the place for close association of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not associate closely with kings, princes, great ministers, or government officials;
he does not associate closely with various non-Buddhists, brāhmaṇas, Nirgrantha and the like,
N. irgrantha;
nor with composers of secular literature and those who praise and recite non-Buddhist texts,
nor with Lokāyata and counter-Lokāyata adherents;
he also does not associate with those who perform violent games,
wrestling or sumō,
nor with various trick performances such as those by nāgas and the like;
furthermore, he does not associate with chāṇḍālas,
nor with those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, dogs,
or who hunt, fish, or engage in other evil practices.
For people such as these, should they sometimes come,
he will expound the Dharma to them,
harboring no expectations.
He also does not associate with seekers of the Śrāvaka path: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās;
nor does he make inquiries of them.
Whether in a room,
whether in a place for walking meditation,
or whether in a lecture hall,
he does not dwell together with them.
If by chance they come,
he expounds the Dharma as appropriate
without any expectations.
Wénshū Shīlì,
furthermore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva ought not, regarding the female form,
to dwell on features that arouse lustful thoughts while expounding the Dharma, nor should he delight in seeing them.
If he enters another’s house, he should not speak with young girls, maidens, or widows.
He also should not form close relationships with the five types of impotent men,
nor enter another’s house alone.
If by circumstance it becomes necessary to enter alone,
he should focus single-mindedly on recollecting the Buddha.
If expounding Dharma for women,
he should not bare his teeth in a smile,
nor expose his chest,
not even in Dharma matters should there be intimacy,
much less in other affairs.
He does not delight in keeping young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or boys,
nor does he delight in associating with co-disciples.
He constantly enjoys seated meditation,
dwelling in quiet places,
cultivating and restraining his mind.
Wénshū Shīlì,
this is called the first place for close association.”
“Next, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty,
in accordance with their true aspect,
being neither inverted, nor moved, nor retrogressive, nor turned back,
like empty space, with no inherent existence.
All routes of language are cut off;
no birth, no coming forth, no arising;
without names, without features, truly empty;
measureless, boundless, without hindrance or obstruction;
existing only on account of conditions;
they are spoken of as arising from inverted views.
Constantly delighting in contemplating such dharma aspects,
this is called the second place for close association of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.”
At that time, the Bhagavān, wishing to
reaffirm this meaning, spoke these verses:
“If there is a Bodhisattva,
in the evil world to come,
with a fearless mind,
who wishes to expound this sūtra,
he should enter the place of practice,
and the place of close association.
Always distancing himself from kings,
and princes,
great ministers and officials,
those who revel in violence,
chāṇḍālas,
non-Buddhists and brāhmaṇas.
He also should not associate closely
with arrogant people,
those attached to the Hīnayāna,
students of the Tripiṭaka,
precept-breaking monks,
so-called arhats,
and bhikṣuṇīs who love frivolity and laughter,
those deeply attached to the five desires,
seekers of present cessation,
or upāsikās—
none should he closely associate with.
If such people
come with good intent
to the Bodhisattva’s place
to hear the Buddha’s path,
the Bodhisattva, with
a fearless mind,
without expectation,
will expound the Dharma for them.
Widows, maidens,
and those who are impotent—
none should he closely associate with,
forming close relationships.
Nor should he associate closely
with butchers, those who dismember,
hunters or fishermen,
those who kill for profit,
those who live by selling meat,
those who trade in female beauty;
with such people,
he should not associate closely.
Violent wrestling,
various playful amusements,
courtesans and the like,
never associate closely with them.
He should not, alone in a secluded place,
expound Dharma for women,
and if he does so,
he must not smile playfully.
When entering a village to beg for food,
he should bring a fellow bhikṣu,
and if there is none,
he should focus solely on recollecting the Buddha.
These are called
the place of practice and the place of close association.
With these two,
he can expound in peace.
Moreover, he does not perceive
higher, middle, or lower dharmas,
conditioned or unconditioned,
real or unreal dharmas;
nor does he discriminate
as to male or female.
He does not obtain any dharma,
does not know or see them;
this is then called
the Bodhisattva’s place of practice.
All dharmas,
are empty and without substance,
not permanently abiding,
without arising or ceasing;
this is called the place
where the wise draw near.
To distinguish in a deluded way,
the existence or nonexistence of dharmas,
their reality or unreality,
arising or non-arising—
in a quiet place,
he cultivates and restrains his mind,
abides unmoved,
like Mount Sumeru.
Contemplating all dharmas
as empty,
like empty space,
lacking solidity.
Not arising or coming forth,
not moving or retreating,
always abiding in sameness;
this is called the place of close association.
If there is a bhikṣu who, after my parinirvāṇa,
enters this place of practice and close association,
when expounding this sūtra,
he will have no fear or weakness.
Sometimes the Bodhisattva
enters a quiet room,
with right mindfulness,
contemplates the dharma according to meaning;
arising from meditation,
for kings,
princes, ministers and people,
brāhmaṇas and others,
he teaches and expounds,
preaching this scripture,
his mind at peace,
without fear or weakness.
Wénshū Shīlì,
this is what is called a Bodhisattva
abiding in the first Dharma,
able in the future age
to expound the Lotus Sūtra.
“Moreover, Wénshū Shīlì,
after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
in the final Dharma age, if one wishes to expound this sūtra,
he should abide in the practice of peaceful dwelling.
Whether teaching by mouth or when reciting the sūtra,
he should not delight in speaking of the faults of others or of other scriptures.
Nor should he disparage other Dharma teachers,
nor speak of others’ good or bad points, strengths or weaknesses.
With respect to those of the Śrāvaka path,
he also neither names them to speak of their faults,
nor does he name them to praise their virtues,
nor does he give rise to a mind of resentment or dislike.
Because he well cultivates such a peaceful and happy mind,
all who hear him do not oppose his intent;
if there are difficult questions,
he does not answer with Hīnayāna teachings,
but only explains them through the Mahāyāna,
enabling them to obtain the wisdom of all modes."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse, saying:
"The Bodhisattva always delights
in peacefully and gently expounding the Dharma;
in a pure place,
he provides beds and seats.
He anoints his body with oil,
bathes away dust and defilement,
puts on new clean robes,
is pure both within and without,
calmly takes his place on the Dharma seat,
and answers according to the questions asked.
If there are bhikṣus,
as well as bhikṣuṇīs,
upāsakas,
and upāsikās,
kings and princes,
ministers, knights, and laypeople,
he explains with subtle and marvelous meanings and with a gentle demeanor.
If there are difficult questions,
he answers them according to their meaning,
using causes, conditions, and analogies
to clarify and distinguish in detail.
With such skillful means,
he causes all to generate the bodhi mind,
gradually increasing and benefiting,
and entering the Buddha path.
He removes thoughts of laziness,
and imaginings of laxity,
and separates from all worries and afflictions,
speaking the Dharma with a mind of compassion.
Day and night he constantly expounds
the unsurpassed teaching of the Path,
using various causes and conditions,
innumerable analogies,
to reveal and show to sentient beings,
causing all to become joyful.
Whether clothing, beds,
food, drink, or medicine,
among these
he expects nothing.
He has but one thought in mind:
for the sake of Dharma expounding and its causes
aspiring to accomplish the Buddha path,
and wishing that all sentient beings do likewise.
This is a vast benefit,
an offering of peace and joy.
After my extinction,
if there are bhikṣus
who can expound this
marvelous *Fǎhuá jīng*,
their minds free of jealousy and anger,
free from all afflictions and obstructions,
also without sorrow,
nor abusive language and insults,
and no fear at all,
nor threats of blades or staves,
nor expulsion;
they dwell in patience.
The wise, in this way, well cultivate their minds,
and can abide in ease and joy
as I have spoken above.
The merit of such a person,
for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, by calculation and analogy,
cannot be exhaustively described.
"Moreover, Mañjuśrī,
Bodhisattva Mahāsattva! In the latter age, when the true Dharma is about to perish,
those who uphold, recite, and read this sūtra,
should not harbor a mind of envy, flattery, or deception,
nor belittle or revile learners of the Buddha path, seeking their faults and shortcomings.
Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, seekers of the Śrāvaka path,
seekers of the Pratyekabuddha path, or seekers of the Bodhisattva path,
one should not trouble them, causing them to doubt and regret.
Nor should one say to them,
'You are far from the Path;
you will never attain the wisdom of all modes.
Why is this so?
You are people of negligence, lax in the Path.'
Nor should one engage in idle debates about the Dharma
or contentious disputes.
One should give rise to great compassion towards all beings,
regard all Tathāgatas as compassionate fathers,
regard all Bodhisattvas as great teachers,
and towards the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions,
always deeply and reverently pay homage.
To all sentient beings,
one expounds the Dharma equally,
in harmony with the Dharma,
not more, not less,
even to those who deeply love the Dharma, one does not expound excessively."
"Mañjuśrī!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in the latter age, when the true Dharma is about to perish,
who accomplishes this third practice of ease and joy,
when expounding this Dharma,
no one can trouble or disturb him;
he obtains good companions who recite and read the sūtra together,
and also draws great assemblies to come and listen and receive it.
Having heard, they uphold it;
having upheld it, they recite it;
having recited it, they expound it;
having expounded it, they write it,
or have others write it,
offering the scripture rolls with
respect, honor, and praise."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse, saying:
"If one wishes to expound this sūtra,
one must put aside jealousy, anger, and arrogance,
a mind of flattery, deception, or hypocrisy,
and always cultivate straightforward conduct.
Do not belittle or disparage others,
nor debate the Dharma frivolously;
do not cause others to doubt and regret,
saying, 'You shall not attain Buddhahood.'
This son of the Buddha, expounding the Dharma,
is always gentle, harmonious, and patient,
compassionate toward all,
never giving rise to a mind of laziness.
The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions,
practicing the path for the sake of sentient beings,
should give rise to a mind of reverence;
these are my great teachers.
Towards all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones,
regard them as the supreme father,
eradicate thoughts of arrogance,
and expound the Dharma without obstruction.
Such is the third Dharma;
the wise should uphold it,
single-mindedly practice this conduct of peace and joy,
and be revered by countless assemblies.
"Moreover, Mañjuśrī!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in the latter age, when the true Dharma is about to perish,
who upholds the *Fǎhuá jīng*,
should generate great compassion toward those at home and those who have left home,
and great pity for those who are not Bodhisattvas.
One should make this reflection:
'Such persons are truly losing greatly.
The Tathāgata, by skillful means and in accord with circumstances, expounds the Dharma;
yet they neither hear, know, nor are aware,
they neither ask about, believe in, nor understand it.
Even though these people neither ask about, believe in, nor understand this sūtra,
when I attain Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi,
wherever I may be,
with my power of spiritual penetration and wisdom, I will guide them,
enabling them to abide in this Dharma.'
Mañjuśrī!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, after the extinction of the Tathāgata, who accomplishes this fourth Dharma,
when expounding this Dharma, is without fault;
he is always supported and revered by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
kings, princes, ministers, people,
brāhmaṇas, laymen, and so forth,
and the deities of empty space,
also, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, constantly attend upon him.
Whether in a village, a city, or an empty forest,
if someone comes to ask difficult questions,
the deities, day and night, for the sake of the Dharma, will always guard and protect him,
causing all listeners to attain joy.
Why is this so?
Because this sūtra is always protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Mañjuśrī!
This *Fǎhuá jīng*—
in measureless worlds,
even its name cannot be heard,
much less obtained, upheld, recited, and read."
Mañjuśrī!
It is like a powerful Wheel-Turning Sage King,
wishing by his might and majesty to subdue all countries,
while the minor kings do not obey his orders;
then the Wheel-Turning King raises various armies and goes to punish them.
The king, seeing that among the soldiers and multitudes there are those who perform meritorious deeds in battle,
is greatly delighted,
and following the merit, he rewards them:
he may grant them fields and houses, villages and cities;
or bestow on them clothing and magnificent ornaments;
or give them all kinds of precious treasures:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, carnelian, coral, amber,
elephants, horses, chariots, male and female servants, and people.
Yet the luminous jewel from his topknot he does not give to them.
Why is this so?
Because only the king himself has this one jewel upon his crown;
if he were to give it away,
all his kinsmen and retainers would surely be greatly astonished.
“Wénshū Shīlì!
The Rú lái is also thus:
by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he attains the Dharma land and realm,
becomes king over the Three Realms,
yet the demon kings do not willingly submit.
The Rú lái’s worthy and holy generals battle against them,
and those who perform meritorious deeds,
their hearts are also filled with joy;
among the four assemblies, he expounds various sūtras for them,
to delight their minds,
bestowing upon them meditation, liberation, undefiled root powers, and the treasures of the Dharma,
further granting them the city of Nirvāṇa,
declaring they have attained extinction,
guiding their hearts, causing all to rejoice,
yet not speaking to them of this Dharma Flower Sūtra.
“Wénshū Shīlì!
It is like a wheel-turning king, who, seeing among his troops those with great achievement,
is deeply joyful at heart,
and bestows upon them the rare and hard-to-believe jewel, which has for long been kept in his topknot, never giving it to anyone lightly,
but now he gives it to them.
In the same way, the Rú lái
is the Great King of Dharma in the Three Realms,
using the Dharma to teach and transform all beings.
He sees his worthy and holy army
battling together with the demons of the five aggregates, the demons of afflictions, and the demon of death;
when there are great feats performed,
the three poisons are destroyed,
the Three Realms are left behind,
the net of demons is broken—
then the Rú lái is likewise filled with great joy.
This Dharma Flower Sūtra can enable beings to attain all-knowledge;
yet all the worlds, with their many resentments, find it difficult to believe;
what was not previously spoken is now spoken.
Wénshū Shīlì!
This Dharma Flower Sūtra is the supreme teaching of all Rú láis;
it is the deepest among all their teachings,
and in the end, it is granted,
like the powerful king long protecting the luminous jewel;
now he finally gives it away.
Wénshū Shīlì!
This Dharma Flower Sūtra is the secret treasury of all Buddhas and Rú lái;
it stands foremost among all sūtras,
guarded through the long night and never falsely proclaimed;
only now, today, is it expounded to you and the others.”
Then the Bhagavān, wanting to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
Always practicing patience,
having compassion for all,
only then can one expound
the sūtra praised by Buddhas.
In the later evil ages,
those who uphold this sūtra,
whether householders or those who have left home,
as well as those who are not Bodhisattvas,
should give rise to compassion;
such people do not hear,
do not believe in this sūtra,
thus incur great loss.
I, having attained Buddhahood,
by various expedient means,
teach this Dharma,
causing beings to abide therein.
It is like a mighty
wheel-turning king,
who, when there are military achievements,
rewards and bestows many things:
elephants, horses, chariots,
adornments for the body,
as well as fields and houses,
villages and cities,
sometimes clothing,
various precious treasures,
servants, wealth—joyfully granted.
If anyone is brave and valiant,
capable of difficult deeds,
the king removes from his topknot
the luminous jewel and bestows it upon them.
The Rú lái is the same,
being the Dharma King of all teachings,
with great power of patience,
a treasury of wisdom,
and great compassion,
teaching the world according to Dharma.
Seeing all people,
enduring all sufferings,
seeking liberation,
battling against all demons,
he, for these beings,
teaches various Dharmas,
by great expedient means
expounds these various sūtras.
Having discerned that beings
have gained their strength,
only at the end
does he preach this Dharma Flower.
Like the king removing his topknot,
bestowing the luminous jewel.
This sūtra is supreme,
foremost among all sūtras;
I always guard and protect it,
never freely revealing it;
now is the right time,
and I speak it for you all.
After my extinction,
those who seek the Buddha path,
desiring peace and safety,
and wish to expound this sūtra,
should approach
and rely on these four methods.
Those who read this sūtra
will always be free from worry and suffering;
also free from sickness or pain,
with a bright and radiant appearance,
not subject to poverty,
meanness, or ugliness.
Beings will delight in seeing them,
as if admiring worthies and saints;
the heavenly youths
will serve them.
Knives and cudgels will not assail them,
poison will not harm them,
and if anyone abuses them,
their mouths will be stopped up.
They will travel unafraid,
like a lion king,
their wisdom shining
like the sun’s radiance.
Even in dreams,
they will only see marvelous things:
seeing various Rú láis,
seated on lion thrones,
surrounded by bhikṣu assemblies,
expounding the Dharma.
They will also see dragon deities,
asuras, and others,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
respectfully with joined palms,
and see themselves
expounding the Dharma.
They will also see various Buddhas,
their bodies golden-hued,
emitting immeasurable light,
illuminating everything,
and with Brahma-voices
proclaiming the Dharma.
The Buddhas, for the four assemblies,
teach the unsurpassed Dharma,
they see themselves amid the assembly,
joining their palms, praising the Buddha,
joyfully hearing the teachings,
making offerings,
attaining dhāraṇī,
and realizing non-retrogressive wisdom.
The Buddhas know their minds
have penetrated the Buddha way,
and immediately grant them prediction,
for perfect and supreme awakening:
‘You, good man!
In a future lifetime,
will attain immeasurable wisdom,
the great path of the Buddha.
Your land will be pure and adorned,
vast and unmatched.’
There will also be the four assemblies,
joining their palms to listen to the Dharma.
They will also see themselves
in mountains and forests,
cultivating wholesome practices,
realizing ultimate reality,
profoundly entering meditation,
and viewing the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The Buddhas’ bodies are golden-hued,
adorned by a hundred blessings,
hearing the Dharma, they preach to others,
such fine dreams always occur.
They also dream they become kings,
forsaking palaces and kinsfolk,
along with the five sensual pleasures,
proceeding to the bodhi site.
Beneath the tree of awakening,
they are seated on a lion throne,
seeking the path for seven days,
attaining the wisdom of Buddhas.
Having accomplished supreme enlightenment,
they arise and turn the Dharma wheel,
preaching to the four assemblies,
for a thousand, ten thousand, hundred million kalpas,
they preach the undefiled marvelous Dharma,
and rescue immeasurable beings.
Afterward, they enter Nirvāṇa,
like an extinguished lamp or spent smoke.
If, in a later evil age,
one speaks this supreme Dharma,
that person obtains great benefits,
such as the above merits.
At that time, the many Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who had come from other lands and realms—
their number exceeding the sands of eight Ganges Rivers—
rose in the midst of the great assembly,
joined their palms in reverence, bowed, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Bhagavān!
If you permit us, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
to diligently and zealously protect, recite, transcribe, and make offerings to this scripture in this Saha world,
then we shall widely expound it in this land.”
Then the Buddha said to the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas:
“Stop, good men!
There is no need for you to uphold this scripture.
Why is that?
In my own Saha world there are already sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
and each Bodhisattva has sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges as attendants.
These beings, after my parinirvāṇa, will be able to protect, recite, and widely expound this scripture.”
When the Buddha had spoken these words,
the three thousand great chiliocosms of the Saha world quaked and split apart,
and from within, innumerable tens of thousands of millions of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas leapt forth simultaneously.
All these Bodhisattvas had golden bodies,
the thirty-two marks,
immeasurable radiance,
and had always dwelled beneath this Saha world, in the sky of this realm.
These Bodhisattvas, upon hearing the voice of Śākyamuni Buddha,
emerged from below.
Each Bodhisattva was the foremost leader of an assembly,
each leading sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges in their retinue;
not to mention those leading fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand times the sands of the Ganges;
furthermore, even those with only one Ganges, half a Ganges, a quarter,
or as little as a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or nayuta portion of a Ganges;
not to mention those with a thousand, ten thousand, or nayuta in their retinues;
not to mention those with a hundred million followers;
not to mention those with ten million, one million, or even ten thousand;
not to mention those with one thousand, one hundred, or even ten;
not to mention those with five, four, three, two, or a single disciple;
let alone those who come alone, delighting in solitary practice.
Such as these,
innumerable and boundless, beyond calculation and analogy.
When these Bodhisattvas had arisen from the earth,
each proceeded through the sky to the jeweled, wondrous stūpa of Duōbǎo Tathāgata and to Śākyamuni Buddha.
When they had arrived,
they bowed their heads at the feet of the Two Bhagavāns,
and at the lion throne beneath the jeweled trees where the Buddhas sat, also performed obeisance,
circled three times to the right,
joined their palms reverently,
and praised the Buddha with various methods of Bodhisattva praise,
standing respectfully to one side,
rejoicing and gazing up at the Two Bhagavāns.
These Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, from the very first moment of their appearance,
praised the Buddha with various methods of Bodhisattva praise,
and such a time endured for fifty kalpas of lesser duration.
During this time, Śākyamuni Buddha sat silently,
and the fourfold assembly also remained silent for fifty kalpas of lesser duration;
by the Buddha’s spiritual power,
the great assembly felt as if it were but half a day.
At that time, the fourfold assembly,
also due to the Buddha’s spiritual power,
saw the Bodhisattvas filling the skies of innumerable hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds.
Amongst this assembly of Bodhisattvas were four leaders:
the first was named Shàngxíng,
the second Wúbiānxíng,
the third Jìngxíng,
the fourth Ānlìxíng.
These four Bodhisattvas were the highest and foremost leaders of the assembly,
who, at the front of the gathering,
together joined their palms,
looked upon Śākyamuni Buddha and inquired, saying:
“Bhagavān!
Are you free from illness and distress,
at ease in your conduct?
Of those to be led to liberation, is their reception of your teaching easy?
Does the Bhagavān experience no fatigue?”
Thereupon these four great Bodhisattvas spoke in verse, saying:
“The Bhagavān is at ease,
little illness, little distress,
teaching and transforming living beings,
is free from exhaustion or weariness.
And, as for these living beings,
are they readily receptive to instruction?
Does the Bhagavān
suffer no fatigue?”
At that time the Bhagavān, amidst the great assembly of Bodhisattvas, declared:
“So it is, so it is! Good men!
The Tathāgata is at ease,
with little illness or distress;
living beings are easy to teach and liberate,
and there is no weariness.
Why is this?
Because these beings, from innumerable past lifetimes, have always been guided by me,
have honored and made offerings to past Buddhas,
and planted all kinds of good roots.
When these living beings first behold my body,
they hear what I teach and instantly accept, believe, and enter the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
except those who have previously practiced the śrāvaka path.
As for these individuals, I now also enable them to hear this scripture
and enter into the Buddha’s wisdom.”
At this time the great Bodhisattvas uttered verses, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
The heroic Bhagavān!
All these living beings,
are easily guided and liberated.
Able to inquire of the Buddhas
the most profound wisdom;
having heard, they believe and practice,
we all rejoice in accord.”
At that time, the Bhagavān praised the leading great Bodhisattvas:
“Excellent, excellent!
Good men!
You have been able to give rise to a mind of rejoicing toward the Tathāgata.”
Thereupon Mílè Bodhisattva and the host of Bodhisattvas as numerous as eight thousand times the sands of the Ganges all thought:
“Since the distant past we have never seen or heard of such a multitude of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas springing forth from the earth,
present before the Bhagavān, joining their palms, making offerings,
and inquiring after the Tathāgata.”
Then Mílè Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
knowing the minds of the eight thousand Ganges sands of Bodhisattvas,
and wishing also to resolve his own doubts,
joined his palms toward the Buddha,
and in verse asked:
“Innumerable thousands of millions,
the great assembly of Bodhisattvas,
never before seen in the past,
we pray the Revered of Two Feet will speak,
from whence have they come,
and for what causes and conditions have they gathered?
With great bodies, great transcendental powers,
wisdom inconceivable,
with resolute aspiration,
bearing great patience,
cherished by all beings—
from where have they come?
Each of these Bodhisattvas,
with their multitude of attendants,
their number immeasurable,
like the sands of the Ganges.
Some great Bodhisattvas
lead sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges;
such a great multitude,
with one mind seek the Buddha-way.
These great teachers,
sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges,
all come to make offerings to the Buddha
and to uphold this scripture.
Some lead fifty thousand Ganges-sands—their number even greater than this.
Forty thousand, thirty thousand,
twenty thousand to ten thousand,
one thousand, one hundred, and so on,
even so far as one Ganges-sand,
half, or a third or quarter,
one part in ten million,
a thousand, ten thousand nayutas,
ten thousand billions of disciples,
down to half a hundred million,
their numbers even greater than above.
From a million to ten thousand,
one thousand and one hundred,
fifty or even ten,
even three, two, or one,
coming alone without a retinue,
delighting in solitary seclusion,
all come before the Buddha,
their numbers surpassing what’s already stated.
Such great multitudes—if someone were to count,
even beyond the kalpas of the Ganges sands,
still could not know them all.
These, beings of great power and virtue,
this assembly of zealous Bodhisattvas,
who instructs and preaches to them,
guides and brings them to accomplishment?
From whom did they first give rise to bodhicitta?
Which Buddha’s Dharma do they declare and praise?
Whose scripture do they uphold and practice?
Which Buddha-way do they cultivate?
Such Bodhisattvas as these,
with supernatural powers and great wisdom,
causing the earth in the four directions to quake and split,
all burst forth from within.
Bhagavān, from the past until now,
never have I seen such a thing;
I pray you will tell the source
and the names of their lands and realms.
I have always wandered in many lands,
but never have seen this assembly;
among all these beings
there is not one that I recognize;
suddenly they have sprung from the earth;
I pray you will declare their causes and conditions.
Now, in this great assembly,
countless hundreds of thousands of millions,
all these Bodhisattvas
desire to know of this matter.
This assembly of Bodhisattvas—the causal origins and outcome,
Bhagavān of immeasurable virtue,
we entreat you alone to resolve the doubts of the assembly.”
At that time, the emanated Buddhas of Shìjiāmóuní,
coming from immeasurable trillions of other lands,
sat cross-legged beneath the various jeweled trees in the eight directions, atop lion thrones.
The attendants of these Buddhas each beheld that great multitude of Bodhisattvas,
who, from the four quarters of the three-thousand-great-thousand worlds, sprang forth from the earth
and dwelled in empty space.
Each addressed their Buddha, saying:
“World-honored One!
From whence have come this countless, boundless, asaṃkhyeya multitude of Bodhisattvas?”
Then the Buddhas each told their attendants:
“Good men! Wait a moment;
there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Mílè—
to whom Shìjiāmóuní Buddha has given a prophecy,
who shall be the next to become a Buddha—
he will ask about this matter;
the Buddha will now answer him;
you all shall naturally hear by virtue of this.”
At that time, Shìjiāmóuní Buddha addressed Mílè Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent!
Āyìduō! You are able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter.
You all should focus your minds as one,
don the armor of diligence,
arouse a resolute mind.
The Tathāgata now wishes to manifest and declare the wisdom of the Buddhas,
the freedom and supernatural power of the Buddhas,
the lion-like energetic strength of the Buddhas,
the awe-inspiring might of the Buddhas.”
At that time, the World-honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke in verse:
“You must be diligent and single-minded;
I wish to speak of this matter.
Do not harbor doubt or regret;
the Buddha’s wisdom is unfathomable.
Now arouse the power of faith,
dwell in patience and goodness;
the Dharma you have not heard before,
now you will all hear.
I now reassure you;
do not harbor suspicion or fear;
the Buddha never speaks falsely;
his wisdom is beyond measure.
The supreme Dharma attained
is so deep as to be inconceivable.
Thus I shall now speak;
all of you, listen single-mindedly.”
When the World-honored One had spoken this verse,
he addressed Mílè Bodhisattva:
“Now in this great assembly, I declare to you all. Āyìduō!
These great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
innumerable and countless asaṃkhyeyas, have sprung forth from the earth,
such as you have not seen before.
After I attained anuttarā samyak-saṃbodhi in this Sàpó world,
I taught, transformed, and directed these Bodhisattvas,
tamed their minds,
and inspired them to arouse the resolve for the path.
These Bodhisattvas all dwell beneath this Sàpó world, in the space of this realm;
in the various scriptures, they read, recite, and skillfully comprehend;
they contemplate, discern, and rightly recall.
Āyìduō! These good men do not relish speaking much in crowds;
they always delight in quiet places,
diligently practicing without ever ceasing;
nor do they depend on humans or devas for support.
They always rejoice in profound wisdom without obstruction,
and constantly delight in the Dharma of the Buddhas, single-mindedly diligent, seeking unsurpassed wisdom.”
At that time, the World-honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke in verse:
“Āyì, you should know!
These great Bodhisattvas,
from countless eons past,
have cultivated the Buddha’s wisdom;
they are all my transformational disciples,
whom I have inspired to arouse the great resolve for the path.
These are my children,
who abide in this world,
always practicing ascetic deeds,
intent on and delighting in solitude,
leaving behind the noisy multitude,
not delighting in much speech.
Such are my children,
studying my Dharma-path,
ever diligent day and night,
for the sake of seeking Buddhahood,
dwelling in the Sàpó world,
in the space below.
Their mindfulness and power are firm,
always diligently seeking wisdom,
preaching various wondrous Dharmas,
without any fear in their hearts.
In the city of Jiāyé,
seated beneath the Bodhi tree,
I attained supreme perfect enlightenment,
and turned the unsurpassed Dharma wheel.
Then I taught and transformed them,
causing them first to arouse the mind for the path;
now they all abide without regressing,
and they will all surely attain Buddhahood.
Now I speak truthfully:
you all must believe with single mind;
from long ages past,
I have taught and transformed these beings.”
At that time, Mílè Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and countless Bodhisattvas
gave rise to doubts and perplexity,
finding it unprecedented and thinking thus:
“How has the World-honored One, in such a short time, taught and transformed these countless, boundless, asaṃkhyeya great Bodhisattvas,
enabling them to abide in anuttarā samyak-saṃbodhi?”
They immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-honored One!
When the Tathāgata was still a prince,
he departed from the Śākya palace,
and not far from Jiāyé city, sitting at the place of enlightenment,
he attained anuttarā samyak-saṃbodhi.
Since then, only a little more than forty years have passed.
World-honored One!
How, in such a short time, can one have performed such great works of the Buddha,
through the Buddha’s power, through the Buddha’s merits,
and taught, transformed, and led such an innumerable assembly of great Bodhisattvas,
who are to attain anuttarā samyak-saṃbodhi?
World-honored One! This assembly of great Bodhisattvas,
even if someone were to count for trillions of eons, could not exhaust their number, nor reach their limit.
These have, from remote ages past,
under innumerable, boundless Buddhas,
planted all good roots,
perfected the Bodhisattva path,
and constantly cultivated pure conduct.
World-honored One! Such a matter is hard to believe in the world.
It is like someone who, handsome and black-haired, at the age of twenty-five,
points to a hundred-year-old person and says:
‘This is my son.’
The hundred-year-old also points to the youth and says:
‘This is my father, who begot us.’
Such a thing is hard to believe.
So it is with the Buddha:
since attaining the Way, actually not long ago,
yet this great multitude of Bodhisattvas
has, for countless trillions of eons,
for the sake of Buddhahood, diligently practiced,
skillfully entering and dwelling in countless hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis,
attained great supernatural powers,
long cultivated pure conduct,
skillfully trained in order in all good Dharmas,
adept at questions and answers,
the jewels among humans,
extremely rare in all the world.
Now today, the World-honored One says:
‘When I attained Buddhahood,
I first inspired them to arouse the mind,
taught, transformed, and directed them,
leading them toward anuttarā samyak-saṃbodhi.’
The World-honored One has attained Buddhahood but recently
and yet can perform such great meritorious deeds.
Though we indeed believe that the Buddha speaks as appropriate,
never has the Buddha’s word been false,
the Buddha’s knowledge is thoroughly pervasive.
Yet, Bodhisattvas newly resolved, after the Buddha’s extinction, if they hear these words,
may not believe or accept them,
but instead give rise to the cause and conditions for the offense of destroying the Dharma.
Indeed, World-honored One!
We pray you will explain and remove our doubts,
and so that in future generations, when good men hear of this,
they too will not have doubts.”
At that time, Mílè Bodhisattva wished to restate this meaning
and spoke in verse:
“The Buddha long ago, born of the Śākya lineage,
left home near Jiāyé,
sat beneath the Bodhi tree,
since then not much time has passed.
These Buddha-children,
their number beyond reckoning,
have long practiced the Buddha-path,
abiding in supernatural powers,
well-learned in the Bodhisattva way,
unstained by worldly Dharmas,
like a lotus in water,
spring forth from the earth.
All arise with hearts of reverence,
abiding before the World-honored One.
This matter is difficult to conceive;
how can it be believed?
The Buddha attained the Way quite recently,
yet he has accomplished so much.
We pray you will dispel the doubts of the assembly,
and explain truly and distinctly.
It is like a young man,
aged just twenty-five,
pointing to a hundred-year-old son,
with white hair and wrinkled face,
and claiming: These are my children;
the son also says: this is my father.
The father is young, yet the son is old—
such a thing is never believed by the world.”
The World-Honored One is just so,
having attained enlightenment not long ago.
These many Bodhisattvas,
their resolve is steadfast and without cowardice,
have, from innumerable kalpas past,
practiced the Bodhisattva path,
skilled in answering difficult questions,
their minds free from fear,
with a mind firmly set on patience,
upright and possessing great majesty and virtue,
praised by Buddhas in the ten directions.
They are well able to explain and distinguish teachings,
not delighting in crowds,
always preferring meditation,
seeking the Buddha-path,
dwelling suspended in empty space below.
We have heard from the Buddha,
and have no doubt about this matter.
We wish that the Buddha, for the sake of the future,
may expound and cause us to understand.
Should there be anyone who,
regarding this sūtra,
harbors doubt or disbelief,
he will surely fall into the evil realms.
We now wish for an explanation,
of how these innumerable Bodhisattvas,
in such a short time,
were guided to arouse the aspiration
and abide in the non-retreating ground?”
