Then the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattvas and the great assembly:
“Good sons! You must trust and understand the truthful words of the Tathāgata.”
He again addressed the assembly:
“You must trust and understand the truthful words of the Tathāgata.”
Yet again, he addressed the great assembly:
“You must trust and understand the truthful words of the Tathāgata.”
At that time, the multitude of Bodhisattvas, with Mílè at their head,
joined their palms and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! We beg that you speak it,
and we shall trust and receive the words of the Buddha.”
In this way, after repeating their plea three times, they again said:
“We beg that you speak it; we shall trust and receive the words of the Buddha.”
Then the World-Honored One, knowing the Bodhisattvas had urged him three times without ceasing, addressed them:
“You must listen carefully to the secret, supernal powers of the Tathāgata.
All the heavenly beings and humans, as well as Asuras in the world, all say:
‘Now, Shìjiāmóuní Buddha, after leaving the Śākya prince’s palace,
not far from the city of Jiāyé, sat at the place of enlightenment
and attained Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.’
However, good sons!
In truth, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been countless, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of nayutas of kalpas.
Suppose five hundred thousand myriads of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya trichiliocosms were ground to dust,
and passing eastward over five hundred thousand myriads of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya countries you drop a speck of dust,
and proceed east in this way, dropping all the dust;
good sons, what do you think?
Can the number of those worlds be conceived or calculated?”
Mílè Bodhisattva and the assembly all said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! Those worlds are innumerable and boundless;
no calculation can know them,
nor can mental power reach them.
Even all the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, with faultless wisdom,
cannot conceive or know their limits.
Though we abide in the Avīvara ground,
we too cannot fathom such a thing.
World-Honored One! Such worlds are innumerable and boundless.”
Then the Buddha told the great Bodhisattva assembly:
“Good sons!
Now I will clearly declare this to you:
Take all the worlds mentioned, both with dust and without, and form them all into dust;
assign one kalpa to each particle.
The time since I achieved Buddhahood
exceeds even this by hundreds of thousands of myriads of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Since then,
I have constantly been in this Sahā world teaching the Dharma and guiding beings,
and in hundreds of thousands of myriads of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya countries elsewhere, also leading and benefiting sentient beings.
Good sons!
During this time, I spoke of Rándēng Buddha and others,
and I spoke of their entry into Nirvāṇa;
all this was by skillful means and suitable explanations.
Good sons!
If any beings come to me,
with the Buddha-eye I observe whether their faculties are keen or dull, whether they have faith,
and teach and convert them as they can be saved,
manifesting myself wherever needed, under various names, of various ages,
and also speak of entering Nirvāṇa,
as well as teaching the subtle Dharma by many skillful means.
I can cause beings to give rise to joyful hearts.
Good sons!
The Tathāgata sees that there are sentient beings who delight in lesser doctrines, whose virtue is slight and obstructions heavy;
for such people I say: ‘I left home not long ago, and attained Anuttarā Samyaksaṃbodhi.’
But in reality, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been unimaginably long;
it is only with skillful means that I teach and convert beings,
to bring them into the Buddha-path,
so I speak in this way.
Good sons!
All the scriptures taught by the Tathāgata
are for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
sometimes referring to myself,
sometimes referring to others,
sometimes manifesting myself,
sometimes manifesting others,
sometimes speaking of my own experiences,
sometimes speaking of others’,
and in all that is said, all is true and not false.
Why is this?
The Tathāgata knows and sees, as they really are, the characteristics of the three realms:
there is no birth or death, no retreating or emerging,
neither abiding in the world nor entering extinction,
not real nor unreal,
not the same nor different;
not seeing the three realms as the three realms.
Such matters the Tathāgata sees clearly, with no error.
Because all sentient beings have various natures, various desires, various actions,
and various thoughts and discriminations,
wanting them to give rise to good roots,
he teaches the Dharma by various causes and conditions, analogies, and terms.
His work as a Buddha
has never, for a moment, been neglected.
Thus,
since I attained Buddhahood,
an exceedingly great and long time has passed;
my lifespan is measureless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
perpetually abiding, never perishing.
Good sons!
The lifespan I completed in my former Bodhisattva practice is not yet exhausted,
nor is the measure of it twice told.
Yet even now, it is not that I truly enter extinction,
but I announce: ‘I am about to enter Nirvāṇa.’
The Tathāgata, by such skillful means, teaches and converts beings.
Why is this?
If a Buddha were to dwell long in the world,
people of shallow virtue would not plant wholesome roots,
being poor, lowly,
greedy for and attached to the five desires,
caught in the net of recollection and false views.
If they saw that the Tathāgata was always present and never perished,
they would become proud and arrogant, and take things lightly,
unable to give rise to thoughts of rarity or a heart of reverence.
Therefore, the Tathāgata teaches through skillful means:
‘Bhikṣus, you should know that it is difficult for Buddhas to appear in the world.’
Why is this?
Because those of shallow virtue may pass through countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, and yet not see a Buddha;
or they might see, or might not see.
Thus, because of this, I say:
‘Bhikṣus, it is difficult to see the Tathāgata.’
Hearing such words,
these sentient beings must give rise to thoughts of rarity;
their hearts will cherish yearning,
admiring and thirsting for the Buddha,
thereby planting wholesome roots.
That is why, even though the Tathāgata does not truly enter extinction,
still he says he enters Nirvāṇa.
Again, good sons!
All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, their Dharma is just so,
in order to deliver sentient beings, and are truly not false.
Suppose there is a good physician,
wise and intelligent,
well-versed in prescriptions and medicines,
skilled in treating all diseases.
He has many sons—ten,
twenty, even a hundred or more.
Because of business, he travels to another country far away.
While he is gone, his sons drink poison,
and the poison takes effect and causes them confusion;
they fall down and roll on the ground.
At this time, their father returns home;
the sons have drunk poison,
some lose their right minds,
some do not,
and from afar, seeing their father,
they are all greatly delighted, bow down, and make inquiries:
‘Welcome home in safety.
We have been foolish and ignorant, and by mistake have taken poison.
We beg you to heal and save us, and grant us long life.’
The father, seeing his children’s distress,
according to all the medical texts,
searches for fine herbs,
whose color, fragrance, and taste are all complete,
grinds, sifts, and mixes them
and gives them to his sons to take,
saying:
‘This is a great, beneficial medicine;
its color, fragrance, and taste are all perfect.
You should take it; it will quickly remove your distress, and you will have no further troubles.’
Among the sons, those not out of their minds, seeing the excellent medicine, its color and fragrance both good,
immediately take it,
and all their illnesses are healed.
Those who have lost their minds, though they see their father come and are also joyful and make inquiries,
ask for healing,
but even when given the medicine, are unwilling to take it.
Why is this?
The father had this thought:
"This child is to be pitied,
for he has been poisoned
and his mind is completely confused.
Though he is glad to see me and seeks help and treatment,
though the medicine is good, he refuses to take it.
Now I must use skillful means to make him take this medicine."
Then he spoke, saying:
"You should know! I am now old and weak,
and my death has come.
Here is this fine medicine, now left here;
you may take it—do not worry you will not recover."
Having thus instructed them,
he went to another country and sent a messenger back to tell them:
"Your father has died."
At this time, when the sons heard their father had abandoned them in death,
they became greatly sorrowful and thought:
"If our father were here, out of his compassion for us,
he could see and protect us,
but now he has left us and died far off in another country."
Each considered himself orphaned and exposed, with nothing more to rely on,
always filled with grief and emotion.
Then their minds awakened,
and they came to know that the color and flavor of this medicine were fragrant and good,
whereupon they took it and drank it,
and all their poisoning and sickness were healed.
When the father heard that his sons were all recovered,
he immediately returned home
and had them all see him.
"Good men!
What do you think?
Is there anyone who could say this skilled physician was guilty of falsehood?"
"No, World-honored One!"
The Buddha said: "So it is with me.
Since becoming a Buddha, through immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of millions of nayuta asamkhyeya kalpas,
for the sake of sentient beings,
by the power of skillful means, I have said that I will be extinguished,
yet no one is able to, according to Dharma, speak of my faults as falsehood."
Then the World-honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse, saying:
"Since I attained Buddhahood,
the countless kalpas that have passed
are measureless hundreds of thousands of millions,
kalpas as many as the grains of the Ganges.
I have constantly expounded Dharma, teaching and transforming,
to an innumerable multitude of billions
enabling all to enter the Buddha Way.
From then until now, throughout incalculable kalpas,
for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
I, with skillful means, appear to enter nirvāṇa,
and yet in truth do not pass away,
but always abide here, teaching Dharma.
I always abide here,
and with the power of various supernormal abilities
cause deluded sentient beings,
though near, not to see me.
When the multitude see my extinction,
they make widespread offerings and worship my relics,
all cherishing longing and yearning,
their hearts arising in thirst and admiration.
When beings have become faithful and receptive,
pure and gentle in intent,
single-mindedly seeking to see the Buddha,
not sparing even their lives,
then I, together with the Saṅgha,
appear together on Gridhrakūṭa,
and at that time I tell them:
'I am always here, never extinct.
It is only by the power of skillful means
that I show extinction and non-extinction.'
In other lands there are sentient beings
who are respectful, believing and delighting;
I likewise am among them,
teaching them the unsurpassed Dharma.
You do not hear this,
but only think I have entered extinction.
I see all sentient beings
submerged in suffering and trouble,
so I do not manifest my body,
causing them to develop longing,
and, as their minds are filled with yearning,
I then emerge and teach the Dharma.
Such is the power of my supernormal abilities;
through innumerable kalpas,
I am always on Gridhrakūṭa
and in other places of dwelling.
When beings think the kalpa is ending,
and a great fire consumes the world,
my land is then safe and secure,
always filled with gods and humans.
Gardens and groves, pavilions and towers,
all adorned with various jewels,
jewel-trees with profuse blossoms and fruit,
where beings take their pleasure and delight.
All the gods beat heavenly drums,
constantly producing all kinds of music,
and rain down māndārava flowers,
scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
My pure land is not destroyed,
but beings perceive it as being consumed,
and, full of grief and fear,
such suffering and distress abound.
All such sinful sentient beings,
because of the causes and conditions of evil karma,
pass countless kalpas
without ever hearing the name of the Three Jewels.
For all who practice virtue,
who are gentle and upright,
they all see my body
here, teaching the Dharma.
At times, before this assembly,
I speak of the Buddha’s lifespan as immeasurable;
to those who see the Buddha after a long time,
I speak of the Buddha being difficult to encounter.
My wisdom and power are thus,
radiant with limitless wisdom,
a lifespan of numberless kalpas,
attained through long cultivation.
All you of wisdom,
do not harbor doubts in this,
but should cut them off and end them forever,
for the Buddha’s words are true, never false.
Just like a good physician who,
for the sake of curing his delirious sons,
is actually alive but says he is dead—
none can call these words a lie.
I too am the father of the world,
saving all those suffering and afflicted;
for those deluded and ordinary,
though actually abiding, I speak of extinction.
Because they always see me,
they develop arrogance and self-indulgence,
abandon themselves to the five desires,
and fall into evil destinies.
I always know of sentient beings,
those who follow the Path, those who do not follow the Path,
and according to who can be saved,
I teach them various dharmas.
I always consider,
by what means might sentient beings
attain the unsurpassed wisdom
and quickly accomplish Buddhahood.
At that time, the great assembly, hearing the Buddha speak of his lifespan being so long through many kalpas,
innumerable, limitless, asamkhyeya sentient beings attained great benefit.
Then the World-honored One said to Mílè Púsà Móhēsà:
"Āyìduō!
When I preach of the Thus Come One’s lifespan being long,
six hundred and eighty million nayuta Ganges-sands of sentient beings
attain the forbearance of the unproduced dharmas.
There are a thousand times as many Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
who attain the dhāraṇī of retention.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of one world, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
attain the unhindered eloquence of joyful speech.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of one world, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
attain innumerable hundreds of thousands of millions of revolving dhāraṇīs.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of three thousand great thousand worlds, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
become able to turn the wheel of the non-retreating Dharma.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of two thousand middle-sized lands, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
become able to turn the wheel of the pure Dharma.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of small thousand lands, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
will attain Anuttara Samyaksaṃbodhi in eight lifetimes.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of four continents, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
will attain Anuttara Samyaksaṃbodhi in four lifetimes.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of three continents, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
will attain Anuttara Samyaksaṃbodhi in three lifetimes.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of two continents, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
will attain Anuttara Samyaksaṃbodhi in two lifetimes.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of one continent, Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas
will attain Anuttara Samyaksaṃbodhi in one lifetime.
Again, as many as the dust-motes of eight worlds, all sentient beings give rise to the mind of Anuttara Samyaksaṃbodhi."
When the Buddha spoke of these Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas attaining great benefit in Dharma,
in the sky, there rained down māndārava and great māndārava flowers,
scattering below the countless billion-jeweled trees and lion seats of each Buddha,
and upon the lion seats in the seven-jewel stūpas, over Shìjiāmóuní Buddha and Duōbǎo Tathāgata long passed into extinction,
and also scattered over all the great Bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
Again, there rained fine powdered chandana and aloeswood and such scents.
In the air, divine drums sounded by themselves,
producing wondrous, deep, far-reaching music.
Again, a thousand kinds of heavenly garments rained down,
streaming with various necklaces, pearl necklaces, maṇi jewel necklaces, and as-you-will jewel necklaces,
pervading the nine directions.
Censers of precious fragrance burned priceless incense,
naturally wafting everywhere, as offerings to the great assembly.
Upon each Buddha, there were Bodhisattvas, upholding banners and canopies,
rising in order up to the Brahmā Heavens.
These Bodhisattvas used their exquisite voices to sing innumerable verses praising all Buddhas.
At this time, Mílè Púsà rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder,
joined his palms before the Buddha,
and spoke in verse, saying:
The Buddha expounds the rare Dharma,
never heard before in the past;
the Shìzūn possesses great power,
his lifespan is beyond measure.
Innumerable Buddha-children,
on hearing the Shìzūn’s discernment,
and attaining benefit from the Dharma,
are filled with joy throughout their bodies.
Some abide on the stage of non-retrogression,
some attain dhāraṇī,
some can speak delightfully and unobstructedly,
and have command of myriad recitations and concentration.
There are those bodhisattvas, as numerous as dust motes in a great trichiliocosm,
each and every one able to turn
the wheel of non-retreating Dharma.
Again, in a medium trichiliocosm,
there are bodhisattvas as numerous as dust motes,
each and every one able to turn
the wheel of pure Dharma.
Again, in a small trichiliocosm, bodhisattvas as numerous as dust motes,
each remaining with eight more births,
will attain Buddhahood.
Again, among 432 such four-continent worlds, bodhisattvas as numerous as dust motes,
are reborn by number and become Buddhas.
Or in a single four-continent world, bodhisattvas as numerous as dust motes,
each with only one remaining birth,
will attain omniscience.
All such beings as these,
on hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and distant,
obtain boundless, undefiled, and pure retribution.
Again, in eight worlds, sentient beings as numerous as dust motes,
on hearing the Buddha teach about lifespan,
all give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
The Shìzūn teaches boundless, inconceivable Dharmas,
providing great benefit,
like the endless expanse of space.
Heavenly maṇḍārava and great maṇḍārava flowers rain down,
Shì and Brahmā gods as numerous as the sands of the Ganges come from countless Buddha-lands.
Rain of chandana and agarwood, falling profusely and chaotically,
descend like birds flying down through the sky,
making offerings scattered before the various Buddhas.
Divine drums in the sky,
emit wondrous sounds of themselves;
heavenly garments, in myriad forms,
whirl and come tumbling down.
Multiple precious censers,
burn incomparable incense,
spontaneously pervading everywhere,
offering to all Shìzūn.
The congregation of great bodhisattvas,
holds banners and canopies of seven treasures,
wondrous and tall, in myriad varieties,
ascending in order to the Brahmā heavens.
Before each and every Buddha,
jeweled banners are hung with supreme pennants,
and in thousands and millions of verses,
they chant praises to the Tathāgatas.
Such various events,
never before seen,
on hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is boundless,
all are filled with joy.
The Buddha’s name is heard in the ten directions,
widely benefiting sentient beings,
all are endowed with wholesome roots,
thus aiding the unsurpassed mind.
At that time, the Buddha said to Mílè Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: "Āyìduō!
If there are sentient beings who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is thus long and far-reaching,
and are able even to give rise to one thought of faith and understanding,
the merits they obtain are without limit or measure.
If there are good men or good women,
for the sake of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
through eighty thousand million nayuta kalpas,
who practice the five pāramitās— dāna-pāramitā,
śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā—
except prajñā-pāramitā,
even if the merits from this practice are compared with the above merits, one hundredth, one thousandth, hundred thousand millionth part cannot match a single part,
so much so that calculation, simile, and analogy cannot know them.
If good men or good women have such merit,
they will never regress from Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, the Shìzūn, desiring to reiterate this meaning,
spoke verses, saying:
“If one seeks the wisdom of the Buddha,
for eighty thousand million,
nayuta kalpas,
practices the five pāramitās.
In all those kalpas,
offering alms and making offerings to Buddhas,
as well as to pratyekabuddhas and disciples,
together with the assembly of bodhisattvas.
With rare and wondrous food and drink,
the finest clothing and bedding,
sandalwood-adorned meditation halls,
with gardens and groves for decoration.
Such giving and charity,
of all kinds, of subtle excellence;
throughout these countless kalpas,
dedicating all to the Buddha Way.
If, further, one upholds the precepts,
pure without flaw or breach,
seeking the unsurpassed path,
praised by all Buddhas.
If further, one practices forbearance,
abiding in the land of gentleness,
even if all manner of evil comes forth,
the mind remains unmoved.
Should those who have gained the Dharma
harbor excessive pride,
and therefore belittle and harrass,
such things one can also forbear.
If further, one is diligently vigorous,
with resolve and mindfulness always firm,
for countless kalpas,
without ever slacking for a moment.
Also, for innumerable kalpas,
dwelling in quiet seclusion,
whether sitting or walking,
constantly keeping the mind clear and free from drowsiness.
Because of such causes and conditions,
one is able to generate all meditative concentrations,
for eighty billion kalpas,
the mind abides undisturbed.
Holding this single-minded merit,
vowing to seek the unsurpassed path,
I will obtain all-knowledge,
and exhaust the limits of all meditative states.
Such a person, throughout hundreds of thousands,
and myriads of million kalpas,
performs these meritorious acts,
as explained above.
If good men or women,
on hearing me speak of lifespan,
even for a single moment give rise to faith,
their merits surpass the above.
If people are entirely free from
all doubt and regret,
and in the depth of their hearts instantly believe,
their merit is truly like this.
Bodhisattvas who,
for incalculable kalpas have cultivated the Way,
on hearing me speak of lifespan,
are able to believe and accept.
All such people
receive this scripture on their crown,
vowing that in the future,
I may have a long life and save sentient beings.
As now, the Shìzūn,
the king among the Shì clan,
roars the lion’s roar at the place of enlightenment,
fearlessly teaching the Dharma.
We, in future ages,
will be universally revered,
when seated at the site of enlightenment,
will speak of lifespan just the same.
If there are those of deep resolve,
pure and upright,
much learned and able to retain,
understanding the Buddha’s teaching according to its meaning,
such as these,
in this matter have no doubts.”
Again, Āyìduō!
If any hear of the Buddha’s life being long and distant,
and understand the intent of his words,
such a person’s merit is immeasurable and limitless,
capable of giving rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
How much more so for widely hearing this sūtra, or teaching others to hear,
or themselves upholding it, or instructing others to uphold,
or themselves copying it, or instructing others to copy,
or offering flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, pennants, silk canopies,
incense oils, ghee lamps, in order to make offerings to the sūtra scroll.
Such a person’s merit is measureless and boundless,
and can give rise to omniscience.
Āyìduō!
If good men or good women,
on hearing me speak of my long lifespan,
believe and understand with deep faith,
such will truly see the Buddha always at Qíshuā Quěshān,
surrounded by great bodhisattvas and the multitude of śrāvakas, expounding the Dharma.
They will also see this Sahā world,
with ground of crystal, broad and even,
Jāmbūnada gold marking the eight highways,
rows of jeweled trees, all terraces, towers and pavilions are made entirely of jewels,
and the assembly of bodhisattvas all abide therein.
If there is anyone able to contemplate thus,
know that this is the mark of deep faith and understanding.
Again, after the extinction of the Tathāgata,
if someone hears this scripture and does not slander or revile it,
but gives rise to a heart of rejoicing, you should know that this already counts as profound faith and understanding;
how much more so for those who read, recite, accept, and uphold it!
Such persons are as if they carry the Tathāgata upon their heads.
"Āyìduō!
These good men and good women need not, for my sake, further build stūpas or temples,
nor construct monastic dwellings, or provide the four requisites to support the Saṅgha.
Why is this so?
Because these good men and good women who receive, uphold, and recite these scriptures
are as if they have already erected stūpas, built monastic dwellings, and made offerings to the Saṅgha.
It is as if they have erected a stūpa of the Buddha's relics made of the seven precious substances,
soaring high and wide, gradually narrowing until it reaches the realm of Brahmā,
adorned with hanging banners, canopies, and myriad jeweled bells,
flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, anointing incense, burning incense, all manner of drums and musical performances, flutes, pipes, konghou,
various dances and entertainments,
using exquisite voices to sing hymns and praises;
it is as if during innumerable kalpas, their offerings were already made in this way.
Āyìduō!
If, after my passing, anyone hears this scripture and is able to accept and uphold it,
whether writing it themselves or teaching others to write it,
it is as if they have built and erected a monastic dwelling,
using red sandalwood to make thirty-two halls and chambers,
each as tall as a palm tree,
beautiful, grand, and exquisitely adorned,
able to accommodate hundreds and thousands of monks within,
with gardens, groves, bathing pools, promenades for walking meditation, meditation caves,
and with clothing, food, beds, bedding, hot baths, and medicines—
everything needed for comfort is fully supplied within.
Such monks’ dwellings and pavilions, hundreds, thousands, myriads, and millions in number, limitless in quantity,
are used for making present offerings to me and to the monastery of monks.
Therefore I say:
"After the extinction of the Tathāgata, if there are those who accept, uphold, read, recite, or expound this on behalf of others,
whether by copying it themselves or teaching others to copy it, or by making offerings to the scripture scrolls,
there is no need any longer to erect stūpas and temples, or build monasteries, or make offerings to the monastic community."
How much more so for those who are able to uphold this scripture,
along with practicing giving, maintaining precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom—
their merit is supreme,
immeasurable and boundless.
Just as space in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below is immeasurable and boundless,
so too is the merit of such people immeasurable and boundless;
they quickly attain all-knowledge.
If someone reads, recites, accepts, and upholds this scripture and expounds it for others,
whether writing it themselves or teaching others to write it,
is further able to erect stūpas and build monasteries, make offerings and praise to the Śrāvaka monks,
and also praise the merit of bodhisattvas with hundreds, thousands, myriads, and millions of ways of praise,
and, further, for others, in accordance with occasion and principle, explain and expound this Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra,
is also able to purely maintain precepts,
dwells together with the gentle and harmonious,
enduring insults without anger,
his mind resolute,
always esteeming sitting meditation and attaining deep absorptions,
diligent, courageous, and skillful in gathering all good dharmas,
of keen faculties and wisdom, able to skillfully answer difficult questions.
Āyìduō!
If, after my passing, good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this scripture,
they possess such good merits,
and you should know that these people are already on the path to enlightenment,
close to Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, seated beneath the bodhi tree.
"Āyìduō!
These good men and good women, whether sitting, standing, or walking,
in these places it is fitting to erect a stūpa,
and all gods and humans should make offerings just as to a Buddha’s stūpa."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further proclaim this doctrine,
spoke in verse, saying:
If after my extinction,
one is able to respectfully uphold this scripture,
the blessings of this person are countless,
as has been expounded above;
thus are all offerings
perfected in every way.
By erecting a stūpa of relics,
adorned with the seven treasures,
its spires exceedingly high and broad,
gradually narrowing, reaching Brahmā’s heaven,
with jeweled bells in their thousands, millions, and billions,
ringing with wondrous sounds as wind stirs them.
And for countless kalpas,
one makes offerings at this stūpa,
with flowers, incense, necklaces,
heavenly garments and musical performances,
lamps of burnished oil and ghee,
burning brightly on every side.
In the later days of the law,
those who are able to maintain this scripture
are thus, as above, perfect in all offerings.
If one can uphold this scripture,
it is as if the Buddha were present,
and, with ox-head sandalwood,
builds monasteries and makes offerings.
There are thirty-two halls,
each as tall as seven tala trees,
complete with choice food and fine robes, with beds and couches fully supplied,
accommodating hundreds and thousands,
with gardens, groves, and bathing pools,
promenades for walking meditation and meditation caves,
all finely adorned in every way.
If one has a heart of faith and understanding,
accepts, upholds, reads, recites, and copies this scripture,
or teaches others to copy it,
and makes offerings to the scripture scrolls,
scattering flowers, powdered incense,
and using sūmanā, campaka, atimuktaka, anointing with fragrant oil so that lamps always burn,
making such offerings,
one attains immeasurable merit,
as vast and boundless as space,
and their blessings are likewise.
How much more for those who uphold this scripture,
and also practice giving, maintain precepts,
are patient and delight in meditation,
do not harbor anger or harsh speech,
honor stūpas and temples,
are humble toward all monks,
renounce arrogance,
constantly contemplate wisdom,
do not become angry when questioned,
and skillfully give explanations accordingly;
if one can practice in this way,
their merit cannot be measured.
If you see a Dharma teacher
accomplished in such virtues,
you should scatter heavenly flowers
and drape them in heavenly garments,
prostrate, putting your head and face at their feet in reverence,
giving rise to a mind regarding them as a Buddha.
You should also think thus:
"Before long, they will proceed to the bodhi tree,
attain the unconditioned, undefiled state,
and greatly benefit both humans and gods."
Wherever they abide and dwell,
whether walking, sitting, lying down,
or expounding even a single verse,
in such a place a stūpa should be erected,
adorned and made exquisitely fine,
and with various offerings presented.
Where the Buddha’s children abide,
it is the Buddha’s own use,
and he is always present therein,
walking, sitting, and lying down.
The fifth scroll of the Miàofǎ Liánhuā Jīng
The sixth scroll of the Miàofǎ Liánhuā Jīng
Translated under imperial command by the Tripiṭaka master
Jiūmóluóshí of the country of Qiuci in Later Qin
At that time, Mílè Púsà Móhēsà said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
If there are good men or good women
who, having heard this Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra, rejoice accordingly,
how much merit do they acquire?"
and spoke these verses:
After the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa,
if there be those who hear this scripture,
and are able to rejoice accordingly,
how much merit do they gain?
At that time, the Buddha said to Mílè Púsà Móhēsà:
"Āyìduō! After the extinction of the Tathāgata,
if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and others, whether wise or not, whether old or young,
having heard this scripture, rejoice accordingly,
and after leaving the assembly,
go elsewhere,
whether to a monastery,
a quiet and solitary spot,
a city, town, street, village, or countryside,
and, according to what they have heard,
explain and proclaim it for parents, relatives, good friends, and acquaintances as best they are able—
these people,
after hearing, rejoice accordingly,
and in turn pass it on to others;
those others, upon hearing,
also rejoice and in turn pass it on to others.
In this way, passing on from one to another, up to the fiftieth person.
Āyìduō! The merit of this fiftieth good man or good woman who rejoices,
I will now explain to you;
listen well.
Suppose in four hundred billion asaṃkhyeya worlds, that all sentient beings in the six paths and four kinds of birth—
those born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation,
those with form, without form,
with perception, without perception,
neither with perception nor without perception,
those without legs, with two legs, four legs, or many legs—
so long as they are included among the number of sentient beings;
if there were someone seeking merit,
who, according to their desires, gave them all manner of delightful things,
to each and every sentient being
giving the entire continent of Jambudvīpa filled with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, coral, amber,
all kinds of wondrous treasures,
elephants, horses, carriages,
palaces and towers all made of the seven precious substances—
such a great benefactor,
having conducted such giving for eighty years,
then thinks thus:
“I have already provided beings with the means of enjoyment,
according to their wishes and desires.
Yet all these beings are already aged, over eighty years old,
their hair white and faces wrinkled,
close to death, with little time left to live.
I ought to instruct them with the Buddha’s teaching.”
Then he gathered these beings,
proclaimed the teaching and transformation,
demonstrated, guided, benefitted, and filled them with joy.
All at once, all attained the fruit of Śrótāpánna,
Sakṛdāgāmin,
Anāgāmin,
Arhat,
exhaustively ended all defilements,
and gained complete mastery in profound meditation,
possessing the eight liberations.
“What do you think,
would the merit gained by this great benefactor be much or not?”
Mílè addressed the Buddha:
“World-honored One!
This person’s merit is indeed great,
boundless and immeasurable.
If this benefactor only gave beings all manners of pleasures,
his merit would be measureless;
how much more so to enable them to attain the fruit of Arhat.”
The Buddha told Mílè:
“I shall now speak to you clearly.
Suppose this person, using all kinds of pleasures,
makes offerings to the beings of the six realms in four hundred myriads of millions of asaṃkhyeya worlds,
and also enables them to attain the fruit of Arhat,
the merit thus gained cannot compare to that of the fiftieth person
who rejoices upon hearing even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra,
not even a hundredth, a thousandth, a hundred thousand myriadth part, nor any fraction,
even by calculation or analogy it cannot be known.
“Āyìduō!
In this way, the merit of the fiftieth person in succession who hears and rejoices at the Lotus Sūtra
is already boundless, innumerable, asaṃkhyeya;
how much more so for one who is among the initial congregation to hear it and rejoice, whose merit is yet greater,
beyond all measure and comparison, boundless, innumerable, asaṃkhyeya.
Further, Āyìduō!
If for the sake of this sūtra, a person goes to a monastic dwelling,
whether sitting or standing, and listens and receives it for even a brief moment,
on account of this merit,
wherever they are reborn they will receive excellent and splendid elephants, horse chariots,
jewel-studded carriages and palanquins,
and even ride in celestial palaces.
If moreover there is someone who sits at a place where the teaching is expounded,
and another comes,
encourages them to sit and listen,
or shares their seat and lets them sit,
the merit of this person, wherever they are reborn, will be to obtain the seat of Śakra,
or the seat of Brahmā,
or the seat of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Āyìduō! If there is yet another, who says to someone else,
‘There is a sūtra named the Lotus Sūtra; let us go and listen together,’
and they accept this invitation,
and even listen for but a short time, the merit of this person, wherever they are reborn, will be to be born together with Dhāraṇī Bodhisattvas,
sharp of faculties and wisdom, for
hundreds of thousands of kalpas they will never become mute,
their breath will be free of foulness, their tongue ever without infirmity, the mouth also without ailment, the teeth neither dirty, blackened, yellow, nor sparse,
nor absent, nor misaligned, nor crooked,
the lips neither drooping nor curled, neither coarse nor rough, neither ulcerated nor inflamed,
nor damaged, nor twisted,
neither thick nor large,
nor swarthy, and without anything repulsive.
The nose neither flat nor misshapen, nor crooked or distorted,
the complexion not dark,
not narrow nor long,
nor sunken or twisted,
with no appearance that is displeasing in any way.
The lips, tongue, and teeth will all be beautiful and fine,
the nose long and straight,
the face full and complete,
eyebrows high and long,
forehead broad and proper,
endowed with all marks of humanity,
wherever they are born,
they will see Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and faithfully accept the teaching.
“Āyìduō! Now consider this:
to just encourage one person to go to listen to the Dharma,
the merit is thus,
how much greater for one who single-mindedly listens to, recites,
and among the congregation, explains for others
and puts the teaching into practice as it is expounded?”
At that time, the World-honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning,
spoke these verses:
If someone among an assembly,
hears this sūtra,
even if only a single verse,
rejoices and passes it on to others,
and in this way, through repeated instruction,
it reaches to the fiftieth,
the final person who earns the merit,
I shall now distinguish for you.
Suppose there is a great benefactor,
who supplies untold multitudes,
each filled to the age of eighty,
with whatever their hearts desire.
Seeing their signs of decline,
with hair white and face wrinkled,
teeth sparse and form withered,
knowing that death is not far,
I ought now to teach them,
to lead them to the fruit of the path.
Then, skillfully, I explain
the true Dharma of nirvāṇa:
“The world is inconstant for all,
like a bubble of water, a foam, or a flame.
You all should
quickly give rise to a mind of revulsion and detachment.”
All who hear this Dharma,
all attain Arhatship,
endowed with the six spiritual powers,
the three insights and eight liberations.
Yet that final, fiftieth one,
hearing but a single verse and rejoicing,
that person’s merit surpasses the former,
beyond analogy or comparison.
In this way, from one to another in succession,
the merit yet is boundless;
how much more so for those at the Dharma assembly
who at the beginning hear and rejoice?
If one encourages a person,
and leads them to hear the Lotus Sūtra,
saying, “This sūtra is deep and wonderful,
difficult to encounter in thousands or tens of thousands of kalpas,”
and they accept the invitation and go to listen,
and even if they listen for but a moment,
the merit and good retribution of such a person,
I shall now explain in detail.
Life after life they will have no afflictions of the mouth,
their teeth never sparse, yellow, nor black,
lips not thick, curled, or incomplete,
no detestable features,
tongue not dry, blackened, or short,
nose tall, elegant, and straight,
forehead broad and even,
countenance and features dignified and handsome,
beloved by those who see them,
breath free of foul odor,
always sandalwood fragrance
issuing from their mouth.
Should anyone purposefully go to the monastic dwelling,
wishing to hear the Lotus Sūtra,
and, in a brief hearing, feel joy,
I shall now tell of the merit.
In subsequent lives among gods and humans,
they will obtain marvelous elephants and horse carriages,
jewel-studded palanquins,
and ride in celestial palaces.
If at the place the Dharma is expounded,
one encourages others to sit and listen to the sūtra,
the reward from such merit and cause
is to obtain the seat of Śakra, Brahmā, or the Wheel-Turning King.
How much more for those who single-mindedly listen,
grasp the meaning and purport,
and practice it as it is taught,
whose merit cannot be measured.
At that time the Buddha addressed Chángjīngjìn Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
“Should any good man or good woman accept and uphold this Lotus Sūtra,
whether by reading, reciting, explaining,
or copying it,
these people will gain eight hundred merits of the eyes, twelve hundred merits of the ears,
eight hundred merits of the nose, twelve hundred merits of the tongue, eight hundred merits of the body, and twelve hundred merits of the mind.
With these merits adorning their six faculties, all will be rendered pure.
These good men or good women,
with the pure fleshly eyes given by their parents,
will see all mountains, forests, rivers, and seas within and beyond the three-thousand great-thousand world,
from the lowest Avīci hell to the highest Heaven of the Summit,
and will also see all beings therein,
as well as their karmic causes and conditions, retributions, and places of birth—beholding and knowing them all.”
Then the World-honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“If, among the great assembly,
with a fearless mind,
one proclaims this Lotus Sūtra,
listen to the merit thus gained.
Such a person gains eight hundred,
supreme merits of the eye,
and, being thus adorned,
his eyes become exceedingly pure.
With the eyes given by his parents,
he sees the three-thousand lands,
sees within and without Mount Meru,
Sumeru as well as the Iron Ring Mountains,
and all other mountains and forests,
great seas, lakes and rivers,
down to Avīci hell,
up to the Summit of Existence,
and all the beings therein—he sees them all without exception.
Though he has yet to gain the divine eye,
his fleshly eye has such power.”
“Next, always be diligent!
If a good man or good woman accepts and upholds this scripture,
whether they read, recite, explain, or copy it,
they will obtain one thousand two hundred merits of the ear.
With such pure ears,
they will hear, within the Trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra world, from Avīci Hell below up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Nonperception above, all types of inner and outer languages and sounds—
sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and carriages,
sounds of weeping and crying, sounds of grief and sighing, sounds of conches, drums, bells, and chimes,
sounds of laughter and speech, men’s voices, women’s voices, boys’ and girls’ voices,
sounds of the Dharma, sounds of non-Dharma,
sounds of suffering and of happiness,
voices of ordinary people, voices of sages,
sounds of joy and of displeasure,
sounds of Devas, Lóng, Yèchā, Qiántàpó, Āxiūluó, Jiālóuluó, Jǐnnàluó, Móhóluójiā,
sounds of fire, water, and wind,
sounds of hell beings, animals, and hungry ghosts,
voices of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs,
voices of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
voices of bodhisattvas and Buddhas—
in brief,
all sounds, both internal and external, within the Trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra world, even without having attained the divine ear, with the pure, ordinary ear born of father and mother,
all can be heard and known, each type of sound clearly distinguished, and the faculty of hearing will not be harmed.”
Then the World-honored One, wishing to again declare this meaning, spoke in verse:
“With the ears born of father and mother,
pure, without defilement,
using this ordinary ear to hear
all the sounds in the three thousand worlds;
sounds of elephants, horses, carriages, and oxen,
sounds of bells, chimes, conches, and drums,
music of qín, sè, kōnghóu,
and the tones of shāo and dí flutes,
pure and fine singing,
which one hears without attachment,
innumerable sorts of human voices,
all can be understood.
One also hears the sounds of Devas,
subtle and marvelous songs,
and the voices of men and women,
boys and girls.
In mountains, streams, and perilous valleys,
the voice of Jiālínpínqié,
and such birds as mìngmìng,
all their songs are heard.
In hell, innumerable sufferings,
all kinds of wailing and tormenting cries,
the hunger and thirst cries of hungry ghosts,
seeking food and drink,
all kinds of Āxiūluó,
living by the great sea,
when speaking together,
produce a great sound.
Thus, one who teaches the Dharma
while dwelling here,
hears all these sounds from afar
and the faculty of hearing is not harmed.
In the worlds of the ten directions,
cries and calls of birds and beasts,
the one who teaches the Dharma
hears them all.
And in the heavens of the Brahmā world,
the heavens of Rājyābhā and Śubhakṛtsna,
even up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Nonperception,
all voices and speeches,
the Dharma teacher dwelling here
can hear them all.
All assemblies of bhikṣus,
and all bhikṣuṇīs,
whether reading and reciting the scriptures,
or teaching them to others,
the Dharma teacher dwelling here
can hear them all.
Further, all bodhisattvas,
when reading and reciting the scriptures,
or teaching them for others,
editing and compiling explanations of their meanings,
all such voices
can be heard.
The Buddhas, great noble honored ones,
teaching and transforming living beings,
in great assemblies
expound wondrous Dharma,
and one who holds this Lotus Sūtra,
can hear them all.
In the Trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra worlds,
every kind of sound, both internal and external,
from Avīci Hell below
to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Nonperception above,
all such sounds are heard,
yet the faculty of hearing is not harmed,
as the ear is sharp and keen,
and all can be distinguished and known.
Those who hold this Lotus Sūtra,
even without attaining the divine ear,
but only using the ordinary ear with which they were born,
already receive merits such as these.”
“Next, always be diligent!
If a good man or good woman accepts and upholds this scripture,
whether reading, reciting, explaining, or copying it,
they will accomplish eight hundred merits of the nose.
With such pure nasal faculties,
they will smell, throughout the Trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra world, above and below, inside and outside, all kinds of fragrances—
the fragrance of sūmànnà flowers, zhētí flowers,
mòlì flowers, zhānpò flowers, bōluóluó flowers,
red lotus fragrance, blue lotus fragrance, white lotus fragrance,
flower tree fragrance, fruit tree fragrance,
zhāntán, chénshuǐ, duōmóluóbá, duōjiāluó fragrances,
and tens of thousands of blended incenses,
whether in powder, ball, or ointment form—
those who uphold this scripture, while dwelling here,
can distinguish them all.
They can further discern the scents of sentient beings—
the scent of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and others,
the scent of men, women, boys, and girls,
and the fragrances of grasses, trees, and thickets—
whether near or far,
all such scents can be perceived, all distinguished without error.
Those who uphold this scripture,
even dwelling here,
also perceive the scents of the Devas above—
fragrances of the bōlìzhìduōluó and jūpítuóluó trees,
and the fragrances of mántuóluó flowers, máhāmántuóluó flowers,
mánshūshā flowers, máhámánshūshā flowers,
zhāntán, chénshuǐ, and various fragrance powders,
and all mixed flower fragrances—
such blended heavenly aromas,
there is none that cannot be perceived.
One also smells fragrances of the bodies of Devas—
when Shìdìhuán Yīn is in the splendid palace, enjoying the five desires and amusements;
or in the Wondrous Dharma Hall, when teaching the Devas of Trāyastriṃśa;
or playing in gardens;
and also the body scents of other heavenly males and females,
all are sensed from afar.
Thus, gradually, up to the Brahmā worlds,
and as high as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Nonperception, the body scents of all these Devas are perceived,
along with the scents of incenses burned by Devas.
And the scents of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas,
all can be distinctly sensed from afar,
and their locations discerned.
Even upon perceiving these fragrances,
the faculty of the nose is not harmed or in error,
and if wishing to distinguish and explain for others,
one remembers without mistake.”
Then the World-honored One, wishing to again declare this meaning,
spoke in verse:
“This person’s nose is pure;
in this world,
all scents, whether fragrant or foul, are fully perceived.
Sūmànnà, zhētí,
duōmóluó, zhāntán,
chénshuǐ and cassia fragrances,
various flower and fruit scents,
and the scents of sentient beings—
the scent of men and women—
those who teach the Dharma from afar
by smelling their scent, locations are known.
Great Power Cakravartin King,
the lesser Cakravartins and their sons,
their ministers and all those of the inner court,
by scent, their locations are known.
All rare and precious jewels worn on the body,
the treasures hidden in the earth,
and jewel maidens of the Cakravartin King,
by scent, their locations are known.
The ornaments adorning people,
clothing and necklaces,
various ointment fragrances,
by their scent, the body is known.
The Devas, whether walking, sitting,
at play or in divine transformations,
those who uphold this Lotus Sūtra
know all by their scent.
Trees, flowers, fruits,
even the fragrance of ghee,
when those who uphold the scripture are here,
all their locations are known.
In deep and dangerous mountain places,
when zhāntán trees bloom,
those beings dwelling within
can be known by their scent.
In Iron Encircled Mountains and great oceans, the sentient beings within the earth,
those who hold the scripture know by fragrance,
and all their locations are known.
Males and females of Āxiūluó,
and their many followers,
whenever fighting or playing,
can all be known by their scent.
In wild and rugged places,
lions, elephants, tigers, wolves,
wild oxen, water buffalo, and the like,
by scent, their places are known.
If there is a pregnant woman,
before the gender of the child is known,
whether it is without root or not human,
upon smelling the fragrance, all can be known.
Relying on the power of smelling fragrance,
one knows when a woman has newly conceived,
whether the pregnancy will come to fruition or not,
and whether there will be an easy birth and a fortunate child.
Relying on the power of smelling fragrance,
one knows what male or female persons are thinking,
whether it be thoughts of desire, attachment, ignorance, or anger,
as well as who is cultivating good.
All the hidden treasures in the earth,
all the precious things of gold and silver,
and all that is stored in bronze vessels,
can all be known by smelling the fragrance.
All kinds of various ornaments,
whose value no one can recognize,
by smelling the fragrance one knows their worth,
their origins and location.
All the flowers in the heavens,
such as màn tuó and màn shū shā,
pō lì zhì duō trees,
can all be known by smelling the fragrance.
All the heavenly palaces,
distinctions of superior, middle, and lower,
adorned with multitudes of precious flowers,
can all be known by smelling the fragrance.
Gardens, groves, and magnificent halls of heaven,
various observation towers and wondrous Dharma halls,
wherein beings enjoy themselves,
can all be known by the fragrance.
Whenever devas are hearing the Dharma,
or indulging in the five desires,
coming and going, walking, sitting, lying down,
all can be known by the fragrance.
The garments worn by heavenly maidens,
adorned with beautiful flowers and fragrance,
as they circle and play,
all can be known by the fragrance.
Thus, ascending ever higher,
even up to the realm of Fàn shì,
whether entering or emerging from meditation, all can be known by the fragrance.
The light-sound, all-pure heavens,
even up to the summit of existence,
when a being is first born or passes away,
all can be known by the fragrance.
As for the Bhikṣu congregation,
who always diligently apply themselves to the Dharma,
whether sitting or walking,
or reading and reciting scriptures,
or sitting in meditation beneath a forest tree,
intently focused in meditation,
one who holds the scriptures smells the fragrance
and knows precisely where they are.
For Bodhisattvas whose resolve is firm,
whether sitting in meditation or reciting scripture,
or expounding Dharma for others,
all can be known by the fragrance.
Wherever there is a World-Honored One,
revered by all,
who speaks Dharma with compassion for the multitude,
all can be known by the fragrance.
Sentient beings in the presence of Buddha,
on hearing the sutra, are all filled with joy,
and cultivate according to the teaching,
all can be known by the fragrance.
Although they have not yet attained the Bodhisattva’s undefiled Dharma-produced nose,
these upholders of the sūtra
first obtain this mark of the nose.”
“Moreover, Cháng Jīngjìn,
if good men and good women uphold this sūtra,
whether reading, reciting, explaining, or copying it,
they gain one thousand two hundred merits of the tongue.
Whether things are good or bad in form, beautiful or not,
or things that are bitter and astringent,
when they touch the root of the tongue, all become exquisite in flavor, like heavenly nectar,
with nothing unpleasant.
If, using their tongue, they expound teachings before the assembly,
they bring forth profound and wondrous tones,
which can enter the listener’s heart,
and all are made joyful and delighted.
Moreover, all the sons and daughters of devas, the Shì and Fàn devas,
upon hearing these profound, wondrous sounds and orderly explanations,
all come to listen.
And also nāgas and nāga maidens, yèchā and yèchā maidens,
gandharva and gandharva maidens,
asura and asura maidens,
kalavinka and kalavinka maidens,
kiṁnara and kiṁnara maidens,
mahoraga and mahoraga maidens,
all come in person to reverently serve and make offerings, for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
As well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
kings, princes, ministers, and attendants,
minor wheel-turning kings, great wheel-turning kings, the seven treasures, a thousand sons, and all their inner and outer retinue,
ride in their palaces,
and all come together to listen to the Dharma,
because the Bodhisattva is skillful in explaining the Dharma.
Brahmans, lay people, and the citizens within the realm,
throughout their entire lives, serve and make offerings.
Moreover, all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas constantly rejoice to see him.
Wherever this person is,
the buddhas all turn toward that place to proclaim the Dharma,
and he can uphold all the Buddha’s teachings,
and further bring forth profound and wondrous Dharma sounds.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse, saying:
“This person’s root of the tongue is pure,
never tasting anything foul,
whatever he eats and tastes,
all turns to sweet nectar.
With profound, pure, wondrous voice,
he speaks Dharma in the great assembly,
using various causes and similes,
to guide the minds of sentient beings,
those who hear are all joyful,
offering superb offerings.
Devas, nāgas, yèchā,
and asura and others,
all with reverent hearts,
come together to hear the Dharma,
this speaker of Dharma,
if he wishes with his marvelous voice,
to resound throughout the three thousand worlds,
it will come as he wills.
Minor and great wheel-turning kings,
and their retinue of a thousand sons,
with joined palms in reverent minds,
constantly come to listen and receive the Dharma.
Devas, nāgas, yèchā,
rākṣasa, piśāca,
also with joyful hearts,
constantly delight in coming to make offerings.
Fàn tiān kings, Māra kings,
Freedom and Great Freedom,
and all such multitudes of devas,
constantly come to where he is.
The buddhas and their disciples,
hearing his Dharma voice,
constantly think of and protect him,
sometimes even appearing in person.”
“Moreover, Cháng Jīngjìn,
should good men and good women uphold this sūtra,
whether reading, reciting, explaining, or copying it,
they acquire eight hundred merits of the body.
They gain a purified body,
like pure crystal,
pleasing to all who see.
Because the body is pure,
the sentient beings throughout the three thousand great chilicosms, at the time of birth or death,
high or low, beautiful or ugly,
born in good places or evil places,
all appear within it.
And the Iron Encircling Mountain, Great Iron Encircling Mountain,
Mí lóu Mountain, Mahā Mí lóu Mountain and all other mountains,
and all beings therein,
all appear within it.
From the deepest Avīci Hell,
up to the Summit of Existence,
all places and sentient beings are all manifest within it.
Whether a śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, or buddha preaches the Dharma,
all their forms and images appear within the body.”
Then the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke a verse, saying:
“If one upholds the Lotus Sūtra,
his body is very pure,
like that pure crystal,
pleasing to all beings who see.
Like a pure and bright mirror,
showing all forms and appearances,
the Bodhisattva’s pure body
reflects all that exists in the world,
known only to himself,
invisible to others.
Within the three thousand worlds,
all sentient beings,
devas, humans, asuras,
beings of hell, ghosts, and animals,
all such forms and images,
appear within his body.
The palaces of devas and others,
even up to the Summit of Existence,
the Iron Encircling and Mí lóu,
Mahā Mí lóu Mountains,
all great oceans and waters,
all appear within his body.
All Buddhas and Śrāvakas,
the Buddha's sons, Bodhisattvas, and the like,
whether alone or among the assembly,
when expounding the Dharma, always manifest themselves.
Though they have not yet attained the stainless [state],
the wondrous body of Dharma-nature,
with its ever-pure constant essence,
manifests all things within it.」
「Further, Cháng Jīngjìn!
If good men or good women, after the Tathāgata’s passing, uphold this sūtra,
whether by reading, reciting, explaining, or copying it,
they will obtain twelve hundred merits of the mind.
With this pure root of mind,
even upon hearing just a single verse or phrase,
they thoroughly comprehend limitless, boundless meanings.
Having understood these meanings,
they can expound upon a single phrase or verse for a month, four months, or even a year;
all the Dharma they speak, following the intent and meaning,
never contradicts reality.
If they speak of worldly texts, governing words, or livelihoods,
all is in harmony with the correct Dharma.
For all the beings of the six realms throughout the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds,
the tendencies, actions, and idle talk of their minds—they fully comprehend.
Though they have not yet attained stainless wisdom,
their faculty of mind is as pure as this.
Whatever such a person contemplates, considers, or says,
is always the Buddha Dharma,
without any falsehood.
This, too, is as the Buddhas of the past have spoken in their sūtras.」
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
「This person’s mind is pure,
bright, sharp, and without defilement;
with this wondrous faculty of mind,
he knows higher, middle, and lower teachings.
Even upon hearing a single verse,
he comprehends limitless meanings.
Step by step, he properly expounds them,
for four months, or even a year.
Within or beyond this world, all beings—
whether devas, nāgas, humans,
yaksas, ghosts, spirits, and so on—
within the six destinies,
whatever thoughts they harbor,
due to upholding the Dharma Flower Sūtra,
he understands them all at once.
Buddhas of the ten directions, innumerable,
with the hundredfold adorned marks,
expound the Dharma for sentient beings;
he fully hears and can receive it.
He ponders limitless meanings,
and his preaching is likewise limitless.
From beginning to end, he forgets nothing,
because he upholds the Dharma Flower Sūtra.
He thoroughly knows all dharma characteristics,
passing through the sequence of meanings,
and reaches the terms and expressions,
expounding as he understands.
Whatever this person says,
is all the Dharma of the former Buddhas.
Because he expounds this Dharma,
he fears nothing in the assembly.
Whoever upholds the Dharma Flower Sūtra, his faculty of mind is thus pure;
though he has not yet gained the stainless [state],
he already possesses such qualities.
This person who upholds this sūtra
abides on the rare, wondrous ground.
For all sentient beings,
he brings joy, love, and respect.
He is able, with myriad kinds
of skillful speech,
to distinguish and expound the Dharma,
all because he upholds the Dharma Flower Sūtra.」
At that time, the Buddha said to Dé Dàshì Púsà Móhēsà:
“You should now know!
If any bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā upholds the Dharma Flower Sūtra,
and anyone uses harsh words, reviles, or slanders them,
such a person will incur great retribution,
as previously stated;
the merit gained by the upholders is as just explained—
eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all purified.
Dé Dàshì,
in the remote past,
beyond countless, boundless, inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
there was a Buddha named Wēi Yīn Wáng, the Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Complete in Right and Universal Knowledge,
Perfect in Clarity and Conduct,
Well-gone, Knower of the World, Peerless Hero, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Men,
Buddha, World-Honored One.
The kalpa was called Lí Shuāi, and the land was named Dà Chéng.
That Buddha, Wēi Yīn Wáng, in that world,
spoke the Dharma for the devas, humans, and asuras.
For those seeking śrāvaka-hood,
he taught the Four Noble Truths,
to deliver them from birth, aging, illness, and death,
and attain final nirvana.
For those seeking pratyekabuddhahood,
he expounded the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
For the bodhisattvas
who aspired to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
he preached the Six Pāramitās, leading to the supreme wisdom of a Buddha.
Dé Dàshì,
that Buddha Wēi Yīn Wáng
lived for four hundred trillion nayutas of Ganges sands of kalpas.
The duration of the True Dharma age
was as many kalpas as dust motes in a single Jambudvīpa,
while the Semblance Dharma age
lasted as many kalpas as dust motes in the Four Continents.
Having greatly benefited beings,
that Buddha then entered nirvana.
After the extinction of the True and Semblance Dharma,
another Buddha again appeared in that land,
also called Wēi Yīn Wáng, the Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings,
Complete in Universal and Right Knowledge, Perfect in Clarity and Conduct, Well-gone, Knower of the World,
Peerless Hero, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Men, Buddha, World-Honored One.
In this way, in succession, there were twenty trillion Buddhas,
all with the same name.
After the very first Wēi Yīn Wáng Tathāgata entered nirvana,
following the end of the True Dharma,
during the Semblance Dharma,
arrogant bhikṣus grew in great power.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva-bhikṣu named Cháng Bù Qīng.
Dé Dàshì,
why was he named Cháng Bù Qīng?
Whatever this bhikṣu saw—
be they bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—
he always bowed to and praised them, saying:
‘I deeply respect you all,
and would not dare to slight or despise you.
Why is this?
You are all practicing the bodhisattva path and will become Buddhas.’
Yet this bhikṣu did not devote himself to reading or reciting scriptures,
but only practiced bowing in reverence.
Even when he saw the Four Assemblies from afar,
he would purposely approach them and bow, praise, and speak as follows:
‘I dare not slight you all.
You all will become Buddhas.’
Among the Four Assemblies,
some became angry
and impure in mind.
They abused and cursed him, saying:
‘Where has this witless bhikṣu come from
who goes about saying, “I don’t slight you,”
and confers on us the prediction that we will become Buddhas?
We don’t accept such deluded predictions.’
So, over the course of many years,
he was continually reviled.
He did not give rise to anger,
but always said:
‘You will become Buddhas.’
When he spoke these words,
the crowd would sometimes attack him with sticks, wood, tiles, or stones,
so he would flee and stay far away,
but still cried aloud:
‘I would not dare to slight you all.
You all will become Buddhas.’
Because he always spoke these words,
the arrogant bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās gave him the name “Cháng Bù Qīng.”
When this bhikṣu was near death,
he heard in the air the full extent of the Dharma Flower Sūtra as previously expounded by Wēi Yīn Wáng, containing twenty thousand myriads of verses.
He was able to accept and retain it all
and immediately attained the purified faculty of eye as described above,
as well as the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Having attained the purity of the six faculties,
his lifespan was further extended by two hundred myriads of nayuta years,
throughout which he widely expounded the Dharma Flower Sūtra for people.
At that time, the arrogant Four Assemblies—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
looked down on this person and labeled him “Bù Qīng.”
But seeing that he had now attained great supernatural powers,
eloquence in debate, and the strength of great quiescence,
and hearing what he taught,
they all believed, submitted to, and followed him.
This bodhisattva then transformed countless millions,
causing them to abide in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
After death,
he encountered two thousand billion Buddhas,
all named Rì Yuè Dēng Míng,
and in their Dharma, he preached the Dharma Flower Sūtra.
Due to these causes and conditions,
he again encountered two thousand billion Buddhas,
all called Yún Zìzài Dēng Wáng,
and among these Buddhas,
he accepted and upheld, read and recited
and taught this scripture for the sake of the Four Assemblies,
thereby attaining ever-pure vision,
and pure faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Among the Four Assemblies, his mind was fearless in expounding Dharma.
Dé Dàshì,
this Cháng Bù Qīng Púsà Móhēsà
made offerings to countless Buddhas,
revered, honored, and praised them,
and planted various roots of goodness.
Later he again encountered myriad Buddhas,
and in their teaching he likewise expounded this scripture,
and with merit thus perfected, he will become a Buddha.
To attain great power!
What do you think?
At that time, was Constant Reverence Bodhisattva a different person?
It was my very self.
If, in previous lives, I had not accepted, upheld, recited, and expounded this sūtra for others,
I would not have so swiftly attained Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because, in the presence of former Buddhas, I accepted, upheld, recited, and expounded this sūtra for people,
I quickly attained Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta!
At that time the four assemblies— —bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— —
scorned and belittled me in anger,
and for two hundred billion kalpas, they would not encounter Buddhas, would not hear the Dharma, nor see the Saṅgha,
and for a thousand kalpas endured great suffering in Avīci Hell.
When these sins were exhausted,
they again encountered Constant Reverence Bodhisattva,
who instructed and transformed them toward Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
what do you think?
At that time, the four assemblies who constantly slighted this Bodhisattva,
were they different people?
Now, in this assembly, these five hundred Bodhisattvas such as Bǎtuópóluó,
and these five hundred bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs such as Shīzǐ Yuè,
and these five hundred upāsakas such as Sīfó,
all are those who do not turn back from Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta!
You should know that this Dharma Flower Sūtra
greatly benefits all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
and can enable them to reach Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, after the Tathāgata's extinction, should always accept and uphold, recite, explain, and copy this sūtra."
At that time, the World Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke in verse:
“In the distant past there was a Buddha,
named Wēiyīn Wáng,
whose miraculous wisdom was limitless,
guiding all beings,
heavenly beings, humans, dragons, and spirits,
were all together devoted in offering.
After this Buddha’s extinction,
when the Dharma was about to disappear,
there was a Bodhisattva,
named Constant Reverence.
At that time, the four assemblies
were attached to the Dharma.
Constant Reverence Bodhisattva
would go before them
and speak to them, saying:
‘I do not belittle you;
for you are all practicing the Way,
and shall all become Buddhas.’
After these people heard him,
they despised, reviled, and berated him;
but Constant Reverence Bodhisattva
was able to patiently endure it.
When those transgressions were exhausted,
at their final moment,
they heard this sūtra,
and their six faculties became pure.
Due to spiritual powers,
their lifespan was increased,
and they again, for the sake of others,
widely expounded this sūtra.
All those attached to the Dharma
were taught and transformed by the Bodhisattva,
and brought to dwell in the Buddha Way.
When Constant Reverence reached his end,
he encountered innumerable Buddhas,
and, because he expounded this sūtra,
he attained measureless blessings,
gradually perfected merit and virtue,
and swiftly accomplished the Buddha Way.
At that time, Constant Reverence
was my very self.
Those four assemblies,
attached to the Dharma,
when they heard Constant Reverence’s words:
‘You shall become Buddhas,’
by means of this causation,
encountered innumerable Buddhas.
This assembly’s Bodhisattvas, the company of five hundred,
together with the four assemblies,
the faithful men and women,
now before me,
are those who are listening to the Dharma.
In former lives,
I encouraged these people
to receive and accept this sūtra—
the foremost Dharma—
revealing and teaching it to people,
bringing them to abide in Nirvāṇa,
to receive and uphold
this sūtra for life after life.
For billions upon billions of kalpas,
to incalculable time,
only then could they hear
this Dharma Flower Sūtra.
For billions upon billions of kalpas,
to incalculable time,
the Buddha, World Honored Ones,
at that time expounded this sūtra.
Therefore, practitioners,
after the Buddha’s extinction,
who hear this sūtra,
should not give rise to doubt or confusion.
You should wholeheartedly,
widely expound this sūtra,
encountering Buddhas life after life,
and swiftly accomplish the Buddha Way.”
At that time, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the dust of a thousand worlds, who sprang up from the earth,
all, before the Buddha, single-mindedly joined their palms,
gazed up reverently at his honored face,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World Honored One! After the Buddha’s extinction,
in all the lands where the World Honored One’s manifestations pass into extinction,
we will widely expound this sūtra.
Why is this so?
We ourselves also wish to obtain this true, pure, great Dharma,
to accept and uphold, recite, explain, and copy it, and make offerings to it.”
At that time, the World Honored One,
in the presence of Mañjuśrī and countless hundreds, thousands, myriads, and millions of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas long dwelling in the Sahā World,
together with all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, the heavens, dragons, yaksas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans,
before these entire assemblies, manifested great spiritual power,
extending his broad and long tongue so that it reached to the Brahmā world,
and from every pore emitted immeasurable, innumerable rays of light,
illuminating all worlds of the ten directions.
All Buddhas under jeweled trees and upon lion thrones did likewise—
they extended their broad, long tongues and emitted immeasurable light.
When Śākyamuni Buddha and all the Buddhas beneath jeweled trees manifested their spiritual power,
for a hundred thousand years,
thereafter, returned and withdrew their tongues.
At the same time, they cleared their throats
and snapped their fingers together,
and these two sounds resounded through the worlds of Buddhas in all ten directions,
causing the earth to quake in six ways.
All the living beings therein,
gods, dragons, yaksas,
gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas,
humans and non-humans,
through the Buddha’s spiritual power,
could all see this Sahā world, with its innumerable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas under jeweled trees and on lion thrones;
and see Śākyamuni Buddha together with Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata,
in the jeweled stupa, seated on the lion throne;
and also see immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of millions of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the four assemblies, reverently encircling Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having seen this,
they all experienced great joy,
something never known before.
Immediately, the gods in the sky, with loud voices, proclaimed:
“Beyond this innumerable, boundless, hundred thousand million asaṃkhyeya worlds,
there is a land called Sahā;
within it there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni,
who is now, for all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, preaching the Mahāyāna Sūtra called the Sublime Dharma Lotus Flower;
he teaches the Bodhisattva path,
protected and cared for by the Buddhas.
All of you should deeply rejoice in your hearts,
and should also bow and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.”
Those sentient beings, hearing the voices from the sky,
joined their palms and turned toward the Sahā world, saying:
“Namo Śākyamuni Buddha! Namo Śākyamuni Buddha!”
And with all kinds of flowers, incense, jeweled necklaces, banners, and canopies,
along with various excellent adornments, rare and wondrous treasures,
all were scattered at a distance toward the Sahā world.
All the offerings, coming from the ten directions like clouds gathering,
were transformed into jeweled canopies, covering all the Buddhas above.
Then all the worlds of the ten directions became unhindered and as one Buddha land.
At that time, the Buddha said to the great assembly of Bodhisattvas such as Sthāvirā:
“The spiritual powers of the Buddhas are thus;
immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable.
If I, by means of these spiritual powers, for the sake of entrustment, were to speak of the merits of this sūtra, for infinite, boundless, hundreds of thousands of millions of asankhyeya kalpas,
I could not exhaust them.
To put it briefly,
all the Tathāgata’s possessions, all his sovereign spiritual powers,
all his secret storehouses, all his most profound matters, are all declared and clearly revealed within this sūtra.
Therefore all of you, after the Tathāgata’s extinction,
should single-mindedly accept and uphold, recite, expound, and copy it,
and practice as taught.
In any land,
if there are those who accept and uphold, recite, expound, and copy,
and practice as taught,
or where the scripture stays,
be it in gardens, forests, under trees, in monasteries,
in laypeople’s houses,
in halls and pavilions,
in valleys or wastelands,
in all these places there should be built stupas and offered veneration.
Why is this?
You should know that these places are truly the sites of enlightenment,
where Buddhas attain Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,
where Buddhas turn the Dharma wheel,
and where Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa.”
At that time, the World Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke in verse:
"The various Buddhas who save the world,
abide in great supernatural power;
for the delight of sentient beings,
they manifest immeasurable divine abilities.
The marks of their tongues reach up to Brahmā Heaven,
and their bodies emit countless rays of light.
For those who seek the Buddha path,
these rare and marvelous events are revealed.
The breath and voice of the Buddhas,
and the sound of their snapping fingers,
are heard throughout the countries of the ten directions,
and the earth shakes in six ways.
Because, after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa,
there are those able to uphold this sūtra,
all Buddhas rejoice,
and manifest immeasurable supernatural power.
Because of entrusting this sūtra,
they praise those who receive and keep it;
throughout countless kalpas,
still its praises cannot be exhausted.
The merit and virtue of such a person
is boundless and without limit,
like the empty space of the ten directions,
unattainable are its boundaries.
Those able to uphold this sūtra
are those who have already seen me,
have seen Duōbǎo Fó,
and the various emanated bodies;
and have also seen me today
teaching and transforming the various Bodhisattvas.
Those able to uphold this sūtra
enable myself and my emanations,
as well as Duōbǎo Fó after nirvāṇa,
all to be delighted.
The Buddhas presently in the ten directions,
as well as those of the past and future,
will likewise be seen, worshipped,
and thus be made joyful.
The secret and essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas sitting in the place of enlightenment,
those able to uphold this sūtra
will also soon obtain.
Those able to uphold this sūtra,
regarding all meanings of the Dharma, words and terms, will joyfully explain without end,
like the wind in the sky;
nothing can hinder them.
After the Tathāgata's extinction,
they will know all the teachings given by the Buddha,
the causes and conditions, and the order thereof,
following the meaning and speaking it as it truly is;
as the light of sun and moon,
can dispel all darkness.
Such a person, acting in the world,
can dispel the darkness of sentient beings,
teach boundless Bodhisattvas,
ultimately abiding in the One Vehicle.
Therefore, those who are wise,
hearing these meritorious benefits,
after my parinirvāṇa,
should receive and uphold this sūtra.
This person, with regard to the Buddha-path,
will have no doubts whatsoever."
At that time, Shìjiāmóuní Fó rose from his Dharma seat,
displayed great supernatural powers,
and with his right hand touched the crowns of innumerable Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
and spoke these words:
"Through countless hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhyeyas of kalpas,
I have cultivated this hard-to-attain Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma;
now I entrust it to you all.
You should wholeheartedly circulate this Dharma,
broadly increasing it."
In this way, he touched the crowns of the multitude of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in samādhi and said:
"Through countless hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhyeyas of kalpas,
I have cultivated this hard-to-attain Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma;
now I entrust it to you all.
You should receive, uphold, recite, and widely proclaim this Dharma,
so that all sentient beings everywhere may hear and know it.
Why is this?
The Tathāgata has great compassion,
is free from all stinginess,
and is also without fear;
he is able to give to sentient beings the wisdom of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and the spontaneous wisdom.
The Tathāgata is the great patron of all sentient beings.
You should likewise learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata,
and do not give rise to stinginess.
In the future,
if there are good men or good women who have faith in the wisdom of the Tathāgata,
you should expound this Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra
so that they may hear and know it,
in order to help them attain Buddha-wisdom.
If there are sentient beings who do not believe or accept,
then among the other, deeper Dharma of the Tathāgata,
you should reveal, teach, benefit, and bring them joy.
If you are able to do so,
then you will have repaid the kindness of the Buddhas."
Then the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing the Buddha's words,
were all filled with great joy throughout their bodies,
and became ever more respectful,
bending, bowing their heads,
joining their palms to the Buddha,
and together voiced these words:
